```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [-3, 3], "xLabel": "x", "yLabel": "residual", "points": [{"at": [1, 2.1], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [2, 0.8], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3, -0.4], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [4, -1.2], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5, -1.6], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [6, -1.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [7, -0.9], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [8, 0.1], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [9, 1.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}], "caption": "A curved residual pattern: a straight line is not the right model"}
```

A fan shape looks different: no curve, but the residuals spread out as $x$ grows.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [-3, 3], "xLabel": "x", "yLabel": "residual", "functions": [{"f": "0", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [1, 0.3], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [1.5, -0.4], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [2, 0.2], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3, -0.6], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3.5, 0.8], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [4, -0.3], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5, 1.1], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5.5, -1.2], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [6, 0.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [7, -1.7], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [7.5, 1.9], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [8, -0.8], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [9, 2.4], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [9.5, -2.2], "color": "#2c5e8f"}], "caption": "A fan-shaped residual plot: the line's form is fine, but predictions are less precise for large x"}
```

## The coefficient of determination r²

The square of the correlation, $r^2$, is called the **[[coefficient of determination]]**. It
has a clean meaning: the fraction of the variation in $y$ that is accounted for by the
linear relationship with $x$.

$$r^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y - \hat{y})^2}{\sum (y - \bar{y})^2} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}.$$

Why: $\text{SST} = \sum (y - \bar{y})^2$ is the total variation in $y$ — the squared
error you'd make predicting every $y$ by $\bar{y}$, ignoring $x$. $\text{SSE}$ is the
squared error left after using the line. So $1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ is the fraction
of the original squared error that the line removes.

For the training data: $\text{SST} = S_{yy} = 10$ (from the correlation lesson), and
$\text{SSE} = 0.16 + 0.64 + 1 + 1.44 + 0.36 = 3.6$. So $r^2 = 1 - 3.6/10 = 0.64$, which is
$0.8^2$. ✓

Interpretation template: "About 64% of the variation in skill score is accounted for by
the linear relationship with weeks of training."

Going back from $r^2$ to $r$: $r = \pm\sqrt{r^2}$, with the sign of the slope. If
$r^2 = 0.81$ and the slope is negative, $r = -0.9$.

## The standard deviation of the residuals

The typical size of a prediction error is measured by

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (y - \hat{y})^2}{n - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{SSE}}{n-2}}.$$

We divide by $n - 2$ because two quantities (slope and intercept) were estimated from the
data. For the training data, $s = \sqrt{3.6/3} \approx 1.10$: predictions of skill
score are typically off by about 1.1 points. $r^2$ is a percentage with no units; $s$ is
in the units of $y$. Report both.

Putting the checks in order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Checking whether a straight line is a good model
  accDescr: Fit the least-squares line and make a residual plot. If the residuals curve, the form is wrong, so try a transformation as in the next lesson. If they fan out, the line's form is fine but errors grow with x, so be careful with predictions at large x. If they show random scatter, report r squared and s. Then look for a point with an extreme x value. If there is one, refit without it and compare to see whether it is influential. If not, use the line within the range of the data.
  A["Fit the least-squares line"] --> B["Make a residual plot"]
  B --> C{"What pattern do the residuals show?"}
  C -- Curve --> D["Wrong form: try a transformation"]
  C -- "Fan shape" --> E["Form OK, but errors grow with x"]
  C -- "Random scatter" --> F["Report r squared and s"]
  F --> G{"Any point with an extreme x?"}
  G -- Yes --> H["Refit without it and compare"]
  G -- No --> I["Use the line within the data range"]
```

## Outliers, leverage and influential points

*AP exam scope:* the AP Statistics framework that took effect in the 2026–27 school year
removed the topic "analyzing departures from linearity," which covered this section's
outliers, high-leverage points and influential points (and the transformations of the next
lesson). The ideas are still standard in introductory college statistics and worth knowing
when you read any regression, but they are no longer tested on their own.

- An **[[outlier]]** in regression is a point with a large residual — far from the line in
  the $y$ direction.
- A point has high **[[leverage]]** if its $x$ value is far from $\bar{x}$. Such points pull on
  the line like a long lever.
- A point is **[[influential]]** if removing it would markedly change the slope, intercept
  or correlation. High-leverage points are often influential, especially when they don't
  follow the pattern of the rest.

An influential point may have a *small* residual — because it has pulled the line
toward itself. So don't hunt for influential points by looking at residuals; refit
without the point and compare.

```plot
{"x": [0, 16], "y": [0, 12], "xLabel": "x", "yLabel": "y", "points": [{"at": [1, 4], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [2, 5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3, 4.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [4, 6], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5, 6.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [6, 7.5], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [15, 2], "label": "P", "color": "#c53030"}], "functions": [{"f": "3.233 + 0.671*x", "dashed": true}, {"f": "5.998 - 0.180*x", "color": "#c53030"}], "caption": "One high-leverage point P flips the slope (dashed: fit without P; solid: fit with P)"}
```

The three kinds of unusual point side by side. Each panel has the same eight points plus one
circled point, with the line fitted with it (solid) and without it (dashed).

![Three scatterplots of the same eight points rising along a line, each with one extra circled point. Point A, at x = 4.5 and well above the others, is an outlier with a large residual; the line with it is only slightly higher than the line without it. Point B, at x = 16 and lying on the trend of the other points, has high leverage but follows the pattern, so the two lines coincide. Point C, at x = 16 and far below the trend, is influential: it drags the fitted line almost flat, while the line without it rises steeply.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The numbers behind the panels: without the circled point the line is $\hat{y} = 2.125 + 0.475x$
with $r \approx 0.97$. A sits at $x = 4.5$, the mean of the other $x$ values, so it has the least
possible leverage: adding it only raises the intercept a little (to about 2.48), keeps the slope at 0.475, and lowers $r$ to about 0.70, and A's
residual (about 2.9) is the largest in any panel. Adding B leaves the line almost unchanged
and raises $r$ to about 0.99. Adding C drops the slope to about 0.01 and $r$ to about 0.04, yet
C's residual (about −1.7) is *smaller* than A's: C has pulled the line toward itself.

### Example 1

A regression of salary on years of experience for 30 employees gives $r = 0.52$. One
employee, the founder, has 40 years of experience while everyone else has under 15.
Removing the founder changes $r$ to 0.31 and the slope from 2.1 to 1.2 (thousands per
year). The founder is influential: one point accounts for a large share of the apparent
relationship. Report both analyses and explain.

### Example 2

For a regression of fuel used (gallons) on distance (miles) with $\hat{y} = 0.4 + 0.035x$,
a trip of 300 miles used 11.9 gallons. Find and interpret the residual.

1. $\hat{y} = 0.4 + 0.035(300) = 0.4 + 10.5 = 10.9$ gallons.
2. Residual $= 11.9 - 10.9 = 1.0$ gallon.
3. This trip used 1 gallon *more* than the line predicts — the point is above the line.

### Example 3

A study reports $r^2 = 0.36$ and a negative slope. What is $r$? $r = -\sqrt{0.36} = -0.6$.
Only 36% of the variation in the response is explained by the linear relationship.

## Common mistakes

- Computing a residual as predicted minus observed.
- Saying "$r^2 = 0.64$ means the line is correct 64% of the time" or "64% of the points
  are on the line." It is a fraction of *variation* explained.
- Forgetting the sign when taking $\sqrt{r^2}$.
- Judging fit by $r^2$ alone; a curved pattern can have a high $r^2$. Check the residual plot.
- Assuming an influential point must have a big residual.

## Key points

- Residual $= y - \hat{y}$; residuals of an LSRL sum to 0.
- Residual plot: random scatter means a line fits; curves or fans signal problems.
- $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$: fraction of variation in $y$ explained by the line.
- $s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)}$: typical prediction error, in $y$'s units.
- Outliers have big residuals; high-leverage points have extreme $x$; influential points
  change the fit when removed.

lessons.title: Transformations to achieve linearity
lessons.body:
## When the residual plot curves

The last lesson showed how a curved residual plot signals that a straight line is the
wrong model. Many real relationships are curved: populations grow exponentially, the
weight of an animal grows like a power of its length, the brightness of a light falls
off with the square of distance. Rather than learn a new fitting method for each curve,
statisticians *transform* one or both variables so that the relationship becomes
linear, fit a least-squares line to the transformed data, and then transform back to
make predictions.

*AP exam scope:* transformations to achieve linearity were part of the "analyzing
departures from linearity" topic, which the AP Statistics framework removed starting in the
2026–27 school year. Treat this lesson as enrichment if you are preparing for a current AP
exam; it remains part of many college statistics courses and of older AP exams.

## The idea in one line

If $y$ depends on $x$ in a known curved way, find a function that "undoes" the
curvature. Logarithms are the workhorse because they turn multiplication into addition
and powers into multiplication:

$$\log(ab) = \log a + \log b, \qquad \log(a^k) = k \log a.$$

Either common logs ($\log_{10}$) or natural logs ($\ln$) work, as long as you undo with
the matching inverse ($10^{(\cdot)}$ or $e^{(\cdot)}$).

## Exponential models: transform y

An **[[exponential model]]** has the form $y = ab^x$: each unit increase in $x$ multiplies
$y$ by the constant factor $b$ (growth if $b > 1$, decay if $0 < b < 1$). Taking logs:

$$\log y = \log a + x \log b.$$

That is a straight line in $x$ and $\log y$, with intercept $\log a$ and slope $\log b$.
So: *if a plot of $\log y$ against $x$ is linear, an exponential model fits*.

## Power models: transform both

A **[[power model]]** has the form $y = ax^p$. Taking logs:

$$\log y = \log a + p \log x.$$

This is linear in $\log x$ and $\log y$ with slope $p$. So: *if a plot of $\log y$
against $\log x$ is linear, a power model fits*. Power models describe geometric scaling
(area grows like length², volume like length³) and many physical laws.

| Model | Linearizing plot | Fitted line | Back-transform |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exponential $y = ab^x$ | $\log y$ vs. $x$ | $\widehat{\log y} = c + dx$ | $\hat{y} = 10^{c + dx}$ |
| Power $y = ax^p$ | $\log y$ vs. $\log x$ | $\widehat{\log y} = c + d\log x$ | $\hat{y} = 10^{c}x^{d}$ |
| Square-root-type | $\sqrt{y}$ vs. $x$ (or $y$ vs. $\sqrt{x}$) | $\widehat{\sqrt{y}} = c + dx$ | $\hat{y} = (c + dx)^2$ |

## Choosing a transformation

1. Plot $y$ against $x$ and look at the residual plot from a straight-line fit. A
   systematic curve says "transform."
2. Try the candidate transformations and plot each one.
3. Choose the one whose scatterplot is most linear *and* whose residual plot shows
   random scatter. A higher $r^2$ alone is not enough — check residuals.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a transformation
  accDescr: Start when the residual plot from a straight-line fit of y on x is curved. Plot log y against x. If that plot is linear with random residuals, use an exponential model. If not, plot log y against log x. If that is linear with random residuals, use a power model. If neither works, try another re-expression such as a square root. Whichever model you choose, fit the least-squares line to the transformed data and back-transform its predictions.
  A["Residual plot of y on x is curved"] --> B{"log y vs x: linear, random residuals?"}
  B -- Yes --> C["Exponential model: y = a times b to the x"]
  B -- No --> D{"log y vs log x: linear, random residuals?"}
  D -- Yes --> E["Power model: y = a times x to the p"]
  D -- No --> F["Try another re-expression, such as a square root"]
  C --> G["Fit the line to the transformed data, then back-transform predictions"]
  E --> G
```

### Example 1: exponential growth

A colony of bacteria is counted each hour:

| Hour $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count $y$ | 20 | 31 | 44 | 70 | 105 | 160 |

A straight line fitted to $y$ gives $r = 0.957$, but its residual plot is clearly curved
(positive at the ends, negative in the middle). Plotting $\log_{10} y$ against $x$ gives
an almost perfect line ($r = 0.9996$), with least-squares fit

$$\widehat{\log y} = 1.3006 + 0.1802x.$$

Predict the count at hour 6:

1. $\widehat{\log y} = 1.3006 + 0.1802(6) = 2.3818$.
2. Undo the log: $\hat{y} = 10^{2.3818} \approx 241$.

Interpretation of the slope: $10^{0.1802} \approx 1.51$, so the model says the count is
multiplied by about 1.51 each hour (51% growth per hour).

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 6], "y": [1.1, 2.6], "xLabel": "hour", "yLabel": "log count", "points": [{"at": [0, 1.301], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [1, 1.491], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [2, 1.643], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3, 1.845], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [4, 2.021], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5, 2.204], "color": "#2c5e8f"}], "functions": [{"f": "1.3006 + 0.1802*x", "color": "#c2570c"}], "caption": "After taking log of the counts, the points lie on a line"}
```

Back on the original scale, the back-transformed model follows the counts closely, while the
straight line fitted to the raw counts ($\hat{y} \approx 3.95 + 27.09x$) runs below the points at
both ends and above them in the middle: exactly the curved residual pattern (positive, then
negative, then positive) described above.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 6], "y": [0, 250], "xLabel": "hour", "yLabel": "count", "points": [{"at": [0, 20], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [1, 31], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [2, 44], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [3, 70], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [4, 105], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [5, 160], "color": "#2c5e8f"}], "functions": [{"f": "10^(1.3006 + 0.1802*x)", "color": "#c2570c", "label": "ŷ = 10^(1.3006 + 0.1802x)"}, {"f": "3.952 + 27.086*x", "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [5.3, 112], "text": "straight line"}], "caption": "Bacteria counts with the back-transformed exponential model (solid) and the straight-line fit (dashed)"}
```

### Example 2: a power model

For a set of animals, $x$ = body length (m) and $y$ = mass (kg). A plot of $\ln y$ against
$\ln x$ is linear with fitted line $\widehat{\ln y} = 0.5 + 1.5\ln x$. Predict the mass
of an animal 4 m long.

1. $\ln 4 \approx 1.3863$, so $\widehat{\ln y} = 0.5 + 1.5(1.3863) = 2.5794$.
2. $\hat{y} = e^{2.5794} \approx 13.19$ kg.

Equivalently the model is $\hat{y} = e^{0.5}x^{1.5}$, and $e^{0.5} \cdot 4^{1.5} = 1.6487 \times 8 \approx 13.19$.

### Example 3: reading a fitted model

A model for a car's value is $\widehat{\log_{10}(\text{value})} = 4.5 - 0.06(\text{age})$. What
does the slope say? Each additional year multiplies the predicted value by
$10^{-0.06} \approx 0.871$ — about a 12.9% loss per year. A new car ($\text{age} = 0$) is
predicted to be worth $10^{4.5} \approx \$31{,}623$.

## Cautions

- Predictions must be **[[back-transformed]]**: if you fit $\log y$, the line predicts
  $\log y$, not $y$.
- Residuals and $r^2$ of the transformed fit are on the transformed scale.
- Extrapolation is even riskier with exponential models, which grow without bound.
- Logs require positive values.

## Common mistakes

- Reporting $\widehat{\log y}$ as the prediction of $y$.
- Using $10^{(\cdot)}$ to undo a natural log (or $e^{(\cdot)}$ to undo $\log_{10}$).
- Choosing a model by $r^2$ without checking the residual plot.
- Confusing the models: $\log y$ vs. $x$ linear means exponential; $\log y$ vs. $\log x$
  linear means power.

## Key points

- Transform to make a curved relationship linear, fit the LSRL, then back-transform.
- Exponential $y = ab^x$ ↔ $\log y$ linear in $x$; slope $\log b$, so $b = 10^{\text{slope}}$.
- Power $y = ax^p$ ↔ $\log y$ linear in $\log x$; slope $p$.
- Judge a transformation by a straight scatterplot and a patternless residual plot.

lessons.title: Two-way tables and conditional distributions
lessons.body:
## Relationships between categorical variables

Scatterplots and correlation need two *quantitative* variables. When both variables are
categorical — age group and preferred transit mode, treatment and outcome, gender and
voting choice — the data go into a two-way table, and relationships show up as
differences between conditional distributions. These ideas lead directly to conditional
probability (Module 5) and the chi-square test (Module 9).

## Two-way tables

A **[[two-way table]]** (contingency table) counts individuals by two categorical variables
at once: one variable's categories label the rows, the other's label the columns.

A transit survey of 200 commuters:

| Age group | Train | Bus | Car | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Under 30 | 30 | 20 | 10 | 60 |
| 30–50 | 25 | 15 | 40 | 80 |
| Over 50 | 15 | 10 | 35 | 60 |
| Total | 70 | 45 | 85 | 200 |

Each inner cell is a *joint* count: 30 commuters are *both* under 30 *and* take the
train. The totals in the margins are the *marginal* counts.

![The transit survey table drawn as a grid with four highlighted cells. The cell 30 (under 30, train) is marked joint count. The cell 60 at the end of the under-30 row is marked row total. The cell 70 at the bottom of the train column is marked column total. The cell 200 in the bottom right corner is marked grand total.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Three kinds of distribution

- The **[[marginal distribution]]** of one variable uses the row or column totals, divided by
  the grand total. Mode of transit: train $70/200 = 35\%$, bus $22.5\%$, car $42.5\%$. It
  ignores the other variable completely.
- The **[[joint distribution]]** divides each cell by the grand total: $30/200 = 15\%$ of all
  commuters are under-30 train riders.
- A **[[conditional distribution]]** describes one variable *among individuals with a given
  value of the other*: divide by that row's (or column's) total, not the grand total.

Conditional distribution of mode for each age group:

| Age group | Train | Bus | Car |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 30 | $30/60 = 50\%$ | $33.3\%$ | $16.7\%$ |
| 30–50 | $31.25\%$ | $18.75\%$ | $50\%$ |
| Over 50 | $25\%$ | $16.7\%$ | $58.3\%$ |

Each row adds to 100%.

## Association

Two categorical variables are **[[associated]]** if the conditional distributions of one
variable differ across the categories of the other. Here the share of car commuters
rises from 16.7% (under 30) to 58.3% (over 50), so age group and transit mode are
associated. If every age group had the same distribution as the overall 35/22.5/42.5 split,
there would be no association.

A **[[segmented bar chart]]** (one bar per age group, each scaled to 100% and divided by
mode) or a **[[side-by-side bar chart]]** shows the comparison at a glance.

A **[[mosaic plot]]** is a segmented bar chart with one extra feature: each bar's *width* is
proportional to the size of its group. Here the under-30 bar would be 60 units wide, the 30–50
bar 80 units wide and the over-50 bar 60 units wide. The heights of the segments still show
each group's conditional distribution, the widths show the marginal distribution of age
group, and the area of each rectangle is proportional to its cell count.

```plot

```

### Example 1

Using the table, find (a) the percent of all commuters who drive, (b) the percent of
train riders who are over 50, and (c) the percent of over-50 commuters who take the train.

1. (a) Marginal: $85/200 = 42.5\%$.
2. (b) Condition on train riders (column total 70): $15/70 \approx 21.4\%$.
3. (c) Condition on over-50s (row total 60): $15/60 = 25\%$.

Parts (b) and (c) use the same cell, 15, but different denominators — the "given" group
determines the denominator. Mixing them up is the most common error with two-way tables.

To pick the denominator, ask what group the percent is *of*:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the denominator in a two-way table
  accDescr: Ask what group the percent is of. If it is a percent of everyone in the table and describes one variable, such as the percent who drive, it is marginal: divide a row or column total by the grand total. If it is a percent of everyone and describes both variables at once, such as the percent who are under 30 and drive, it is joint: divide the cell by the grand total. If it is a percent of one group only, such as among over-50 commuters, it is conditional: divide the cell by that group's row or column total.
  A["What group is the percent of?"] --> B{"Everyone in the table?"}
  B -- Yes --> C{"Does it describe one variable or both?"}
  C -- "One, such as 'drive'" --> D["Marginal: row or column total ÷ grand total"]
  C -- "Both, such as 'under 30 and drive'" --> E["Joint: cell ÷ grand total"]
  B -- "No, one group, such as 'among over-50s'" --> F["Conditional: cell ÷ that group's total"]
```

## Simpson's paradox

Combining groups can reverse an association. Two hospitals treat patients in mild or
severe condition:

| | Hospital A survived | A total | Hospital B survived | B total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mild | 590 | 600 | 870 | 900 |
| Severe | 210 | 400 | 30 | 100 |
| All | 800 | 1000 | 900 | 1000 |

### Example 2

Which hospital has the better survival rate?

1. Overall: A $800/1000 = 80\%$, B $900/1000 = 90\%$ — B looks better.
2. Mild patients: A $590/600 \approx 98.3\%$, B $870/900 \approx 96.7\%$ — A is better.
3. Severe patients: A $210/400 = 52.5\%$, B $30/100 = 30\%$ — A is better.

A is better for *both* kinds of patients but worse overall, because A treats far more
severe cases (40% of its patients versus 10% for B), and severe cases have lower survival
anywhere. Condition severity is a lurking variable. This reversal is **Simpson's
paradox**: always ask whether a third variable could be hiding inside aggregated data.

### Example 3: reading the conditional distribution the other way

Among the 85 car commuters in the transit survey, what is the distribution of age group?

Divide each car count by the car column total: under 30, $10/85 \approx 11.8\%$; 30–50,
$40/85 \approx 47.1\%$; over 50, $35/85 \approx 41.2\%$. These add to 100%. Compare with the
marginal age distribution for everyone: $60/200 = 30\%$, $40\%$, $30\%$. Drivers are older
than commuters overall — the same association seen from the other direction. Whether you
condition on rows or on columns, an association shows up as conditional distributions that
differ from the marginal one; choose the direction that matches the question being asked
(here, "who drives?" rather than "how do young people travel?").

## Common mistakes

- Using the grand total as the denominator for a conditional percentage.
- Confusing "percent of train riders who are over 50" with "percent of over-50s who take
  the train."
- Concluding there's no association because the counts in a column are similar — compare
  percentages within groups, not raw counts.
- Ignoring possible lurking variables when combining groups.

## Key points

- Two-way tables count individuals by two categorical variables; inner cells are joint
  counts, margins are marginal counts.
- Marginal: total ÷ grand total. Joint: cell ÷ grand total. Conditional: cell ÷ the
  total of the given row or column.
- Variables are associated when conditional distributions differ across groups.
- Simpson's paradox: an association can reverse when a lurking variable is ignored.

lessons.title: The mathematics of least squares
lessons.body:
## Where the formulas come from

The least-squares regression lesson stated two formulas, $b = r\,s_y/s_x$ and
$a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$, and the residuals lesson stated a third, $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$.
Each came with a sentence of intuition, but none was proved. This honors lesson proves all
three using nothing beyond algebra (no calculus), and the proofs pay off: they explain why the
line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, why the residuals always add to zero, why the
"fraction of variation explained" happens to be the square of the correlation, and why the
standard deviation of the residuals divides by $n - 2$.

Throughout, use the shorthand from the correlation lesson:

$$S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \quad S_{yy} = \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2, \quad S_{xy} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}).$$

Note that $S_{yy}$ is the same as SST, and that $r = S_{xy}/\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$.

## A short history

The method was first published by the French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805, in
an appendix to a work on the orbits of comets; he called it the *méthode des moindres carrés*.
Carl Friedrich Gauss published his own account in 1809 and said he had been using the method
since 1795, which started a long priority dispute. Gauss also showed why squares are natural
when measurement errors follow a normal curve. Astronomers and surveyors used it for most of a
century before Galton and Pearson brought it to biology and the social sciences.

## Step 1: the mean minimizes squared deviations

Take any list of numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ with mean $\bar{d}$, and any constant $c$. Write
$d_i - c = (d_i - \bar{d}) + (\bar{d} - c)$ and square:

$$\sum (d_i - c)^2 = \sum (d_i - \bar{d})^2 + 2(\bar{d} - c)\sum (d_i - \bar{d}) + n(\bar{d} - c)^2.$$

The middle sum is zero, because deviations from the mean always add to zero. So

$$\sum (d_i - c)^2 = \sum (d_i - \bar{d})^2 + n(\bar{d} - c)^2.$$

The first term doesn't depend on $c$, and the second is never negative. The total is smallest
when $c = \bar{d}$: *the mean is the single number closest to a list in the squared-error
sense*. This one fact does most of the work below.

## Step 2: the best intercept for any slope

Fix any slope $b$. The squared error of the line $y = a + bx$ is

$$\text{SSE}(a, b) = \sum \big(y_i - a - bx_i\big)^2 = \sum (d_i - a)^2, \quad \text{where } d_i = y_i - bx_i.$$

By Step 1, the best $a$ is the mean of the $d_i$, which is $\bar{y} - b\bar{x}$. So whatever
slope you choose, the best line with that slope passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. That
proves the intercept formula, and it shows why the least-squares line goes through the point
of means.

## Step 3: the best slope, by completing the square

Put $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ back in. Each error becomes
$y_i - \bar{y} - b(x_i - \bar{x})$, so

$$\text{SSE}(b) = \sum \big[(y_i - \bar{y}) - b(x_i - \bar{x})\big]^2 = S_{yy} - 2bS_{xy} + b^2 S_{xx}.$$

That is a quadratic in $b$ that opens upward. Completing the square:

$$\text{SSE}(b) = S_{xx}\left(b - \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\right)^2 + S_{yy} - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}.$$

The squared term is zero exactly when $b = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, which is the least-squares slope.
Because $S_{xy} = (n - 1)\,r\,s_x s_y$ and $S_{xx} = (n - 1)s_x^2$, this equals
$r\,s_y/s_x$, the formula from the lesson.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1.6], "y": [0, 10], "xLabel": "slope b of a line through (3, 5)", "yLabel": "SSE", "functions": [{"f": "10*(x - 0.8)^2 + 3.6", "color": "#2c5e8f"}], "points": [{"at": [0.8, 3.6], "color": "#c2570c"}, {"at": [0.6, 4.0]}], "labels": [{"at": [0.95, 2.8], "text": "b = 0.8, SSE = 3.6"}, {"at": [0.3, 3.0], "text": "b = 0.6, SSE = 4.0"}], "caption": "Training data: SSE(b) = 10(b − 0.8)² + 3.6 is a parabola with its lowest point at the least-squares slope"}
```

Putting Steps 2 and 3 together gives one identity for *any* line $y = a + bx$, with
$\hat{b} = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $\hat{a} = \bar{y} - \hat{b}\bar{x}$ the least-squares values:

$$\text{SSE}(a, b) = \text{SSE}_{\min} + S_{xx}(b - \hat{b})^2 + n\big(\bar{y} - a - b\bar{x}\big)^2.$$

The second term is the price of a wrong slope; the third is the price of missing the point of
means.

### Example 1: checking a line that isn't the best

For the training data $(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 7), (5, 6)$ we know $n = 5$, $\bar{x} = 3$,
$\bar{y} = 5$, $S_{xx} = 10$, $S_{xy} = 8$, $S_{yy} = 10$, and the least-squares line
$\hat{y} = 2.6 + 0.8x$ has $\text{SSE}_{\min} = 3.6$. How much worse is the line $y = 3 + 0.6x$?

1. Directly: the line predicts $3.6, 4.2, 4.8, 5.4, 6.0$, so the errors are
   $-0.6, 0.8, -0.8, 1.6, 0$ and $\text{SSE} = 0.36 + 0.64 + 0.64 + 2.56 + 0 = 4.2$.
2. From the identity: slope penalty $10(0.6 - 0.8)^2 = 0.4$; the line's height at $\bar{x}$ is
   $3 + 0.6(3) = 4.8$, so the means penalty is $5(5 - 4.8)^2 = 0.2$.
3. Total: $3.6 + 0.4 + 0.2 = 4.2$. ✓ Both routes agree, and the identity also says *why* the
   line is worse: mostly its slope.

## Step 4: why r² is the square of r

At the best slope, the completed square leaves

$$\text{SSE}_{\min} = S_{yy} - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}} = S_{yy}\left(1 - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}\right) = \text{SST}\,(1 - r^2).$$

Divide by SST and rearrange: $1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} = r^2$. The residuals lesson
*defined* $r^2$ as a fraction of variation explained; this shows that fraction really is the
correlation squared. It also proves $|r| \le 1$, because SSE can't be negative, and that
$|r| = 1$ exactly when SSE $= 0$, which means every point is on the line.

## The sum-of-squares decomposition

Each point's deviation from the mean splits into two pieces:

$$\underbrace{y_i - \bar{y}}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}}_{\text{explained by the line}} + \underbrace{y_i - \hat{y}_i}_{\text{residual}}.$$

Here $\hat{y}_i$ is the **[[fitted value]]**, the line's prediction at the observed $x_i$.

![The training data with the least-squares line and a dashed horizontal line at the mean of y, 5. For the point (4, 7), a purple bar shows the total deviation y minus y-bar = 2 from the mean line up to the point. Beside it, a green bar from the mean line up to the line's fitted value 5.8 shows the explained part, 0.8, and an orange bar from the fitted value up to the point shows the residual, 1.2.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Squaring and adding over all points, the cross term $2\sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})(y_i - \hat{y}_i)$
turns out to be zero (see the next section), which leaves the **[[sum-of-squares decomposition]]**

$$\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE},$$

where $\text{SSR} = \sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2$ is the **[[regression sum of squares]]**. Since
$\hat{y}_i - \bar{y} = \hat{b}(x_i - \bar{x})$, it equals $\hat{b}^2 S_{xx}$. Then
$r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST}$ as well. (Some books call SSR the "model" sum of squares, and a
few use "SSR" for the *residual* sum of squares, so check the definition before you use a
formula from another source.)

### Example 2: the decomposition for the training data

1. $\text{SST} = S_{yy} = 10$.
2. $\text{SSR} = \hat{b}^2 S_{xx} = 0.8^2 \times 10 = 6.4$.
3. $\text{SSE} = 3.6$ (from the residuals lesson's table).
4. Check: $6.4 + 3.6 = 10$. ✓ And $r^2 = 6.4/10 = 0.64 = 0.8^2$.

For the single point $(4, 7)$ in the picture: total $7 - 5 = 2$, explained $5.8 - 5 = 0.8$,
residual $7 - 5.8 = 1.2$, and $0.8 + 1.2 = 2$. The squares do *not* add for one point
($0.64 + 1.44 \ne 4$); the decomposition holds only for the sums over all points.

## Two facts about the residuals

Write $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = (y_i - \bar{y}) - \hat{b}(x_i - \bar{x})$.

- *They add to zero.* $\sum e_i = 0 - \hat{b} \cdot 0 = 0$, because deviations from a mean
  add to zero.
- *They are uncorrelated with $x$.* $\sum (x_i - \bar{x})e_i = S_{xy} - \hat{b}S_{xx} = 0$
  because $\hat{b} = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$.

The second fact explains a feature of residual plots: after a least-squares fit, a residual
plot against $x$ never shows a straight-line tilt. Any pattern left over is a curve, a fan
or an unusual point. The two facts together also make the cross term above vanish, since each
$\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}$ is a multiple of $x_i - \bar{x}$.

## Why n − 2

Because the $n$ residuals must satisfy those two equations, only $n - 2$ of them can vary
freely: given any $n - 2$ residuals, the last two are forced (as long as those two points have
different $x$ values). So the residuals carry $n - 2$
degrees of freedom, and

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\text{SSE}}{n - 2}}.$$

This mirrors the $n - 1$ in the ordinary standard deviation, where one equation
($\sum(y_i - \bar{y}) = 0$) costs one degree of freedom. Combining with Step 4 gives a
shortcut from summary statistics:

$$\text{SSE} = (n - 1)s_y^2(1 - r^2).$$

### Example 3: s from summary statistics

A regression on $n = 20$ points has $s_y = 5$ and $r = 0.6$. Find SSE and $s$.

1. $\text{SST} = (n - 1)s_y^2 = 19 \times 25 = 475$.
2. $\text{SSE} = 475(1 - 0.36) = 304$.
3. $s = \sqrt{304/18} = \sqrt{16.89} \approx 4.11$.

Compare: $s_y = 5$ is the typical miss when predicting every $y$ by $\bar{y}$; using the line
cuts it to about 4.11. A correlation of 0.6 sounds strong, but it shrinks the typical error by
only about 18%.

## Why squares and not absolute values?

Minimizing $\sum |y_i - a - bx_i|$ instead gives the **[[least absolute deviations]]** line. It is
more resistant to outliers, much as the median is more resistant than the mean, and it is
used in robust statistics. But it has no simple formula (it is found by an algorithm), it can
have more than one best line, and it has no tidy decomposition like SST = SSR + SSE. Squares
give closed-form answers, a clean link to the mean and to $r$, and (as Gauss showed) the best
estimates when the errors are normal. That is why least squares became the standard, along
with its weakness: like the mean, it is pulled hard by outliers and influential points.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the residuals add to zero for *any* line. They do only for lines through
  $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$; the line $y = 3 + 0.6x$ in Example 1 has residuals adding to 1.0.
- Expecting the decomposition to hold point by point. Total = explained + residual holds for
  each point's deviations, but the *squares* add only after summing over all points.
- Mixing up SSR (regression) with SSE (residual), especially in books that use other letters.
- Dividing SSE by $n$ or $n - 1$ instead of $n - 2$.
- Believing $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ holds for any line. It holds for the
  least-squares line; a worse line has a larger SSE.

## Key points

- The mean minimizes $\sum (d_i - c)^2$. For any slope, this puts the best line through
  $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
- $\text{SSE}(b) = S_{xx}(b - S_{xy}/S_{xx})^2 + S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$, so the best slope is
  $S_{xy}/S_{xx} = r\,s_y/s_x$.
- $\text{SSE}_{\min} = \text{SST}(1 - r^2)$, which proves $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ and $|r| \le 1$.
- $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$ with $\text{SSR} = \hat{b}^2 S_{xx}$, and $r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST}$.
- Residuals add to zero and are uncorrelated with $x$, so they have $n - 2$ degrees of freedom.

lessons.title: Regression to the mean: Galton, fallacies and two regression lines
lessons.body:
## The idea that named regression

The least-squares regression lesson ended with a short section on regression toward the mean:
because $|r| \le 1$, a prediction is never farther from the mean, in standard deviations, than
the value it was predicted from (and is closer whenever $|r| < 1$). That small fact gave regression its name, and it is behind
one of the most common reasoning errors in science, sports and everyday life. This honors
lesson tells where the idea came from, explains why it happens with a simple model of
"skill plus luck," shows how it fools people and how good study design guards against it,
and finishes with a surprise: every scatterplot has *two* regression lines.

## Galton's discovery

In the 1880s the English scientist Francis Galton collected the heights of 205 pairs of
parents and their adult children (930 children, by his count). To put men and women on one
scale he multiplied each woman's height by 1.08, and he summarized each pair of parents by
the **[[mid-parent height]]**, the average of the two parents' (adjusted) heights.

He found that children of unusually tall parents were tall, but on average less unusual than
their parents, and children of short parents were short, but less so. In his 1886 paper,
"Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature," he summarized it this way: a child's
deviation from the average was, on average, about two-thirds of the mid-parent's deviation.
So mid-parents 3 inches above average had children averaging about 2 inches above average.

Galton first suspected a biological pull toward the average. He then noticed the pattern runs
both ways: tall children had parents who were, on average, *less* tall than they were.
Biology can't push a generation toward the mean backward in time, so the effect had to be a
property of imperfectly related measurements. Working out how to measure "imperfectly
related" led Galton to the idea of correlation in 1888, and Karl Pearson turned it into the
formula for $r$ used today.

```plot
{"x": [-2.5, 2.5], "y": [-2.5, 2.5], "equal": true, "xLabel": "z-score of x", "yLabel": "z-score of y", "functions": [{"f": "x", "dashed": true, "label": "SD line"}, {"f": "0.6*x", "color": "#2c5e8f", "label": "y on x"}, {"f": "x/0.6", "color": "#c2570c", "label": "x on y"}], "caption": "In standard units with r = 0.6: the SD line (slope 1), the regression of y on x (slope 0.6) and the regression of x on y (slope 1/0.6 on these axes)"}
```

## The z-score form

In standard units the least-squares line is simply

$$\hat{z}_y = r\,z_x.$$

If $r = 0.6$ and an individual is 2 SDs above the mean in $x$, the predicted $y$ is only 1.2 SDs
above the mean. With $r = 1$ there is no regression; with $r = 0$ every prediction is the mean.
The weaker the relationship, the stronger the pull toward the mean.

Two misreadings are worth heading off.

- Regression to the mean does *not* make a population more uniform over time. In a stable
  population, children's heights are about as spread out as their parents'. The *predictions* are pulled in, but the
  actual values are prediction plus scatter, and the scatter refills the tails. New extreme
  individuals keep appearing; they just aren't the same individuals as before.
- It works in both directions. Predicting parents from children pulls toward the mean too.

## Why it happens: skill plus luck

A simple model makes the effect obvious. Suppose every score is a stable part plus a chance
part:

$$\text{score} = \text{true ability} + \text{luck},$$

with the luck independent from one occasion to the next. Pick the people who did best on the
first test. As a group they have high ability, but they were also, on average, lucky: being in
the top group is easier if luck helped. On a second test the ability carries over and the luck
doesn't, so the group's average falls back toward the mean. The bottom group, on average
unlucky the first time, rises.

In this model, when both tests have the same mean and SD, the correlation between them equals
the share of score variance that comes from ability rather than luck. That share is called the
test's **[[reliability]]**: the correlation between two measurements of the same thing. A very
reliable test (little luck, $r$ near 1) shows little regression; a noisy one shows a lot. (This
is a simplified model: real abilities change, practice helps, and luck isn't always
independent, but it captures why regression happens.)

### Example 1: predicting a retest

A test has mean 100 and SD 15, and a retest has the same mean and SD. Scores on the two
correlate with $r = 0.8$. Predict the retest score of a student who scored 130, and of one who
scored 82.

1. With equal SDs, the line is $\hat{y} = 100 + 0.8(x - 100)$: the predicted distance from the
   mean is 80% of the original distance.
2. Score 130 is 30 above: predicted retest $100 + 0.8(30) = 124$.
3. Score 82 is 18 below: predicted retest $100 + 0.8(-18) = 85.6$.

Both predictions move toward 100 even though nothing happened between the tests. Neither
student "got worse" or "improved"; the line is just accounting for luck.

## The regression fallacy

The **[[regression fallacy]]** is explaining a change that is just regression to the mean by some
cause: a treatment, a punishment, a jinx. It is easy to fall into because extreme cases are
exactly the ones that get attention, and so they are the ones selected for action.

- *Praise and punishment.* The psychologist Daniel Kahneman describes flight instructors in
  the Israeli Air Force who believed that praising a very good landing made the next one worse
  and shouting at a bad landing made the next one better. Both patterns are what regression
  predicts when landings vary partly by chance, with no effect from praise or shouting at all.
- *Sports.* A player with an outstanding first season usually has a less outstanding second
  one (the "sophomore slump"). Magazine-cover "jinxes" are popular stories with the same
  explanation: athletes make the cover after unusually good stretches.
- *Medicine and policy.* Patients often join a study or see a doctor when their symptoms
  are at their worst, so many improve whatever is done. Road-safety cameras are often placed at
  sites that just had an unusually bad year, so crash counts there tend to fall even without the
  camera.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How the regression fallacy arises
  accDescr: A group is chosen because its first measurement was extreme. A treatment or other event follows. A second measurement is taken, and it is closer to the mean because the luck that made the first one extreme does not repeat. The change is then wrongly credited to the treatment. The remedy is a comparison group that was chosen the same way but did not get the treatment, ideally by random assignment.
  A["Choose people because their first score was extreme"] --> B["Something happens: a treatment, praise, a camera"]
  B --> C["Measure again: scores move toward the mean"]
  C --> D{"Is there a comparison group chosen the same way?"}
  D -- No --> E["Fallacy risk: the change gets credited to the treatment"]
  D -- Yes --> F["Credit only the difference between the two groups"]
```

The defense is a **[[control group]]** chosen the same way (Module 4): if equally extreme people
who got no treatment improve just as much, the treatment did nothing. Random assignment among
the selected people makes the two groups regress by the same amount on average.

### Example 2: did the tutoring work?

A school gives a reading test (mean 100, SD 15) and enrolls the lowest-scoring students in a
tutoring program. Their first-test average was 75. On a retest with the same mean and SD their
average is 85, a 10-point gain. Past data show $r = 0.7$ between test and retest. How much of
the gain could be regression?

1. The line predicts $100 + 0.7(75 - 100) = 100 - 17.5 = 82.5$ with no tutoring at all.
2. Regression alone accounts for $82.5 - 75 = 7.5$ of the 10 points.
3. Only about $85 - 82.5 = 2.5$ points are left that tutoring might explain, and even that
   needs a control group of similar students to confirm, since other things (practice with the
   test, for example) can raise retest scores. (Using the line to predict a group's average
   assumes the relationship is linear across the range; it is an approximation.)

## Two regression lines and the SD line

The line for predicting $y$ from $x$ minimizes vertical misses. The line for predicting $x$
from $y$ minimizes horizontal ones, and it is a different line:

$$b_{y \cdot x} = r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad b_{x \cdot y} = r\,\frac{s_x}{s_y}, \qquad b_{y \cdot x}\, b_{x \cdot y} = r^2.$$

Both lines pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. Between them lies the **[[SD line]]**, which also passes
through the point of means but has slope $\pm s_y/s_x$ (the sign of $r$): it rises one SD of $y$
for each SD of $x$ and runs along the long direction of the cloud of points (exactly along its
long axis when both variables are in standard units). Drawn on the same
$y$-versus-$x$ axes, the line for $x$ on $y$ has slope $1/b_{x \cdot y}$, so for $r > 0$:

$$r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x} \;<\; \frac{s_y}{s_x} \;<\; \frac{1}{r}\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}.$$

The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is flatter than the SD line. Your eye tends to pick the SD
line as "the line through the cloud," but the SD line over-predicts at the extremes: it ignores
the scatter, which is exactly what makes regression to the mean happen. The three lines coincide
only when $|r| = 1$.

### Example 3: both lines from summary statistics

Suppose $r = 0.6$, $s_x = 4$ and $s_y = 10$.

1. Predicting $y$ from $x$: $b_{y \cdot x} = 0.6 \times 10/4 = 1.5$.
2. Predicting $x$ from $y$: $b_{x \cdot y} = 0.6 \times 4/10 = 0.24$.
3. Check: $1.5 \times 0.24 = 0.36 = 0.6^2$. ✓
4. On $y$-versus-$x$ axes, the SD line has slope $10/4 = 2.5$ and the $x$-on-$y$ line has slope
   $1/0.24 \approx 4.17$. So $1.5 < 2.5 < 4.17$: the $y$-on-$x$ line is the flattest.

Inverting $\hat{y} = a + 1.5x$ to "solve for $x$" would give slope $1/1.5 \approx 0.67$ for
predicting $x$, not the correct 0.24. That inverted line is not a regression line.

## Common mistakes

- Treating regression to the mean as a real force that makes people or things more average.
  It is a statement about predictions from imperfectly correlated measurements.
- Crediting a treatment for improvement in a group chosen because it was extreme, with no
  comparison group.
- Expecting the spread of a population to shrink each generation or each season.
- Getting a prediction of $x$ from $y$ by solving the $y$-on-$x$ equation for $x$.
- Thinking the "best-looking" line through a cloud (the SD line) is the least-squares line.

## Key points

- $\hat{z}_y = r\,z_x$: predictions are $|r|$ times as far from the mean, in SDs, as the
  predictor. The weaker the correlation, the stronger the regression.
- Galton (1886): children's height deviations averaged about two-thirds of the mid-parent's.
  The effect runs in both directions, so it is not biological.
- Score = ability + luck explains it: extreme groups were partly lucky, and luck doesn't repeat.
- The regression fallacy credits regression to a cause; control groups chosen the same way
  prevent it.
- The two regression slopes multiply to $r^2$; the SD line lies between the two regression
  lines.

lessons.title: Relative risk, odds ratios and adjusting for a lurking variable
lessons.body:
## One number for a two-way table

The two-way tables lesson compared conditional percents: 50% of under-30 commuters take the
train, 25% of over-50s do. Medicine, public health, insurance and safety engineering compare
groups this way constantly, and they boil each comparison down to one number: "smokers have
about 15 times the risk," "the drug cuts the risk in half," "the odds ratio was 3.5." This
honors lesson defines those numbers, shows why one of them (the odds ratio) is the only
choice for some study designs, and then returns to Simpson's paradox with a tool for fixing
it: standardization.

## The 2×2 table

Most of these measures start from a table with an *exposure* (a treatment, a habit, a risk
factor) in the rows and a yes/no *outcome* in the columns:

| | Outcome | No outcome | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exposed | $a$ | $b$ | $a + b$ |
| Not exposed | $c$ | $d$ | $c + d$ |

The **[[risk]]** of the outcome in a group is the proportion of the group that has it: a
conditional proportion, $p_1 = a/(a + b)$ for the exposed and $p_2 = c/(c + d)$ for the
unexposed. From two risks you can build two comparisons:

- the **[[risk difference]]**, $p_1 - p_2$ (an absolute comparison, often given in percentage
  points);
- the **[[relative risk]]**, $\text{RR} = p_1/p_2$ (a ratio: how many times as likely).

$\text{RR} = 1$ and a risk difference of 0 both mean no association.

## Odds

Gamblers have long described chances as odds. The **[[odds]]** of an event are its probability
divided by the probability that it doesn't happen:

$$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p}, \qquad p = \frac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}.$$

A probability of 0.75 is odds of $0.75/0.25 = 3$ ("3 to 1"); a probability of 0.2 is odds of
$0.25$ ("1 to 4"). In the 2×2 table the odds of the outcome among the exposed are simply $a/b$,
and among the unexposed $c/d$. The **[[odds ratio]]** compares them:

$$\text{OR} = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{ad}{bc}.$$

For a rare outcome, $1 - p$ is close to 1, so odds are close to probabilities and the odds
ratio is close to the relative risk. For a common outcome they can differ a lot, and the odds
ratio is always farther from 1 than the relative risk (unless both equal 1).

### Example 1: all four measures

A study follows 1,200 adults for ten years. Of 400 who exercised regularly, 20 developed heart
disease; of 800 who didn't, 80 did.

1. Risks: $p_1 = 20/400 = 0.05$ (exercisers) and $p_2 = 80/800 = 0.10$.
2. Risk difference: $0.05 - 0.10 = -0.05$, five percentage points lower.
3. Relative risk: $0.05/0.10 = 0.5$. Exercisers had half the risk.
4. Odds: $20/380 \approx 0.0526$ and $80/720 \approx 0.1111$, so
   $\text{OR} = (20 \times 720)/(380 \times 80) = 14{,}400/30{,}400 \approx 0.474$.

The OR (0.474) is close to the RR (0.5) because heart disease was fairly uncommon in both
groups. This is an observational study, so neither number shows that exercise *caused* the
lower risk; people who exercise differ in other ways too.

## Absolute versus relative

Relative risks make striking headlines. "Doubles the risk" sounds alarming, but if the risk
goes from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 the risk difference is one extra case per 10,000 people.
A relative risk of 1.2 for a common condition can matter far more. Always ask for the baseline
risk, or report the risk difference alongside the ratio.

## Why odds ratios: case-control studies

In a **[[case-control]]** study (see the lesson on study conclusions), investigators start with
people who *have* the outcome (cases) and pick a comparison group who don't (controls), then
look back at exposures. The researchers choose how many cases and controls to include, so the
share of the study with the outcome is set by design. Risks computed from the table are
meaningless: double the number of controls and every "risk" changes.

The odds ratio survives. Its formula $ad/bc$ is unchanged if you multiply a whole column (all
the controls, say) by any constant, because the constant appears once on top and once on the
bottom. And the odds ratio of the outcome given exposure equals the odds ratio of exposure given
the outcome, both being $ad/bc$. So the odds of exposure among cases versus controls, which a
case-control study *can* measure, give the same number as the odds ratio for the outcome. When
the outcome is rare in the population, that odds ratio also approximates the relative risk, a
point made by the statistician Jerome Cornfield in 1951 in his work on smoking and lung
cancer.

### Example 2: a case-control study

Researchers find 200 people with a rare illness and 400 similar people without it. Among the
cases, 120 had a certain exposure; among the controls, 120 did.

| | Cases | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| Exposed | 120 | 120 |
| Not exposed | 80 | 280 |

1. Odds of exposure: cases $120/80 = 1.5$, controls $120/280 \approx 0.429$.
2. $\text{OR} = (120 \times 280)/(80 \times 120) = 33{,}600/9{,}600 = 3.5$.
3. Had they chosen 800 controls with the same exposure rate (240 exposed, 560 not):
   $\text{OR} = (120 \times 560)/(80 \times 240) = 67{,}200/19{,}200 = 3.5$, unchanged. The
   "risk of illness among the exposed" would have changed from $120/240 = 50\%$ to
   $120/360 \approx 33\%$, which shows it was never a real risk.
4. Because the illness is rare, exposed people have roughly 3.5 times the risk of the
   unexposed. (Whether the exposure *causes* it is a separate question; case-control studies
   are observational.)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which comparison a study design supports
  accDescr: If the study chose people by their exposure or followed a whole group forward in time, as in a cohort study or an experiment, risks can be computed, so report the risk difference and relative risk, and the odds ratio if wanted. If the study chose people by their outcome, as in a case-control study, risks cannot be computed, so report the odds ratio, which approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare.
  A{"How were people chosen?"} -- "By exposure, or a whole group followed forward" --> B["Risks are meaningful"]
  B --> C["Report risk difference and relative risk"]
  A -- "By outcome: cases and controls" --> D["Risks depend on the design"]
  D --> E["Report the odds ratio"]
  E --> F["Rare outcome: OR is close to RR"]
```

## Simpson's paradox as a weighted average

The two-way tables lesson showed Hospital A beating Hospital B for mild patients (98.3% vs.
96.7% survival) and for severe patients (52.5% vs. 30%), yet losing overall (80% vs. 90%). The
reason is arithmetic. A hospital's overall survival rate is a *weighted average* of its two
stratum rates, weighted by its own case mix:

$$\text{overall} = (\text{share mild})(\text{mild rate}) + (\text{share severe})(\text{severe rate}).$$

Hospital A's patients are 40% severe, B's only 10%. Plot each hospital's overall rate against
the share of severe patients and each hospital moves along its own straight line. A's line is
above B's everywhere, but A sits far to the right, where every hospital does worse.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1.1], "xLabel": "share of patients who are severe", "yLabel": "overall survival rate", "functions": [{"f": "0.98333*(1 - x) + 0.525*x", "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"f": "0.96667*(1 - x) + 0.30*x", "color": "#c2570c"}], "points": [{"at": [0.4, 0.8], "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [0.1, 0.9], "color": "#c2570c"}, {"at": [0.25, 0.86875], "open": true, "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"at": [0.25, 0.8], "open": true, "color": "#c2570c"}], "segments": [{"from": [0.25, 0], "to": [0.25, 0.97], "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [0.82, 0.72], "text": "Hospital A"}, {"at": [0.75, 0.3], "text": "Hospital B"}], "caption": "Filled dots: each hospital's actual mix (A: 40% severe, 80% survive; B: 10% severe, 90% survive). A's line is above B's for every case mix. At a common mix of 25% severe (dashed), A survives 86.9% and B 80.0%."}
```

## Standardization

The fix is to compare the hospitals *as if they had the same case mix*. **[[Standardization]]**
(direct standardization) picks one standard mix, applies each group's own stratum rates to it,
and adds. The results are called adjusted (or standardized) rates. Demographers and public
health agencies routinely use it, for example to compare death rates of regions whose
populations have different age structures. (The honors lesson on causal inference in Module 4
uses the same tool to adjust an observational comparison for a measured confounder.)

### Example 3: adjusting the hospital comparison

Use the two hospitals combined as the standard: 1,500 mild and 500 severe patients, so the
standard mix is 75% mild, 25% severe.

1. Hospital A's rates: mild $590/600 \approx 0.9833$, severe $210/400 = 0.525$.
   Adjusted: $0.75(0.9833) + 0.25(0.525) = 0.7375 + 0.1313 \approx 0.869$, or 86.9%.
2. Hospital B's rates: mild $870/900 \approx 0.9667$, severe $30/100 = 0.30$.
   Adjusted: $0.75(0.9667) + 0.25(0.30) = 0.725 + 0.075 = 0.800$, or 80.0%.
3. On equal footing A is better, 86.9% to 80.0%, which agrees with the comparison inside each
   stratum. A different standard mix changes the adjusted numbers but here can't reverse the
   order, because A is better in both strata.

## A real example: kidney stones

A frequently cited example comes from a 1986 British study (Charig and colleagues) of two
treatments for kidney stones, open surgery and a less invasive keyhole procedure. Overall, the
keyhole procedure succeeded more often: 289 of 350 (83%) versus 273 of 350 (78%). But open
surgery did better for small stones (81 of 87, 93%, versus 234 of 270, 87%) and for large stones
(192 of 263, 73%, versus 55 of 80, 69%). Large stones are harder to treat, and about 75% of the
open-surgery patients had large stones versus about 23% of the keyhole patients. Stone size was
the lurking variable. (Patients weren't randomly assigned, so even the stratum comparisons can
be confounded by things that weren't recorded.)

That caveat is the limit of every adjustment: standardization removes the effect of the
variables you stratify on, and nothing else. Only random assignment balances the lurking
variables nobody measured.

## Common mistakes

- Reporting a relative risk without the baseline risk, so a tiny absolute change sounds huge.
- Calling an odds ratio a relative risk when the outcome is common; then they can be far apart.
- Computing "risks" from a case-control table, where the number of cases was chosen by the
  researchers.
- Flipping the ratio ($p_2/p_1$ instead of $p_1/p_2$). Say which group is on top.
- Treating an adjusted rate as proof of cause. Adjustment handles only the variables you
  adjusted for.

## Key points

- Risk = proportion with the outcome in a group. Risk difference $p_1 - p_2$; relative risk
  $p_1/p_2$.
- Odds $= p/(1 - p)$; odds ratio $= ad/bc$. For rare outcomes, OR ≈ RR.
- Case-control studies can estimate only the odds ratio, because it is unchanged by how many
  cases and controls are sampled.
- An overall rate is a weighted average of stratum rates; different weights cause Simpson's
  paradox.
- Direct standardization applies each group's stratum rates to one standard mix, so groups are
  compared on equal footing (for the measured variables only).

lessons.title: Sampling methods and bias
lessons.body:
## Where data come from

Everything so far assumed the data were in hand. But conclusions are only as good as the
way the data were collected, and no formula can rescue a badly chosen sample. This module
is about collecting data well: this lesson covers samples and surveys; the next two cover
experiments and what each kind of study can conclude.

## Population, sample and sampling frame

The **[[population]]** is the whole group you want information about; a **[[sample]]** is the
part you actually examine. A **[[sampling frame]]** is the list from which the sample is
actually drawn — a list of registered voters, student ID numbers, customer accounts. If
the frame leaves out part of the population, no sampling method can fix it.

## Bad sampling methods

A sampling method is **[[biased]]** if it systematically favors certain outcomes — not just
"off by chance," but off in the same direction every time it is used.

- A **[[convenience sample]]** takes whoever is easiest to reach: shoppers at one mall,
  your friends, the first 50 people through the door. They are rarely representative.
- A **[[voluntary response sample]]** consists of people who choose to respond to an open
  invitation (call-in polls, online reviews, "click to vote"). People with strong —
  usually negative — opinions respond most, so these samples are typically badly biased.

Large size doesn't help: a voluntary response poll of 100,000 people is still biased.
Bias is about *how* individuals are chosen, not how many.

## Random sampling methods

The cure for bias is to let chance choose. **[[Random sampling]]** removes the selector's
preferences and makes it possible to calculate how far the results are likely to be from
the truth.

### Simple random sample

A **[[simple random sample]]** (SRS) of size $n$ is chosen so that every set of $n$
individuals in the population has the same chance of being the sample. To take one:
number the individuals in the frame $1$ to $N$, then use a random number generator (or
a table of random digits) to pick $n$ distinct numbers, skipping repeats and numbers
outside the range.

### Stratified random sample

Divide the population into **[[strata]]** — groups of similar individuals, such as grade
levels, regions or income brackets — and take a separate SRS within each stratum.
Stratifying guarantees every stratum is represented and gives *more precise* estimates
when the strata differ from each other but individuals within a stratum are similar.
With **[[proportional allocation]]**, each stratum's share of the sample matches its share
of the population.

### Cluster sample

Divide the population into **[[clusters]]** — usually location-based groups such as city
blocks, classrooms or train cars — randomly choose some clusters, and include *every*
individual in the chosen clusters. Clusters are used for convenience and cost: it's
cheaper to survey everyone on 5 randomly chosen trains than 200 riders scattered across
the network. Clusters work best when each cluster is a mini-version of the population
(heterogeneous within).

The contrast is the key exam point: *strata are similar inside, and we sample from every
stratum; clusters are mixed inside, and we sample whole clusters*.

The picture below shows four of these methods on the same population of 40 individuals. Dark
dots are the ones chosen.

![Four panels, each showing 40 dots. Simple random sample: 8 dots chosen with no pattern. Stratified random sample: the dots form four colored rows (strata), and 2 dots are chosen in every row. Cluster sample: the dots sit in 8 dashed boxes of 5 (clusters); 2 boxes are chosen and all 5 dots in each are dark. Systematic sample: every 5th dot is chosen, starting from the 3rd, so the chosen dots line up in two columns.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Systematic random sample

Choose a random starting point among the first $k$ individuals in a list, then take every
$k$th individual after it, where $k = N/n$. This is easy in the field (every 20th
customer through a door). It works like an SRS unless the list has a repeating pattern
that lines up with $k$.

### Multistage sampling

Large surveys combine methods: randomly choose counties, then neighborhoods within them,
then households within neighborhoods.

### Example 1

A university has 12,000 undergraduates: 4,200 first-years, 3,300 sophomores, 2,700
juniors and 1,800 seniors. Plan a stratified sample of 400 with proportional allocation.

1. Sampling fraction: $400/12{,}000 = 1/30$.
2. First-years: $4200/30 = 140$; sophomores $110$; juniors $90$; seniors $60$.
3. Check: $140 + 110 + 90 + 60 = 400$. Then take an SRS of the given size within each
   class year.

### Example 2

An inspector wants a 1-in-$k$ systematic sample of 50 welds from a line of 1,000 welds.

1. $k = 1000/50 = 20$.
2. Choose a random start between 1 and 20 — say 13.
3. Inspect welds 13, 33, 53, …, 993 (that is $13 + 20j$ for $j = 0, \dots, 49$).

## Bias in surveys

Even a random sample can produce biased results:

- **[[Undercoverage]]**: some groups are left out of the frame (people without phones or
  internet, people experiencing homelessness).
- **[[Nonresponse bias]]**: chosen individuals can't be reached or refuse, and nonresponders
  differ from responders. Response rates under 20% are common for phone polls.
- **[[Response bias]]**: answers are systematically inaccurate — people overstate voting and
  understate drinking; an interviewer's tone or appearance influences answers.
- *Wording of questions*: "Do you support the reckless plan to raise fares?" pushes
  answers. Loaded words, double negatives and questions that ask two things at once all
  distort results.

Random sampling protects against *selection* bias but not against these.

The chart follows a survey from the population to the recorded answers and shows where each
problem can enter.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where bias can enter a survey
  accDescr: A survey moves from the population to a sampling frame, then to the chosen sample, then to the people who respond, then to the recorded answers. Undercoverage enters between the population and the frame. Selection bias from a nonrandom method and sampling variability enter when the sample is chosen from the frame. Nonresponse bias enters when some chosen people do not respond. Response bias and question wording enter when answers are recorded.
  P["Population: everyone you want to learn about"] --> F["Sampling frame: the list you draw from"]
  F --> S["Chosen sample"]
  S --> R["People who actually respond"]
  R --> A["Recorded answers"]
  P -. "undercoverage" .- F
  F -. "selection bias if not random; sampling variability always" .- S
  S -. "nonresponse bias" .- R
  R -. "response bias, wording" .- A
```

## Sampling variability

Different random samples give different results — this is **[[sampling variability]]**, and
it is not bias. Larger random samples vary less. The rest of the course measures this
variability precisely (margins of error). The goal is a method that is *unbiased* (right
on average) *and* has low variability (consistent from sample to sample).

Think of each sample's estimate as a shot at a target whose bullseye is the true population
value. Bias is how far the center of the shots is from the bullseye; variability is how widely
the shots scatter. A larger random sample tightens the scatter but doesn't move its center.

![Four archery targets, each with ten shots. Low bias, low variability: shots tightly grouped on the bullseye. Low bias, high variability: shots scattered widely but centered on the bullseye. High bias, low variability: shots tightly grouped but off to the upper right. High bias, high variability: shots scattered and centered off to the lower left.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- Calling any sample "random" because no one deliberately chose who's in it — a
  convenience sample is not random.
- Thinking a bigger sample fixes bias.
- Mixing up strata and clusters: you sample *within* every stratum but take *all* of a
  few clusters.
- Describing bias vaguely. Say which direction the estimate would likely be off and why.

## Key points

- Convenience and voluntary response samples are biased; random sampling avoids selection bias.
- SRS: every set of $n$ equally likely. Stratified: SRS within each similar group.
  Cluster: all members of randomly chosen groups. Systematic: every $k$th after a random start.
- Proportional allocation: stratum sample size $= n \times$ (stratum size ÷ $N$).
- Undercoverage, nonresponse, response bias and question wording can bias even random samples.
- Sampling variability is chance variation; larger samples reduce it, but don't reduce bias.

lessons.title: Designing experiments
lessons.body:
## Why experiments

A sample survey observes; an experiment *acts*. If you want to know whether a new
fastener design reduces track defects, whether a tutoring program raises scores, or
whether a drug lowers blood pressure, the most convincing evidence comes from deliberately
imposing the treatment on some units and not others, then comparing. This lesson covers
the vocabulary and the principles that make experiments trustworthy.

## Vocabulary

- **[[Experimental units]]** are the objects to which treatments are assigned; when they are
  people they are called **[[subjects]]**.
- A **[[factor]]** is an explanatory variable the experimenter manipulates; each factor has
  **[[levels]]** (specific values).
- A **[[treatment]]** is a specific condition applied to units — one level of one factor, or
  a combination of levels of several factors.
- The **[[response variable]]** is the outcome measured.

### Example 1

A study tests three fertilizer amounts (none, low, high) and two watering schedules (daily,
every other day) on 60 tomato plants, measuring fruit weight after 10 weeks.

1. Experimental units: the 60 plants.
2. Factors: fertilizer (3 levels) and watering (2 levels).
3. Treatments: every combination, $3 \times 2 = 6$ treatments.
4. Response: fruit weight.
5. With 60 plants and equal group sizes, 10 plants per treatment.

## Four principles of experimental design

1. *Comparison*. Use two or more treatments so outcomes can be compared. Often one
   group gets a **[[control]]** — no treatment, an existing standard treatment, or a placebo.
   Without a comparison group, improvement could be due to time, attention or chance.
2. **[[Random assignment]]**. Use chance to assign units to treatments. Randomization
   creates groups that are roughly equivalent in every respect — measured or not — before
   treatment begins, so differences in response can be attributed to the treatments.
3. **[[Replication]]**. Use enough experimental units in each group that chance differences
   between groups average out. (Replication can also mean repeating the whole experiment.)
4. *Control of other variables*. Keep everything except the treatment the same for all
   groups (same soil, same timing, same measurement procedure) to reduce variability and
   remove alternative explanations.

## Placebos and blinding

People often improve simply because they believe they are being treated — the **placebo
effect**. A **placebo** is a fake treatment (a sugar pill, a sham procedure) given to the
control group so that both groups have the same expectations.

In a **[[blind]]** experiment, subjects don't know which treatment they get. In a
**[[double-blind]]** experiment, neither the subjects nor the people who interact with them
and measure the response know. Double-blinding keeps expectations (and so any placebo
effect) the same in every group and prevents unconscious bias in how outcomes are measured.

## Completely randomized design

In a **[[completely randomized design]]**, all experimental units are assigned to treatments
completely at random. To assign 40 volunteers to two groups of 20: write each name on an
identical slip, shuffle, draw 20 for treatment A; the rest get treatment B. Or number the
subjects 1–40 and use a random number generator to pick 20 distinct numbers.

An outline like the one below is the standard way to describe a design: the units, the random
assignment, the groups and their treatments, and what is compared. This one is the completely
randomized version of Example 3 later in the lesson.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Outline of a completely randomized design
  accDescr: Thirty volunteers are split by random assignment into two groups of 15. Group 1 gets the caffeinated drink and group 2 gets the decaffeinated placebo drink. Both groups take the same reaction-time test, and the mean reaction times are compared.
  V["30 volunteers"] --> RA["Random assignment"]
  RA --> G1["Group 1: 15 volunteers"]
  RA --> G2["Group 2: 15 volunteers"]
  G1 --> T1["Caffeinated drink"]
  G2 --> T2["Decaf drink (placebo)"]
  T1 --> C["Compare mean reaction times"]
  T2 --> C
```

## Blocking

A **[[block]]** is a group of experimental units that are similar in a way expected to affect
the response. In a **[[randomized block design]]**, units are first sorted into blocks, then
randomly assigned to treatments *separately within each block*. Results are compared
within blocks.

Blocking is to experiments what stratifying is to sampling. Its purpose is to *reduce
variability*: by comparing treatments among similar units, differences between blocks
don't blur the comparison. Blocking doesn't replace randomization — randomization still
happens inside each block.

### Example 2

A railway tests two rail lubricants on 40 curves; 20 curves are sharp and 20 are gentle.
Curve sharpness strongly affects wear.

- Completely randomized: assign 20 curves at random to each lubricant. By chance, one
  lubricant might get more sharp curves, inflating its wear.
- Randomized block: block by sharpness. Within the 20 sharp curves, randomly assign 10 to
  each lubricant; do the same within the 20 gentle curves. Compare lubricants within each
  block. The large sharp/gentle difference no longer adds noise.

The outline of the randomized block design shows the random assignment happening twice, once
inside each block:

![Outline of the randomized block design: 40 rail curves split into Block 1, 20 sharp curves, and Block 2, 20 gentle curves. In each block a random assignment sends 10 curves to lubricant A and 10 to lubricant B, and wear is compared within that block.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Matched pairs

A **[[matched pairs design]]** is blocking with blocks of size 2. Either two similar units are
paired and the treatments randomly assigned within each pair (twins, two adjacent plots),
or each unit receives *both* treatments in random order (each driver tests both seat
designs, the order decided by a coin flip). The analysis looks at the *differences* within
pairs, which removes unit-to-unit variation. Randomizing the order guards against
learning or fatigue effects.

Which design to use depends on what you know about the units before the experiment starts:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing an experimental design
  accDescr: First ask whether some variable other than the treatment is expected to strongly affect the response. If not, use a completely randomized design. If so, ask whether units can be formed into pairs of very similar units, or whether each unit can receive both treatments. If yes, use a matched pairs design and randomize within each pair or randomize the order. If no, use a randomized block design: group similar units into blocks and randomly assign treatments within each block.
  Q1{"Is another variable expected to strongly affect the response?"}
  Q1 -- No --> CRD["Completely randomized design"]
  Q1 -- Yes --> Q2{"Can units be paired, or can each unit get both treatments?"}
  Q2 -- Yes --> MP["Matched pairs: randomize within each pair or randomize the order"]
  Q2 -- No --> RB["Randomized block design: randomize within each block"]
```

## Statistical significance (a preview)

If the treatment groups' responses differ, could chance alone — the luck of the random
assignment — explain it? When an observed difference is too large to plausibly be due to
chance, it is called **[[statistically significant]]**. Module 8 makes this precise. For now:
randomization is what makes "chance" calculable, and replication is what lets real effects
stand out from chance.

### Example 3

Design an experiment to test whether a caffeinated drink improves reaction time, using 30
volunteers.

1. Treatments: caffeinated drink vs. an identical-tasting decaffeinated drink (placebo).
2. Randomly assign 15 volunteers to each (completely randomized), or better, use matched
   pairs: each volunteer is tested on two days, once with each drink, in random order.
3. Double-blind: drinks are coded by someone not involved in testing.
4. Control: same time of day, same test, no other caffeine that day.
5. Response: reaction time; compare means (or the mean of the within-person differences).

## Common mistakes

- Confusing random *sampling* (choosing who is in the study) with random *assignment*
  (choosing who gets which treatment).
- Thinking blocking replaces randomization.
- Forgetting that treatments are *combinations* of factor levels in multifactor
  experiments.
- Saying "control" when meaning "control group" — controlling variables and having a
  control group are different ideas.

## Key points

- Units, factors, levels, treatments, response.
- Principles: comparison, random assignment, replication, control.
- Placebos and double-blinding prevent expectation and measurement bias.
- Completely randomized design: assign all units at random. Randomized block: randomize
  within groups of similar units. Matched pairs: blocks of two, analyze differences.
- Statistically significant: too large a difference to attribute to chance.

lessons.title: Observational studies, confounding and scope of inference
lessons.body:
## What can this study conclude?

The last two lessons covered two tools: random sampling and random assignment. They solve
different problems. This lesson ties them together into the single most practical
question in statistics: *given how these data were collected, what conclusions are
justified — and about whom?*

## Observational studies versus experiments

In an **[[observational study]]**, researchers observe individuals and measure variables but
do not influence the responses. Surveys, records reviews and most medical studies of
lifestyle (diet, smoking, exercise) are observational. In an **[[experiment]]**, researchers
deliberately impose treatments.

Observational studies come in flavors:

- **[[Retrospective]]** studies look backward, examining existing data (medical records, past
  maintenance logs).
- **[[Prospective]]** studies follow individuals forward in time, recording outcomes as they
  happen.
- **[[Case-control]]** studies start with people who have an outcome (cases) and similar
  people without it (controls), then compare past exposures. They are efficient for rare
  outcomes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Kinds of studies
  accDescr: Studies divide into experiments, where researchers impose treatments, and observational studies, where they do not. Observational studies include retrospective studies that look back at existing records, prospective studies that follow people forward in time, and case-control studies that start from people with and without an outcome and compare their past exposures.
  ST["Study"] --> EX["Experiment: researchers impose treatments"]
  ST --> OB["Observational study: researchers only observe"]
  OB --> RE["Retrospective: look back at existing records"]
  OB --> PR["Prospective: follow people forward in time"]
  OB --> CC["Case-control: start from the outcome, look back at exposures"]
```

Observational studies are often the only ethical or practical option — you can't assign
people to smoke — but they have a serious weakness.

## Confounding

Two variables are **[[confounded]]** when their effects on the response can't be separated.
A **[[confounding variable]]** is related to the explanatory variable *and* affects the
response, so it offers an alternative explanation for an observed association.

### Example 1

An observational study finds that people who drink moderate amounts of red wine have
lower rates of heart disease than people who drink none. Does wine protect the heart?

Possibly — but moderate wine drinkers also tend to have higher incomes, better diets and
better access to health care, all of which lower heart-disease risk. Income is a likely
confounding variable: it is associated with wine drinking and affects heart health. The
study cannot tell whether wine, income or both are responsible.

![Three boxes joined by arrows. Income, the confounding variable, is at the top, with an arrow labeled related to pointing to moderate wine drinking, the explanatory variable, and an arrow labeled affects pointing to heart disease, the response variable. A dashed two-headed arrow labeled observed association joins wine drinking and heart disease.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Even careful statistical adjustment can only account for confounders that were measured.
Random assignment is the only method that balances *all* potential confounders —
measured and unmeasured — on average. That is why well-designed experiments can show
cause and effect and observational studies, by themselves, generally cannot.

(The terms *lurking variable* and *confounding variable* are close cousins; "lurking"
emphasizes that the variable wasn't measured in the study, "confounding" that its effect
is mixed up with the explanatory variable's.)

## Scope of inference
