questions.stem: Sorted data: 2, 9, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 18, 19, 20. What shape will the normal probability plot (data up, expected z across) have?
choices: It bends downward, with both ends below the line: left-skewed
It bends upward, with both ends above the line: right-skewed
An S shape with steep ends: heavy tails
Close to a straight line: approximately normal
questions.explanation: Look at the gaps: 7, 4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1. The low values are spread far apart and the high values are bunched together. So the plot is steep at the left and flat at the right (concave down): left skew. The long tail is toward small values.

questions.stem: Right-skewed data with only positive values can often be made close to normal by taking the ___ of each value.
questions.explanation: Taking logarithms pulls in large values much more than small ones, which can remove right skew. In Example 3 the repair times' plot had $r = 0.946$; their base-10 logs gave $r = 0.9985$. Square roots also pull in large values, more gently, and can fix milder right skew.

questions.stem: For the repair times in the lesson, a normal model for the raw times says about 3% of repairs take over 20 hours, while a normal model for the logs (which fits) says about 6%. Why can models that agree well near the center differ so much here?
choices: Because 20 hours is below the mean
Because the logs have a smaller standard deviation than the raw times
Because tail proportions depend on the shape of the distribution far from the center, where the models differ most
Because a normal model can never be used for times
questions.explanation: 20 hours is far out in the right tail, and tail areas depend on exactly how the curve thins out there. The right-skewed log model has a longer right tail than the symmetric raw model, so it puts twice as much area beyond 20. Comparing the SD of the logs with the raw SD means nothing, since they are in different units.

questions.stem: Temperatures recorded to the nearest whole degree give a normal probability plot with several short horizontal runs of points, but overall the points follow a straight line. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The data are bimodal
The data have heavy tails
A normal model is ruled out
The runs come from rounding; a normal model is still reasonable
questions.explanation: Rounding makes several values exactly equal, and equal values plot at the same height: horizontal steps. Steps alone are not evidence against normality. Bimodality would show as a gap or cluster; heavy tails as an S shape.

questions.stem: Bolt lengths are normal, and a specification is drawn on the curve. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A normal curve of bolt lengths on an axis from 146 to 155 mm. Two solid vertical lines stand at 147 and 153, and a dashed vertical line at 150.3 through the peak. The small tail left of 147 and the larger tail right of 153 are shaded. Marker 1 is at the top of the line at 147; marker 2 at the top of the line at 153; marker 3 at the top of the dashed line at 150.3; marker 4 on the shaded tail right of 153; marker 5 on the shaded tail left of 147.

choices: Lower specification limit
Upper specification limit
Process mean
Bolts that are too long
Bolts that are too short
Inflection point
Upper fence
questions.explanation: The solid lines at 147 and 153 mm are the specification limits, set by the design. The dashed line through the peak is the process mean, 150.3 mm. The shaded tails are the parts outside the limits: beyond 153 the bolts are too long, below 147 too short. Because the mean is above the middle (150), the right tail is larger.

questions.stem: A specification is 9.1 to 10.9 mm and the process SD is 0.2 mm. $C_p =$ ___. Give only the number.
A specification is 47 to 53 mm. The process has mean 51 mm and SD 0.5 mm. What is $C_{pk}$?
questions.explanation: Distances to the limits: $53 - 51 = 2$ and $51 - 47 = 4$. The nearer is 2, so $C_{pk} = 2/(3 \times 0.5) = 1.33$. (2.00 is $C_p$, which ignores centering; 2.67 uses the farther limit; 0.67 divides by $6\sigma$ instead of $3\sigma$.)

questions.stem: A normal process is centered with $C_p = 1$. About what fraction of its output is out of specification?
questions.explanation: $C_p = 1$ with centering puts each limit $3\sigma$ from the mean. The area beyond $\pm 3\sigma$ is $1 - 0.9973 = 0.0027$, or 0.27% (2,700 ppm). 0.135% counts only one tail; 5% is beyond $\pm 2\sigma$ and 32% beyond $\pm \sigma$.

questions.stem: All four processes have the specification 47 to 53 mm. Put them in order from MOST capable to LEAST capable, judged by $C_{pk}$.
choices: Mean 50, SD 0.5
Mean 51, SD 0.5
Mean 50, SD 1
Mean 51.5, SD 1

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: The range a part must fall in, set by the design or customer
The range the process actually produces, about μ ± 3σ
Width of the specification divided by 6σ, ignoring centering
Distance from the mean to the nearer limit, divided by 3σ
Out-of-spec parts per million
Distance from the mean to the farther limit, divided by 3σ
questions.explanation: Specification limits are requirements; natural variation is what the process does. $C_p$ compares their widths and would be achieved only by a centered process; $C_{pk}$ uses the nearer limit, so it accounts for centering. ppm is the out-of-spec proportion times 1,000,000.

questions.stem: Which of these would raise a process's $C_{pk}$? Select all that apply.
choices: Moving an off-center mean toward the middle of the specification
Reducing the process standard deviation
Widening the specification limits, if the design safely allows it
Measuring more parts without changing the process
Moving the mean toward the nearer limit
questions.explanation: $C_{pk} = \min(\text{USL} - \mu, \mu - \text{LSL})/(3\sigma)$. Centering increases the smaller distance, a smaller $\sigma$ shrinks the denominator, and wider limits increase both distances. Measuring more parts gives a better estimate but does not change the process. Moving toward the nearer limit makes the smaller distance smaller still.

questions.stem: A specification is 9.7 to 10.3 mm. The process is $N(10.2, 0.1)$, so about 16% of parts are too long. Option A: re-center the mean at 10.0 (SD stays 0.1). Option B: cut the SD to 0.05 (mean stays 10.2). Which gives fewer out-of-spec parts?
choices: Option B, about 0.27% out of spec versus 2.3% for A
They are equal, because both double $C_{pk}$
Option A, about 0.27% out of spec versus 2.3% for B
Option B, because reducing σ always helps more than centering
questions.explanation: A: limits at $z = \pm 3$, so $2(0.00135) = 0.27\%$ out. B: the upper limit is $(10.3 - 10.2)/0.05 = 2$ SDs away, so $1 - \Phi(2) \approx 2.3\%$ are too long (the lower limit is 10 SDs away). Here the process was narrow but badly off center, so centering wins. A raises $C_{pk}$ from 0.33 to 1 and B to 0.67, so they don't both double it.

questions.stem: A specification is 147 to 153 mm and the mean is held at 150 mm. For a "six sigma" process, $C_{pk} = 2$. The largest SD that achieves this is ___ mm. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $C_{pk} = 3/(3\sigma) \ge 2$ gives $\sigma \le 3/6 = 0.5$ mm. Then each limit is $3/0.5 = 6$ SDs from the mean.

questions.stem: Six Sigma is often described as "3.4 defects per million." What assumption produces that number?
choices: The mean is assumed to drift $1.5\sigma$ toward one limit, leaving it $4.5\sigma$ away
The limits are exactly $6\sigma$ from a perfectly centered mean
Defects are counted in both tails beyond $3\sigma$
The distribution is assumed to have heavy tails
questions.explanation: With a $1.5\sigma$ drift, the nearer limit is $6 - 1.5 = 4.5$ SDs away, and $1 - \Phi(4.5) \approx 3.4 \times 10^{-6}$. A centered six-sigma process would give only about 0.002 ppm. The $1.5\sigma$ shift is an industrial convention, not a law of statistics.

questions.stem: From 50 measured parts, a centered process has $C_{pk} = 1.33$, and the normal model predicts about 63 out-of-spec parts per million. Why should this prediction be treated with caution?
choices: Because $C_{pk}$ cannot be computed from 50 parts
Because 63 ppm is too high for any real process
Because the normal model always overstates defect rates
Because it depends on the normal curve 4 SDs from the mean, far beyond the data, where heavier tails would mean many more defects
questions.explanation: The limits are $4\sigma$ away, and 50 parts give almost no information about the distribution that far out. If the real tails are heavier than normal, the true rate can be many times 63 ppm. The model can understate defects, not only overstate them.

questions.stem: A process is predicted to produce 63 ppm out of specification. About how many out-of-spec parts would you expect in a run of 40,000 parts?
choices: About 0.25
About 2.5
About 25
About 252
questions.explanation: 63 ppm is a proportion of $63/1{,}000{,}000 = 0.000063$. Expected count: $40{,}000 \times 0.000063 \approx 2.5$ parts.

questions.stem: A process has $C_p = 1.5$ but $C_{pk} = 0.6$. What does this tell you?
choices: The spread is small enough, but the mean is far off center
The process is centered, but the spread is too large
The process is unstable
An arithmetic error, because $C_{pk}$ is always at least $C_p$
questions.explanation: $C_p = 1.5$ says the specification is 1.5 times as wide as $6\sigma$, so the spread would be fine if centered. $C_{pk}$ is much lower only when the mean sits close to one limit. The fix is to re-center. $C_{pk}$ is never more than $C_p$, so this combination is possible. The indices alone cannot show instability; that needs a control chart.

questions.stem: Dashed lines at the mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$ split this scatterplot into four regions. Describe a point in each numbered region and the sign of its product $z_x z_y$.

image.alt: Scatterplot of five points, weeks of training against skill score, with a dashed vertical line at the mean of x, 3, and a dashed horizontal line at the mean of y, 5. Marker 1 is in the upper right region, 2 in the upper left, 3 in the lower left and 4 in the lower right.

choices: x above its mean, y above its mean: positive product
x below its mean, y above its mean: negative product
x below its mean, y below its mean: positive product
x above its mean, y below its mean: negative product
x at its mean, y above its mean: positive product
questions.explanation: Right of the vertical line means $z_x > 0$; above the horizontal line means $z_y > 0$. Upper right: both positive, so the product is positive. Lower left: both negative, and a negative times a negative is positive. Upper left and lower right: one positive and one negative, so the product is negative. A point exactly on a mean line has a z-score of 0 there, so its product is 0, not positive.

questions.stem: For a data set of $n = 5$ points, the products of the z-scores add to $\sum z_x z_y = 3.2$. The correlation is $r =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $r = \dfrac{1}{n - 1}\sum z_x z_y = \dfrac{3.2}{4} = 0.8$. Dividing by $n = 5$ instead gives 0.64, which is the wrong divisor (the standard deviations behind the z-scores use $n - 1$).

questions.stem: Put the steps for computing $r$ by hand with the formula $r = S_{xy}/\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$ in order.
choices: Find the means $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$
Find each deviation $x - \bar{x}$ and $y - \bar{y}$
Multiply each pair of deviations, and square each deviation
Add them up to get $S_{xy}$, $S_{xx}$ and $S_{yy}$
Divide $S_{xy}$ by $\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$
questions.explanation: Each step needs the one before: deviations need the means, products and squares need the deviations, the sums need the products and squares, and $r$ needs the sums. Example 1 in the lesson follows exactly these steps.

questions.stem: Which of these changes leave the correlation $r$ unchanged? Select all that apply.
choices: Converting every $x$ value from inches to centimeters
Adding 10 to every $y$ value
Swapping which variable is called $x$ and which is called $y$
Multiplying every $y$ value by $-1$
questions.explanation: $r$ is built from z-scores, which don't change when you multiply by a positive constant (inches to centimeters) or add a constant. The formula is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, so swapping them doesn't matter. Multiplying by $-1$ flips the sign of every $z_y$, so $r$ changes sign (its size stays the same).

questions.stem: Match each correlation to the scatterplot it best describes (all the plots have a linear form).
choices: Points fall left to right in a tight band
Points rise left to right in a loose cloud
No visible linear trend
All points exactly on a rising line
Points rise steeply but follow a curve
questions.explanation: The sign gives the direction (negative falls, positive rises) and the size gives the strength: $|r| = 0.95$ is a tight band, 0.6 a moderate loose cloud, 0.05 essentially no linear trend, and $r = 1$ only when every point is on a rising line. A curved pattern isn't described well by any value of $r$.

questions.stem: This is the least-squares line $\hat{y} = 2.6 + 0.8x$ for the training data. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: The training data with the least-squares line. Marker 1 is on the data point (4, 7). Marker 2 is on an open circle on the line directly below it. Marker 3 is on a brace between those two. Marker 4 is on a diamond at (3, 5). Marker 5 is where the line meets the vertical axis. Marker 6 is inside a dashed triangle at the right end of the line with a horizontal side of 1 unit and a vertical side up to the line.

choices: Observed value y
Predicted value ŷ
Residual
Point of means (x̄, ȳ)
Intercept
Slope (rise per 1 unit of run)
Outlier
Extrapolation
questions.explanation: 1 is the data point itself, the observed $y = 7$. 2 is the line's prediction at $x = 4$, $\hat{y} = 5.8$. 3 is the vertical gap between them, the residual $7 - 5.8 = 1.2$. 4 is $(3, 5)$, the point of means, which every least-squares line passes through. 5 is the intercept $a = 2.6$, the predicted $y$ at $x = 0$. 6 is a slope triangle: a run of 1 and a rise of 0.8. No point here is far from the pattern (an outlier), and nothing is predicted outside the data (extrapolation).

questions.stem: A least-squares line has slope $b = 3$, and the data have $\bar{x} = 10$ and $\bar{y} = 50$. The intercept is $a =$ ___. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 50 - 3(10) = 20$, so the line is $\hat{y} = 20 + 3x$. Adding instead of subtracting gives 80.

questions.stem: You have $\bar{x}$, $s_x$, $\bar{y}$, $s_y$ and $r$, and want to predict $y$ for a new $x$ inside the data range. Put the steps in order.
choices: Compute the slope $b = r\,s_y/s_x$
Compute the intercept $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$
Write the line $\hat{y} = a + bx$
Substitute the new $x$ into the line
questions.explanation: The intercept formula uses $b$, so the slope comes first; the line needs both; the prediction needs the line. (Before predicting, check that the new $x$ is inside the range of the data; the stem says it is.)

questions.stem: Which statements are true of every least-squares regression line? Select all that apply.
choices: It passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$
Its slope has the same sign as the correlation $r$
It makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible
It stays the same line if $x$ and $y$ swap roles
It passes through at least two of the data points
questions.explanation: $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ puts $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ on the line; $b = r\,s_y/s_x$ with $s_x, s_y > 0$ gives $b$ the sign of $r$; and minimizing $\sum (y - \hat{y})^2$ is the definition. Swapping $x$ and $y$ gives a different line (slope $r\,s_x/s_y$ for predicting $x$). The line need not pass through any data point; in the training data it passes through none.

questions.stem: For a regression of exam score on hours studied, match each part of $\hat{y} = a + bx$ to its meaning.
choices: Predicted change in score for each extra hour studied
Predicted score for a student who studied 0 hours
Predicted score for a given number of hours
How far a student's actual score is from the prediction
Fraction of the variation in scores explained by hours
questions.explanation: The slope is a rate (points per hour), the intercept is the prediction at $x = 0$, $\hat{y}$ is any prediction, and $y - \hat{y}$ is a residual. The fraction of variation explained is $r^2$, which is not part of the equation.

questions.stem: Each panel shows the same eight points plus one circled point, with the line fitted with it (solid) and without it (dashed). Name the kind of point circled in each panel.

image.alt: Three scatterplots of the same eight points rising along a line from x = 1 to 8. Panel 1: marker 1 on an extra point at x = 4.5, well above the other points; the two fitted lines are nearly the same. Panel 2: marker 2 on an extra point at x = 16 that lies on the trend of the others; the two lines coincide. Panel 3: marker 3 on an extra point at x = 16 far below the trend; the solid line with it is almost flat while the dashed line without it rises steeply.

choices: Outlier with a large residual, not influential
High leverage but following the pattern
Influential point
Point of means
questions.explanation: 1 is far from the line vertically (a large residual) but sits in the middle of the $x$ values, so it barely moves the line: an outlier that is not influential. 2 has an extreme $x$ (high leverage), but it lies on the pattern, so the line hardly changes. 3 has an extreme $x$ and is off the pattern, so it drags the slope from about 0.48 to about 0.01: an influential point. None of them is the point of means.

questions.stem: A regression line is $\hat{y} = 12 + 3x$. A data point has $x = 5$ and $y = 30$. Its residual is ___.
questions.explanation: $\hat{y} = 12 + 3(5) = 27$, so the residual is $y - \hat{y} = 30 - 27 = 3$. The point is 3 units above the line. Computing predicted minus observed gives $-3$, the wrong sign.

questions.stem: Match each residual plot pattern to what it tells you about a straight-line model.
left: Random scatter around zero with even spread
Residuals positive at both ends, negative in the middle
Spread of residuals grows as x increases
One residual far larger than all the others
choices: A line is an appropriate model
The relationship is curved
Predictions are less precise for large x
That point is an outlier
The correlation must be exactly zero
questions.explanation: No pattern means the line captured the form. A U-shape (or upside-down U) means curvature the line missed. A fan means the typical error depends on $x$. A single huge residual marks an outlier. A residual plot of a least-squares fit never tells you that $r = 0$.

questions.stem: A least-squares regression has $r^2 = 0.81$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
choices: The correlation is either $0.9$ or $-0.9$
SSE is 19% of SST
About 81% of the variation in $y$ is accounted for by the linear relationship with $x$
81% of the data points lie on the regression line
A straight line is the right form for these data
questions.explanation: $|r| = \sqrt{0.81} = 0.9$, with the sign of the slope. $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$, so $\text{SSE}/\text{SST} = 0.19$. The fraction of variation explained is 81%. $r^2$ says nothing about how many points are on the line, and a curved pattern can still give a high $r^2$, so only the residual plot can confirm the form.

questions.stem: Put the steps for making a residual plot in order.
choices: Fit the least-squares line to the data
Compute the predicted value ŷ for each data point
Subtract to get each residual y − ŷ
Plot the residuals against x
Look for curves, fans or unusual points
questions.explanation: Predictions need the line, residuals need the predictions, the plot needs the residuals, and you can only read the pattern once the plot exists.

questions.stem: A model fitted to transformed data is $\widehat{\log_{10} y} = 0.5 + 0.25x$. At $x = 6$, the predicted value of $y$ (not of $\log y$) is $\hat{y} =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $\widehat{\log y} = 0.5 + 0.25(6) = 2$, so $\hat{y} = 10^2 = 100$. Answering 2 forgets to back-transform.

questions.stem: Each plot below turned out to be straight with random residuals. Match each to the model it supports for the original data.
left: square root of y against x
choices: Exponential model, y = a·b^x
Power model, y = a·x^p
Linear model, y = a + bx
Square-root model, y = (c + dx)²
Logarithmic model, y = a + b·log x
questions.explanation: $y = ab^x$ becomes $\log y = \log a + x\log b$, linear in $x$. $y = ax^p$ becomes $\log y = \log a + p\log x$, linear in $\log x$. A straight $y$-versus-$x$ plot needs no transformation. A straight $\sqrt{y}$-versus-$x$ plot means $\sqrt{y} = c + dx$, so $y = (c + dx)^2$. A model $y = a + b\log x$ would show up as a straight plot of $y$ against $\log x$, which isn't in the list.

questions.stem: Counts that grow by a roughly constant percent each hour need a prediction for a new hour. Put the steps in order.
choices: Fit a line to $y$ against $x$ and see a curved residual plot
Take $\log_{10}$ of every count
Fit the least-squares line of $\log y$ on $x$
Use the line to predict $\log y$ at the new hour
Raise 10 to that power to predict the count
questions.explanation: The curved residual plot is what tells you to transform; you need the logged values before you can fit to them; the fitted line gives a prediction on the log scale; and back-transforming with $10^{(\cdot)}$ (the inverse of $\log_{10}$) turns it into a count.

questions.stem: For which of these relationships would a plot of $\log y$ against $x$ be close to a straight line? Select all that apply.
choices: Value of a savings account earning 4% interest a year, against years
Amount of a radioactive substance left, against time
Area of a circle, against its radius
Distance traveled at a constant 60 km/h, against hours
questions.explanation: Fixed-percent growth and radioactive decay multiply $y$ by the same factor each unit of time, which is exponential: $\log y$ is linear in $x$. Area $= \pi r^2$ is a power model ($\log y$ is linear in $\log x$, not in $x$), and constant-speed distance is already linear in $y$ itself.

questions.stem: A straight line fitted to the raw bacteria counts in the lesson has residuals of about $+16, 0, -14, -15, -7, +21$ for hours 0 to 5. What do these tell you?
choices: The line is a good fit, because the residuals add to about zero
The relationship is curved: the line is too low at both ends and too high in the middle
Hour 5 is an influential point that should be removed
The counts should be modeled with a power model of $y$ against $\log x$
questions.explanation: Positive residuals mean points above the line, so the line is too low at hours 0 and 5 and too high in between: a systematic curve, the signal to transform. Residuals of any least-squares line add to zero, so that proves nothing. Hour 5 follows the curved pattern rather than breaking it. The log of the counts against hour (not against log hour) turned out to be straight.

questions.stem: Four cells of the transit survey table are highlighted. Name each numbered cell.

image.alt: The transit survey table with rows Under 30, 30 to 50, Over 50 and Total, and columns Train, Bus, Car and Total. Marker 1 is on the cell 30 (under 30, train). Marker 2 is on the cell 60 at the end of the under-30 row. Marker 3 is on the cell 70 at the bottom of the train column. Marker 4 is on the cell 200 in the bottom right corner.

choices: Joint count (one combination of both variables)
Row total (marginal count for age group)
Column total (marginal count for transit mode)
Grand total
Conditional percent
questions.explanation: 1: 30 commuters are both under 30 and train riders, a joint count. 2: 60 is everyone under 30, a row total. 3: 70 is everyone who takes the train, a column total. 4: 200 is everyone surveyed. Totals in the margins give the marginal distributions; every cell in the table is a count, not a percent.

questions.stem: In the transit survey, 25 of the 80 commuters aged 30–50 take the train. What percent of commuters aged 30–50 take the train? ___ % (Give the exact value.)
questions.explanation: The group is the 30–50 commuters, so their row total is the denominator: $25/80 = 0.3125 = 31.25\%$. Dividing by the train total (70) answers a different question (what percent of train riders are 30–50), and dividing by 200 gives the joint percent.

questions.stem: Match each statement about the transit survey to the kind of distribution it comes from.
left: 15% of all 200 commuters are under-30 train riders
35% of all 200 commuters take the train
50% of the 60 under-30 commuters take the train
choices: Joint
Marginal
Conditional
Cumulative
questions.explanation: One cell over the grand total ($30/200$) is joint; a total over the grand total ($70/200$) is marginal; a cell over its group's total ($30/60$) is conditional. A cumulative distribution adds up values in order and doesn't apply to these categories.

questions.stem: Look back at the lesson's data on Hospitals A and B. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: A has the higher survival rate for mild patients
A has the higher survival rate for severe patients
B has the higher survival rate when all patients are combined
A severe patient would do better at B, since B's overall rate is higher
The reversal shows that one of the hospitals' rates was miscalculated
questions.explanation: Mild: A 98.3% vs. B 96.7%. Severe: A 52.5% vs. B 30%. Overall: A 80% vs. B 90%. The overall comparison is distorted because A treats far more severe cases (40% vs. 10%), so a severe patient should look at the severe-patient rates, where A is better. The reversal is Simpson's paradox, real arithmetic and not an error.

questions.stem: Put the steps for deciding whether two categorical variables are associated in order.
choices: Decide which variable defines the groups to compare
Divide each cell by its group's total
Compare the conditional distributions across the groups
State whether the variables are associated
questions.explanation: You need to know the groups before you know which totals are the denominators; the conditional distributions come from those divisions; and the conclusion depends on whether the distributions differ.

questions.stem: For the training data ($\bar{x} = 3$, $\bar{y} = 5$, $S_{xx} = 10$, least-squares line $\hat{y} = 2.6 + 0.8x$ with SSE $= 3.6$), by how much does the SSE of the line $y = 2 + x$ exceed 3.6?
questions.explanation: The line $y = 2 + x$ passes through $(3, 5)$, so the means penalty is 0. The slope penalty is $S_{xx}(b - \hat{b})^2 = 10(1 - 0.8)^2 = 0.4$. Directly: the errors are $0, 1, -1, 1, -1$, so SSE $= 4.0 = 3.6 + 0.4$. 0.04 forgets to multiply by $S_{xx}$, 0.2 is just the slope difference $1 - 0.8$ (not squared or multiplied by $S_{xx}$), and 2.0 multiplies $10 \times 0.2$ without squaring.

questions.stem: A least-squares regression has $\text{SST} = 50$ and $\text{SSE} = 18$. The regression sum of squares is $\text{SSR} =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$, so $\text{SSR} = 50 - 18 = 32$, and $r^2 = 32/50 = 0.64$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the lesson's proof that $r^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ in order.
choices: Show that $\sum (d_i - c)^2$ is smallest when $c$ is the mean of the $d_i$
Conclude that, for any slope $b$, the best intercept is $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$
Substitute that intercept to write SSE as a quadratic in $b$ alone
Complete the square to find the best slope $b = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$
Substitute the best slope to get $\text{SSE} = \text{SST}(1 - r^2)$
questions.explanation: Each step uses the previous one: the fact about the mean gives the intercept, the intercept turns SSE into a function of $b$ only, completing the square finds the best $b$, and the leftover constant is $S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2/S_{xx} = \text{SST}(1 - r^2)$.

questions.stem: Which are always true of the residuals $e_i$ from a least-squares line? Select all that apply.
choices: $\sum e_i = 0$
$\sum (x_i - \bar{x})e_i = 0$
The correlation between the residuals and $x$ is 0
$\sum e_i^2 = \text{SST}$
Every residual has the same sign as the slope
questions.explanation: With $e_i = (y_i - \bar{y}) - \hat{b}(x_i - \bar{x})$: the sum is $0 - \hat{b} \cdot 0 = 0$, and $\sum (x_i - \bar{x})e_i = S_{xy} - \hat{b}S_{xx} = 0$. A zero cross-product sum means zero correlation with $x$. $\sum e_i^2$ is SSE, which is less than SST unless $r = 0$. Residuals have both signs; they add to zero.

questions.stem: The picture splits the point $(4, 7)$'s deviation from the mean of $y$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: The training data with the least-squares line and a dashed horizontal line at y = 5. Near the point (4, 7) are three vertical bars: marker 1 on a purple bar from the dashed line up to the height of the point; marker 2 on an orange bar from the line's fitted value up to the point; marker 3 on a green bar from the dashed line up to the fitted value. Marker 4 is on the dashed horizontal line and marker 5 is on the sloped line near its right end.

choices: Total deviation y − ȳ
Residual y − ŷ
Explained part ŷ − ȳ
Horizontal line at the mean of y
Least-squares line
SD line
Leverage
questions.explanation: The total deviation $7 - 5 = 2$ (1) splits into the explained part $5.8 - 5 = 0.8$ (3), from the mean line (4) up to the least-squares line (5), plus the residual $7 - 5.8 = 1.2$ (2) from the line up to the point. Summed over all points, the squares give $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$.

questions.stem: For the training data, every line through $(3, 5)$ with slope $b$ has $\text{SSE}(b) = 10(b - 0.8)^2 + 3.6$. What is the SSE of the line through $(3, 5)$ with slope 1.3?
questions.explanation: $10(1.3 - 0.8)^2 + 3.6 = 10(0.25) + 3.6 = 6.1$. 2.5 is only the penalty; 4.1 adds $0.5$ without squaring or multiplying by 10; 3.6 is the minimum, reached only at $b = 0.8$.

questions.stem: Completing the square leaves the minimum value $\text{SSE}_{\min} = S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$. Which expression is equal to it?
choices: $\text{SST} \cdot r^2$
$\text{SST}(1 - r)$
$\text{SST}(1 - r^2)$
questions.explanation: Factor out $S_{yy}$: $S_{yy}\left(1 - \dfrac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}\right) = S_{yy}(1 - r^2)$, and $S_{yy} = \text{SST}$. $\text{SST} \cdot r^2$ is SSR, the explained part. $1 - r$ forgets to square, and $S_{xx}$ is the spread of $x$, not of $y$.

questions.stem: A regression on $n = 27$ points has $s_y = 4$ and $r = 0.8$. What is the standard deviation of the residuals $s$?
questions.explanation: $\text{SSE} = (n - 1)s_y^2(1 - r^2) = 26 \times 16 \times 0.36 = 149.76$, so $s = \sqrt{149.76/25} \approx 2.45$. $s_y\sqrt{1 - r^2} = 2.40$ effectively divides by $n - 1$; dividing by $n$ gives 2.36; 5.99 forgets the square root.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its description.
choices: Sum of squared deviations of y from its mean
Sum of squared residuals
Sum of squared deviations of the fitted values from the mean of y
SSR divided by SST
Sum of the residuals (always zero)
questions.explanation: SST measures total variation, SSE what the line leaves unexplained, and SSR what it explains, with $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$. Their ratio $\text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ is $r^2$. The plain sum of residuals is zero, which is why it can't measure fit.

questions.stem: Why does $s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n - 2)}$ divide by $n - 2$?
choices: Because two data points always lie exactly on the line
Because the residuals must satisfy two equations, so only $n - 2$ of them are free to vary
Because $n - 2$ makes $s$ smaller than $s_y$
Because the first and last points are excluded from the fit
questions.explanation: The residuals satisfy $\sum e_i = 0$ and $\sum (x_i - \bar{x})e_i = 0$, one equation for each estimated quantity (intercept and slope). Given any $n - 2$ residuals the other two are forced (when their $x$ values differ), so there are $n - 2$ degrees of freedom. No data points are excluded, and the line needn't pass through any data point.

questions.stem: Who first published the method of least squares, and when?
choices: Francis Galton, in 1886
Karl Pearson, in 1896
Carl Friedrich Gauss, in 1795
Adrien-Marie Legendre, in 1805
questions.explanation: Legendre published it in 1805 in a work on comet orbits. Gauss published his account in 1809 and said he had used the method since 1795, which is not the same as publishing it. Galton and Pearson came later and applied regression and correlation to heredity.

questions.stem: Compared with the least-squares line, the least absolute deviations line (which minimizes $\sum |y - \hat{y}|$)
choices: is more resistant to outliers but has no simple formula
always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$
gives the same line whenever the data have no outliers
has the decomposition $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$
questions.explanation: Like the median compared with the mean, absolute deviations are less affected by a far-off point, but the line must be found by an algorithm and can be non-unique. Passing through the point of means and the sum-of-squares decomposition are properties of least squares. The two lines usually differ even without outliers.

questions.stem: For a list of numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$, the sum $\sum (d_i - c)^2$ is smallest when the constant $c$ is the ___ of the list.
questions.explanation: $\sum (d_i - c)^2 = \sum (d_i - \bar{d})^2 + n(\bar{d} - c)^2$, and the second term is zero only when $c = \bar{d}$. (The median minimizes $\sum |d_i - c|$ instead.)

questions.stem: A data set has $S_{xx} = 40$ and least-squares slope $\hat{b} = 1.5$. A line through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ with slope 1.0 has an SSE that exceeds the minimum by how much?
questions.explanation: The slope penalty is $S_{xx}(b - \hat{b})^2 = 40(1.0 - 1.5)^2 = 40 \times 0.25 = 10$. The line goes through the point of means, so there is no intercept penalty. 20 forgets to square the 0.5; 0.25 forgets to multiply by $S_{xx}$; 0.5 is just the slope difference.

questions.stem: Galton found that a child's height deviation from the average was, on average, about two-thirds of the mid-parent's deviation. Mid-parents 4.5 inches above average would have children averaging about how far above average?
choices: 4.5 inches
6.75 inches
3 inches
1.5 inches
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 4.5 = 3$ inches. The children are tall, but less extreme than their parents. 6.75 multiplies by $\tfrac32$ (moving away from the mean), and 1.5 is the one-third that was lost.

questions.stem: A test and a retest both have mean 70 and SD 10, with $r = 0.6$. A student scored 90 on the test. The least-squares prediction of the retest score is ___.
questions.explanation: With equal SDs, $\hat{y} = 70 + 0.6(90 - 70) = 70 + 12 = 82$. In z-scores: $z = 2$, so $\hat{z} = 0.6 \times 2 = 1.2$, which is $70 + 1.2 \times 10 = 82$.

questions.stem: Which of these could be explained by regression to the mean alone, with no real cause? Select all that apply.
choices: Students who scored lowest on a first test score higher on average on a second test
A rookie with an outstanding first season has a less outstanding second season
Patients who join a study when their symptoms are at their worst feel better a month later
In a randomized experiment, the treatment group improves far more than an equally chosen control group
After five heads in a row, a fair coin is more likely to land tails
questions.explanation: The first three all select an extreme first measurement, and luck that doesn't repeat pulls the second measurement toward the mean. In the randomized experiment, the control group regresses too, so a much larger gain in the treatment group is evidence of a real effect. The coin claim is the gambler's fallacy: independent flips have no memory, and regression is about predictions from imperfectly correlated measurements, not about chance "evening out."

questions.stem: A school wants to know whether a tutoring program helps its weakest readers, without being fooled by regression to the mean. Put the steps of a fair study in order.
choices: Give all students a reading pretest
Select the students who score below a cutoff
Randomly assign the selected students to tutoring or no tutoring
Give both groups a reading posttest
Compare the average gains of the two groups
questions.explanation: Selection needs pretest scores; random assignment happens among the selected students so that both groups are equally extreme and regress by the same amount on average; the posttest comes after the program; and only the difference in gains is credited to tutoring.

questions.stem: Two variables have $r = 0.5$ and $s_x = s_y = 10$. Match each line, drawn on $y$-versus-$x$ axes, to its slope.
left: Least-squares line for predicting y from x
Least-squares line for predicting x from y
questions.explanation: $y$ on $x$: $r\,s_y/s_x = 0.5$. SD line: $s_y/s_x = 1$. $x$ on $y$ has slope $r\,s_x/s_y = 0.5$ as a function of $y$; drawn on $y$-versus-$x$ axes its slope is $1/0.5 = 2$. The SD line lies between the two regression lines. 0.25 is $r^2$, the product of the two regression slopes $0.5 \times 0.5$.

questions.stem: The least-squares slope for predicting $y$ from $x$ is 2, and the slope for predicting $x$ from $y$ is 0.32. What is $r$?
questions.explanation: The two slopes multiply to $r^2$: $2 \times 0.32 = 0.64$, so $|r| = 0.8$, and $r$ is positive because both slopes are positive. 0.64 is $r^2$; 1.6 is $2 \times 0.8$.

questions.stem: Because children of very tall parents are on average less tall than their parents, a student concludes that heights will be much less spread out in a few generations. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; regression to the mean shrinks the spread every generation
The spread will shrink only if $r$ is negative
Predictions are pulled toward the mean, but actual heights are prediction plus scatter, so the spread stays about the same
Regression to the mean applies only to test scores, not to heights
questions.explanation: The line pulls predictions in, but individuals scatter around their predictions, and that scatter refills the tails: some children of average parents turn out very tall. The effect also runs backward (tall children's parents are, on average, less tall than they are), which a real shrinking force couldn't do.

questions.stem: Flight instructors noticed that after they praised an excellent landing, the next landing was usually worse, and after they criticized a poor one, the next was usually better. What is the best explanation?
choices: Praise makes pilots overconfident and criticism makes them careful
The instructors judged the landings inconsistently
Pilots deliberately alternate good and bad landings
Landings vary partly by chance, so an extreme landing is usually followed by a less extreme one whatever the instructor says
questions.explanation: This is the regression fallacy that Daniel Kahneman describes. Both patterns are exactly what regression to the mean predicts when performance is skill plus luck, even if praise and criticism have no effect at all. Testing the psychological explanation would need a comparison, such as randomly varying the feedback.

questions.stem: Test A has test–retest correlation 0.9 and Test B has 0.5 (same mean and SD on each pair of sittings). Students who scored 2 SDs above the mean the first time take each test again. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both groups are predicted to score 2 SDs above the mean again
Test A shows more regression, because its correlation is higher
Test B shows more regression: its prediction is 1 SD above the mean, versus 1.8 SDs for A
Neither test shows regression, because the students are the same
questions.explanation: $\hat{z} = r z$: Test A predicts $0.9 \times 2 = 1.8$ SDs, Test B $0.5 \times 2 = 1$ SD. The less reliable test (more luck in each score) shows more regression. Only $r = 1$ would give no regression.

questions.stem: Fathers' and sons' heights have $r = 0.5$, with equal means and SDs. A son is 2 SDs above the mean. Using the least-squares line for predicting fathers from sons, his father is predicted to be
choices: 2 SDs above the mean
4 SDs above the mean
at the mean
1 SD above the mean
questions.explanation: Predicting in the other direction also pulls toward the mean: $\hat{z} = 0.5 \times 2 = 1$. Regression works both ways, which is how Galton realized it wasn't a biological force. 4 SDs comes from inverting the son-on-father line instead of using the father-on-son line.

questions.stem: Two variables have $r = 0.75$. An individual has $z_x = 2$. The least-squares line predicts $\hat{z}_y =$ ___.
questions.explanation: In standard units the line is $\hat{z}_y = r\,z_x = 0.75 \times 2 = 1.5$: half an SD closer to the mean than the predictor.

questions.stem: A test and retest both have mean 100 and SD 15, with $r = 0.6$. Students chosen because they averaged 72 on the test go through a program, then average 84 on the retest. What retest average would regression to the mean alone predict?
questions.explanation: $100 + 0.6(72 - 100) = 100 - 16.8 = 83.2$. So regression alone explains about 11.2 of the 12-point gain, leaving about 0.8 points that the program might explain, and only a control group could confirm even that. 88.8 uses $1 - r = 0.4$ in place of $r$; 72.0 assumes no regression at all ($r = 1$), and 100.0 assumes complete regression ($r = 0$).

questions.stem: Which describes the SD line of a scatterplot with $r > 0$?
choices: It passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ with slope $s_y/s_x$ and is steeper than the least-squares line of $y$ on $x$
It is the least-squares line for predicting $y$ from $x$
It passes through the origin with slope $r$
It is horizontal at $\bar{y}$, one SD above the mean
questions.explanation: The SD line rises one SD of $y$ per SD of $x$ through the point of means, along the long direction of the cloud. The least-squares line has slope $r\,s_y/s_x$, which is flatter when $0 < r < 1$. Slope $r$ through the origin is the regression line in z-scores, not the SD line.

questions.stem: In a cohort study, 30 of 200 exposed people and 10 of 200 unexposed people developed a condition. What is the relative risk (exposed ÷ unexposed)?
questions.explanation: Risks: $30/200 = 0.15$ and $10/200 = 0.05$, so $\text{RR} = 0.15/0.05 = 3$. 0.10 is the risk difference; 3.35 is the odds ratio $(30 \times 190)/(170 \times 10)$; 0.33 divides the wrong way.

questions.stem: A 2×2 table has exposed: 20 with the outcome, 80 without; unexposed: 10 with the outcome, 90 without. The odds ratio is ___.
questions.explanation: $\text{OR} = \dfrac{ad}{bc} = \dfrac{20 \times 90}{80 \times 10} = \dfrac{1800}{800} = 2.25$. The relative risk is $0.20/0.10 = 2$; the odds ratio is farther from 1, as it always is.

questions.stem: Match each measure to how it is computed.
choices: Risk in the exposed minus risk in the unexposed
Risk in the exposed divided by risk in the unexposed
Probability of the event divided by probability it doesn't happen
Odds in the exposed divided by odds in the unexposed
Cell count divided by the grand total
questions.explanation: Risk difference and relative risk compare risks (proportions) by subtraction and division; odds are $p/(1 - p)$; the odds ratio divides two odds, $ad/bc$ in the 2×2 table. A cell over the grand total is a joint proportion.

questions.stem: A case-control study chose 300 people with a disease and 600 without, then recorded past exposure. Which can be estimated directly from its table? Select all that apply.
choices: The odds ratio
The odds of exposure among the cases
The risk of the disease among exposed people in the population
The proportion of the population that has the disease
questions.explanation: The researchers fixed the numbers of cases and controls, so any "risk" or disease proportion from the table reflects that choice (here one-third), not the population. Odds of exposure within the cases or within the controls are real, and the odds ratio $ad/bc$ doesn't depend on how many cases and controls were sampled.

questions.stem: Two hospitals are compared using direct standardization with a standard population that is 70% mild and 30% severe. Put the steps in order.
choices: Split each hospital's patients into mild and severe cases
Compute each hospital's survival rate within each stratum
Multiply each stratum rate by the standard share of that stratum
Add the products to get each hospital's adjusted rate
Compare the two adjusted rates
questions.explanation: Stratum rates need the split, weighting needs the stratum rates, the adjusted rate is the sum of the weighted rates, and the comparison needs both adjusted rates.

questions.stem: An event has probability 0.2. What are its odds?
questions.explanation: $\text{odds} = p/(1 - p) = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25$, "1 to 4." 4 is the odds against the event, and 0.8 is the probability it doesn't happen.

questions.stem: A headline says a food additive "triples the risk" of a rare illness. The risk rises from 1 in 50,000 to 3 in 50,000. What is the risk difference?
choices: 1 in 3
questions.explanation: $3/50{,}000 - 1/50{,}000 = 2/50{,}000 = 0.00004$: two extra cases per 50,000 people. The relative risk is 3 (a 200% increase), which sounds far more alarming. Report both.

questions.stem: In which situation is an odds ratio a good approximation of the relative risk?
choices: When the outcome is common in both groups
Whenever the study is a randomized experiment
When the outcome is rare in both groups
Only when the odds ratio equals 1
questions.explanation: $\text{OR} = \text{RR} \times \dfrac{1 - p_2}{1 - p_1}$. When both risks are small, that last fraction is close to 1. For common outcomes the two can differ a lot whatever the study design. They are exactly equal only at 1, but approximately equal much more widely.

questions.stem: A hospital's survival rate is 90% for mild cases and 50% for severe cases, and 30% of its patients are severe. What is its overall survival rate?
questions.explanation: The overall rate is a weighted average: $0.7(0.90) + 0.3(0.50) = 0.63 + 0.15 = 0.78$. 70% is the unweighted average of 90% and 50%; 62% swaps the weights.

questions.stem: In the 1986 kidney stone study, open surgery had higher success rates than the keyhole procedure for small stones and for large stones, yet a lower success rate overall. Why?
choices: The keyhole procedure was used much more often on small stones, which are easier to treat
Open surgery was used much more often on small stones
The overall rates were computed with the wrong denominators
The study had more keyhole patients than open-surgery patients
questions.explanation: About 77% of keyhole patients had small stones versus about 25% of open-surgery patients. Small stones succeed more often with either treatment, so the keyhole procedure's overall rate is weighted toward the easy cases: Simpson's paradox with stone size as the lurking variable. Each treatment had 350 patients, and the overall rates (289/350 and 273/350) are correct.

questions.stem: The odds of an event are 3 (that is, 3 to 1). Its probability is ___. (Give a decimal or fraction.)
questions.explanation: $p = \dfrac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75$. Check: $0.75/0.25 = 3$.

questions.stem: After standardizing for age, Region X has a lower death rate than Region Y. What can you conclude?
choices: Living in Region X causes people to live longer
Differences in age structure don't explain the gap, but other lurking variables still might
The crude death rates must also favor Region X
Region X's population is younger than Region Y's
questions.explanation: Standardization removes the effect of the variable you stratified on, here age, and nothing else. Income, smoking or health care could still differ. The crude rates can point either way (that's why standardization was needed), and the adjusted comparison says nothing about which population is younger.

questions.stem: In the lesson's case-control example, 120 of 200 cases and 120 of 400 controls were exposed, giving an odds ratio of 3.5. If the researchers had sampled 800 controls with the same exposure rate instead, the odds ratio would be
choices: impossible to compute
questions.explanation: With 240 exposed and 560 unexposed controls, $\text{OR} = (120 \times 560)/(80 \times 240) = 3.5$. Multiplying the whole controls column by 2 puts a factor of 2 on the top and the bottom of $ad/bc$, which cancels. 1.75 and 7 come from dividing or multiplying by the factor of 2 instead of letting it cancel. The "risk among the exposed" would change, which is why case-control studies report odds ratios.

questions.stem: Each numbered panel shows the same population of 40 individuals, with the chosen ones shaded dark. Name the sampling method in each panel.

image.alt: Four panels of 40 dots. Panel 1: 8 dark dots scattered with no pattern. Panel 2: four colored rows of 10 dots with 2 dark dots in every row. Panel 3: eight dashed boxes of 5 dots, with every dot dark in 2 of the boxes. Panel 4: every 5th dot dark, starting from the 3rd, forming two columns.

choices: Simple random sample
Stratified random sample
Cluster sample
Systematic sample
Convenience sample
Voluntary response sample
questions.explanation: 1: chosen dots have no pattern, as in a simple random sample. 2: the rows are strata (similar individuals), and a few are chosen at random from every row, a stratified random sample. 3: whole groups (clusters) are chosen and everyone in them is included, a cluster sample. 4: every 5th individual after a random start, a systematic sample. Convenience and voluntary response samples don't use chance, so a picture can't tell you who would be chosen.

questions.stem: The actual list of individuals from which a sample is drawn, such as a list of registered voters or student ID numbers, is called the ___.
questions.explanation: That list is the sampling frame. If it leaves out part of the population, the survey suffers from undercoverage, and no sampling method applied to the frame can fix it.

questions.stem: Put the steps of taking a simple random sample in order.
choices: Define the population you want to learn about
Build a sampling frame that lists its members
Number the individuals in the frame from 1 to N
Generate random numbers, skipping repeats and numbers outside 1 to N, until n distinct labels are chosen
Contact and measure the chosen individuals
questions.explanation: You must know the population before you can list it, and the list must exist before it can be numbered. Random numbers then pick n distinct labels, and only then are the chosen individuals measured.

questions.stem: Match each survey problem to the kind of bias it causes.
left: An online survey of a town cannot reach residents without internet access
Only 18% of the randomly chosen households return the questionnaire
Students asked face to face by their teacher whether they have cheated mostly say no
A radio station invites listeners to text in their votes
choices: Undercoverage
Nonresponse bias
Response bias
Voluntary response bias
Sampling variability
questions.explanation: Missing internet users are left out of the frame (undercoverage). Chosen households that don't answer cause nonresponse bias. Answers distorted by who is asking are response bias. People who choose to text in form a voluntary response sample. Sampling variability is chance variation between random samples, not bias.

questions.stem: Which of these are random sampling methods? Select all that apply.
choices: Stratified random sample
Cluster sample with clusters chosen at random
Convenience sample
Systematic sample with a random start
Voluntary response sample
questions.explanation: Stratified, cluster and systematic samples all use chance to decide who is chosen (an SRS within each stratum, a random choice of clusters, a random starting point). Convenience and voluntary response samples let the researcher's ease or the respondents' own choice decide, so they are not random.

questions.stem: A polling firm doubles its random sample from 500 to 1,000 people, still dialing only landline numbers. What happens? Select all that apply.
choices: Sampling variability decreases
Undercoverage of people without landlines is removed
Estimates from repeated samples would cluster more tightly
The center of the estimates moves to the true population value
questions.explanation: A larger random sample varies less from sample to sample, so repeated estimates cluster more tightly. But the frame still leaves out people without landlines, so the bias stays: the estimates cluster tightly around the wrong value, like the high bias, low variability target.

questions.stem: This outline shows the rail-lubricant experiment from the lesson. Name each numbered part of the design.

image.alt: An outline: 40 rail curves split into 20 sharp curves and 20 gentle curves. Each of those leads to a blank box, which splits into two boxes of 10 curves, which both lead to one blank box at the bottom.

choices: Block of similar units
Random assignment
Treatment group
Comparison of responses within a block
Random sample from a population
Placebo group
questions.explanation: 1: the 20 gentle curves are a block, units alike in a way that affects wear. 2: inside each block, chance decides which curves get which lubricant. 3: each set of 10 curves receives one lubricant, a treatment group. 4: wear is compared within the block, so the sharp/gentle difference doesn't blur the comparison. The curves were not randomly sampled from a population, and no placebo is involved.

questions.stem: In a randomized block design, units that are similar in a way expected to affect the response are grouped together, and each group is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Each group is a block. Treatments are then randomly assigned separately within each block, and treatments are compared within blocks.

questions.stem: Put the steps of carrying out a randomized block design in order.
choices: Identify a variable expected to affect the response
Sort the units into blocks according to that variable
Randomly assign the treatments separately within each block
Apply the treatments and measure the response
Compare the treatments within each block, then combine the results
questions.explanation: You need the blocking variable before you can form blocks, and randomization happens after blocking, inside each block. Responses can only be compared once treatments have been applied and measured.

questions.stem: Match each feature of a well-designed experiment to its purpose.
choices: Makes treatment groups similar before treatment, in measured and unmeasured ways
Lets chance differences between groups average out
Keeps expectations and measurement the same in every group
Removes variation due to a known variable from the comparison
Lets results generalize to a larger population
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances groups; replication gives enough units for chance to even out; double-blinding equalizes expectations and keeps measurement unbiased; blocking compares like with like. Generalizing to a population needs random sampling, which is not one of these.

questions.stem: In the two-factor tomato experiment of Example 1 (fertilizer: none, low, high; watering: daily, every other day), which of these are treatments? Select all that apply.
choices: Low fertilizer, watered daily
High fertilizer
No fertilizer, watered every other day
Fruit weight after 10 weeks
questions.explanation: In a multifactor experiment a treatment is a combination of one level of each factor, so "low fertilizer, watered daily" and "no fertilizer, watered every other day" are treatments. "High fertilizer" is only a level of one factor, and fruit weight is the response variable.

questions.stem: An observational study finds that moderate wine drinkers have less heart disease. Give the role of each numbered variable.

image.alt: Three boxes: Income at the top, with arrows to Moderate wine drinking at lower left and Heart disease at lower right; a dashed two-headed arrow labeled observed association joins the two lower boxes.

choices: Confounding variable
Explanatory variable
Response variable
Treatment
Experimental unit
questions.explanation: Wine drinking is the explanatory variable and heart disease the response. Income is related to wine drinking and also affects heart health, so it is a confounding variable. Nothing was imposed in this observational study, so there are no treatments or experimental units.

questions.stem: A variable that is associated with the explanatory variable and also affects the response, so that their effects cannot be separated, is called a ___ variable.
questions.explanation: This is a confounding variable: it offers an alternative explanation for the association. "Lurking variable" is a close cousin that stresses the variable wasn't measured in the study.

questions.stem: Match each study to its type.
left: Researchers review ten years of hospital records on patients’ coffee intake and heart attacks
5,000 teenagers are enrolled now, and their screen time and grades are tracked for four years
200 people with a rare disease and 400 similar people without it are asked about past exposures
Volunteers are randomly given a new or a standard sunscreen, and sunburns are recorded
choices: Retrospective study of existing records
Prospective study
Case-control study
Randomized experiment
Matched pairs experiment
questions.explanation: Looking back through existing records is retrospective; enrolling people and following them forward is prospective; starting from people with and without the outcome is case-control; randomly assigning sunscreens is an experiment. Nobody receives both treatments or is paired, so no matched pairs design is described.

questions.stem: Sixty volunteer employees at one company are randomly assigned to standing or regular desks, and the standing-desk group reports significantly less back pain. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.
choices: The standing desks caused less back pain for these volunteers
Standing desks would reduce back pain for all office workers in the country
A cause-and-effect conclusion is possible because desks were randomly assigned
Only an association can be concluded because the subjects were volunteers
questions.explanation: Random assignment supports cause and effect, so the desks caused the difference for these volunteers. The volunteers were not a random sample of office workers, so generalizing to everyone is not justified. Being volunteers limits generalization, not causation.

questions.stem: A stratum of 12,000 people is sampled with 300 respondents. Each respondent’s sampling weight is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Weight $= N_h/n_h = 12{,}000/300 = 40$: each respondent stands for 40 people in the stratum.

questions.stem: Region A has 30,000 households and Region B 20,000. A survey samples 150 households in each: 60% in A and 30% in B say yes. Estimate the proportion of all households that would say yes.
questions.explanation: Weight each region's result by its share of households: $0.6(0.60) + 0.4(0.30) = 0.36 + 0.12 = 0.48$. The unweighted figure $(90 + 45)/300 = 0.45$ treats the regions as equal in size; $0.42$ swaps the shares; $0.60$ is Region A alone.

questions.stem: A survey oversamples a small stratum. Why is the plain average of all responses usually biased?
choices: Oversampling makes the small stratum’s answers less accurate
The small stratum makes up a larger share of the sample than of the population, so its answers count too much
Plain averages are always biased for stratified samples, even with proportional allocation
The large stratum is left out of the sample
questions.explanation: Oversampling gives the small stratum more than its population share of the sample. Unweighted, its answers pull the estimate toward that stratum's results. With proportional allocation every weight is equal, so the plain average is fine; oversampling makes the small stratum's own estimate more precise, not less.

questions.stem: For the survey in which Region A (60% of households) had $\hat{p}_A = 0.60$ and Region B (40%) had $\hat{p}_B = 0.30$, with 150 sampled in each, find the standard error of the stratified estimate.
choices: About $0.039$
About $0.055$
About $0.028$
questions.explanation: $SE = \sqrt{0.6^2 \cdot \dfrac{0.6(0.4)}{150} + 0.4^2 \cdot \dfrac{0.3(0.7)}{150}} = \sqrt{0.000576 + 0.000224} = \sqrt{0.0008} \approx 0.028$. Using $W_h$ instead of $W_h^2$ gives about 0.039; leaving out the weights gives about 0.055; 0.0008 is the variance before taking the square root.

questions.stem: Stratum 1 has 400 units with standard deviation 15; stratum 2 has 600 units with standard deviation 5. With Neyman allocation, how should a sample of 60 be split?
choices: 24 from stratum 1, 36 from stratum 2
30 from each stratum
45 from stratum 1, 15 from stratum 2
40 from stratum 1, 20 from stratum 2
questions.explanation: $N_h S_h$: $400(15) = 6{,}000$ and $600(5) = 3{,}000$, total 9,000. Stratum 1 gets $60 \times 6/9 = 40$ and stratum 2 gets 20. 24 and 36 is proportional allocation (ignores the SDs); 45 and 15 uses the SDs alone (ignores the stratum sizes).

questions.stem: Compared with proportional allocation, Neyman allocation puts a larger share of the sample in strata that
choices: are smaller
have less variability within them
have more variability within them
are cheaper to sample, regardless of variability
questions.explanation: Neyman allocation sets $n_h \propto N_h S_h$, so for a stratum of a given size, a larger standard deviation earns a larger sample. Where everyone is alike, a few observations suffice. Cost enters only through the extended rule $n_h \propto N_h S_h/\sqrt{c_h}$, and it doesn't override variability.

questions.stem: A survey takes everyone in 40 clusters of 30 people ($n = 1{,}200$). The intraclass correlation is about $0.10$. Find the approximate design effect and effective sample size.
choices: $\text{deff} \approx 3.9$; about 308
$\text{deff} \approx 4.0$; about 300
$\text{deff} \approx 2.9$; about 414
$\text{deff} \approx 3.9$; about 4,680
questions.explanation: $\text{deff} \approx 1 + (m - 1)\rho = 1 + 29(0.10) = 3.9$, and $n/\text{deff} = 1200/3.9 \approx 308$. Using $m$ instead of $m - 1$ gives 4.0; forgetting the 1 gives 2.9; multiplying instead of dividing gives 4,680.

questions.stem: Why do cluster samples usually have a design effect greater than 1?
choices: Clusters are always smaller than strata
Cluster samples are not random
Clusters are chosen to be as different from each other as possible
Members of the same cluster tend to be alike, so each extra member adds less new information
questions.explanation: People in one classroom or block share influences, so a second person from the same cluster partly repeats the first. That positive intraclass correlation inflates the variance compared with an SRS of the same size. Cluster samples are random when clusters are chosen at random.

questions.stem: Renters are 50% of a city’s adults but only 30% of a poll’s 300 respondents. Support for a rent-control measure is 80% among renters and 50% among owners in the poll. What is the post-stratified estimate of support?
questions.explanation: Weight each group by its population share: $0.5(0.80) + 0.5(0.50) = 0.65$. The unweighted figure is $(72 + 105)/300 = 59\%$. Using the sample shares in reverse ($0.7(0.80) + 0.3(0.50)$) gives 71%.

questions.stem: A poll is weighted so that its age groups match the census. Which problem can this weighting NOT fix?
choices: Within each age group, the people who answered hold different opinions from those who did not
Younger adults are underrepresented among respondents
Older adults are overrepresented among respondents
The sample’s age mix differs from the population’s
questions.explanation: Post-stratification fixes imbalance on the weighting variable (age) only. If responders differ from nonresponders within an age group, for example in interest in the topic, the weighted estimate is still biased.

questions.stem: The 1936 Literary Digest poll got about 2.4 million ballots back and still predicted the wrong winner. What is its main lesson?
choices: Mail surveys are always less accurate than phone surveys
A huge sample from a slanted frame with heavy nonresponse can still be badly wrong
Its sample was too small to predict a national election
Polls should never use lists of telephone or car owners, whatever the year
questions.explanation: Its frame overrepresented better-off households and fewer than a quarter of those mailed a ballot returned it. Bias comes from how individuals are chosen and who responds, and a bigger sample doesn't shrink it. The problem was not sample size.

questions.stem: Which statements about sampling weights are true? Select all that apply.
choices: With proportional allocation, weighted and unweighted estimates are equal
A sampling weight equals the stratum size divided by the number sampled from it
Weighting removes all nonresponse bias
Oversampling a small stratum makes that stratum’s own estimate more precise
A larger weight means the researchers consider that person’s opinion more important
questions.explanation: Proportional allocation gives every respondent the same weight $N/n$, so weighting changes nothing. A weight is $N_h/n_h$, the number of people a respondent represents, not a measure of importance. Oversampling gives the small stratum more observations, so its own estimate is more precise. Weighting only fixes imbalance on the weighting variables.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Number of population members a respondent represents
Variance under the actual design divided by variance under an SRS of the same size
Size of an SRS that would give the same precision
How alike members of the same cluster are
Reweighting respondents to match known population shares
Taking a larger share of a small stratum than its population share
questions.explanation: These are the definitions from the lesson. The extra description, taking more than a stratum's share of the sample, is oversampling.

questions.stem: Put the steps of planning a survey with Neyman allocation in order.
choices: Estimate each stratum’s standard deviation from a pilot study or past survey
Multiply each stratum’s size by its standard deviation
Divide each product by the sum of all the products
Multiply by the total sample size and round to whole numbers
Take a simple random sample of that size within each stratum
questions.explanation: Neyman allocation is $n_h = n \cdot N_h S_h / \sum N_k S_k$: the standard deviations must be estimated first, then the products formed, turned into fractions, scaled by $n$, and finally the samples drawn.

questions.stem: A survey uses clusters of 11 people with intraclass correlation $0.08$. Its approximate design effect is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\text{deff} \approx 1 + (m - 1)\rho = 1 + 10(0.08) = 1.8$. The survey's variance is about 1.8 times that of an SRS of the same size.

questions.stem: A $2 \times 2$ experiment crosses temperature (low, high) with catalyst (A, B). Mean yields (made-up data): low temperature with catalyst A 50, low with B 56, high with A 60, high with B 74. What is the main effect of temperature?
questions.explanation: Average over catalysts: high $(60 + 74)/2 = 67$, low $(50 + 56)/2 = 53$, so the main effect is $67 - 53 = 14$. 10 is the catalyst's main effect; 24 compares only the extreme cells; 8 is the interaction.

questions.stem: Same experiment. Mean yields (made-up data): low temperature with catalyst A 50, low with B 56, high with A 60, high with B 74. Measured as a difference of differences (effect of catalyst at high temperature minus its effect at low temperature), the interaction is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Catalyst effect at high temperature: $74 - 60 = 14$; at low: $56 - 50 = 6$. Interaction $= 14 - 6 = 8$. (From the other side: temperature adds 10 with A and 18 with B, and $18 - 10 = 8$ again.)

questions.stem: Same experiment. Mean yields (made-up data): low temperature with catalyst A 50, low with B 56, high with A 60, high with B 74. What is the main effect of switching from catalyst A to catalyst B?
questions.explanation: Average over temperatures: B $(56 + 74)/2 = 65$, A $(50 + 60)/2 = 55$, so the main effect is 10. 6 and 14 are the simple effects at low and high temperature; 18 is $74 - 56$, temperature's effect with catalyst B.

questions.stem: On an interaction plot of treatment means, the two lines are parallel. This means
choices: neither factor has any effect
the two factors are confounded
there is no interaction: each factor’s effect is the same at both levels of the other
the experiment was not randomized
questions.explanation: Parallel lines mean the gap between them (one factor's effect) is the same at every level of the other factor, which is the definition of no interaction. The factors can still have large main effects. (With real data, lines are never exactly parallel because of chance.)

questions.stem: Mean test scores: small class with lecture 70, small with discussion 80, large with lecture 75, large with discussion 65. Which summary is best?
choices: Discussion helps in small classes (+10) and hurts in large ones (−10), so report the simple effects
Teaching method has no effect, because its main effect is 0
Class size has no effect, because its main effect is 0
There is no interaction, because the main effect of method is 0
questions.explanation: The main effect of method is $(80 + 65)/2 - (70 + 75)/2 = 0$, but the simple effects are $+10$ and $-10$: the lines cross. With a strong interaction, main effects mislead. Class size's main effect is $(75 + 65)/2 - (70 + 80)/2 = -5$, not 0.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of studying factors one at a time instead of in a factorial design?
choices: It requires random assignment, which factorial designs avoid
It always needs more factors
It cannot use a control group
It can’t detect interactions, so it can mispredict combinations it never tried
questions.explanation: One-factor-at-a-time studies never run the combinations, so an interaction goes unseen and predictions for untried combinations can be wrong. They also use units less efficiently. Both designs should randomize.

questions.stem: In the temperature and catalyst experiment, the true mean yields are 50 (low, A), 56 (low, B), 60 (high, A) and 74 (high, B). A one-factor-at-a-time study starts at low temperature with catalyst A, varies temperature (keeping A), then varies the catalyst (keeping low temperature). What does it predict for high temperature with catalyst B?
choices: 74, exactly right
66, which is 8 below the true 74
70, which is 4 below the true 74
80, which is 6 above the true 74
questions.explanation: Temperature alone: $60 - 50 = +10$. Catalyst alone: $56 - 50 = +6$. Prediction: $50 + 10 + 6 = 66$, but the true mean is 74. The gap of 8 is exactly the interaction, which OFAT can't see.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to test 6 factors, each at 2 levels, in a full factorial design. How many treatments are needed?
questions.explanation: A full factorial uses every combination: $2^6 = 64$. Adding levels gives 12; $6^2 = 36$ squares the wrong number; 32 is $2^5$. Designs this large are why fractional factorial designs exist.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts interaction and confounding?
choices: They are two names for the same thing
Interaction means one factor’s effect depends on another factor; confounding means an outside variable’s effect is mixed up with a factor’s
Interaction can occur only in observational studies
Confounding means the interaction plot’s lines cross
questions.explanation: Interaction is a real feature of how the response behaves, and a balanced factorial experiment is designed to measure it. Confounding is a design flaw: the effect of an unbalanced outside variable can't be separated from the factor's effect.

questions.stem: A $2 \times 2$ factorial experiment uses 48 subjects, 12 per treatment. When estimating the main effect of factor A, how many subjects are compared with how many?
choices: 12 with 12
48 with 48
24 with 24
6 with 6
questions.explanation: Each level of A includes two treatments, $2 \times 12 = 24$ subjects, so every subject contributes. The same 48 subjects, regrouped, give 24 with 24 for factor B too.

questions.stem: Which statements about a balanced $2 \times 2$ factorial experiment with several units per treatment are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Every unit helps estimate both main effects
It can detect an interaction between the factors
If there is an interaction, both main effects must equal 0
Units should be randomly assigned to all four treatment combinations
An interaction means the two factors are confounded
questions.explanation: Each unit sits at one level of A and one level of B, so it counts in both main-effect comparisons, and having all four combinations lets the design see an interaction. Randomize to all four combinations. An interaction does not force the main effects to be 0 (in the quizzes-and-spacing example both main effects and the interaction were positive), and interaction is not confounding.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Change in mean response between two levels of a factor, averaged over the other factor
Effect of a factor at one particular level of the other factor
The effect of one factor depends on the level of another
Runs a planned subset of all the factor combinations
Assigning units to treatments by chance
questions.explanation: These are the definitions from the lesson. Assigning units by chance is random assignment, which every good factorial experiment uses but which is not one of these terms.

questions.stem: Put the steps of running a $2 \times 2$ factorial experiment with 40 subjects in order.
choices: Choose two factors and two levels of each
List the four treatment combinations
Randomly assign 10 subjects to each combination
Apply the treatments and measure the response
Compute the main effects and interaction from the treatment means
questions.explanation: The factors and levels define the combinations; only then can subjects be randomized to them. The analysis needs the measured responses, so it comes last.

questions.stem: In a two-factor experiment, the effect of one factor at a single level of the other factor is called a ___ effect.
questions.explanation: That is a simple effect. If the simple effects of a factor differ across the levels of the other factor, the factors interact.

questions.stem: Why can’t an individual causal effect $Y(1) - Y(0)$ be observed directly?
choices: Potential outcomes are always measured with error
The effect is too small to measure for one person
It can be observed, but only in a large sample
Each unit either gets the treatment or doesn’t, so only one of its potential outcomes is ever seen
questions.explanation: A treated unit's $Y(0)$ is a "what if" that never happened, and vice versa. That is why we estimate average effects, using groups that are comparable.

questions.stem: Four units have potential outcomes $Y(0) = 10, 12, 15, 19$ and $Y(1) = 14, 13, 18, 24$ (units 1 to 4, in order). Find the average treatment effect.
questions.explanation: Individual effects are $4, 1, 3, 5$, so the ATE is $13/4 = 3.25$ (equivalently $17.25 - 14 = 3.25$). 10 is the naive difference if units 3 and 4 chose treatment; 5 is the largest single effect; 17.25 is the mean of $Y(1)$ alone.

questions.stem: Four units have potential outcomes $Y(0) = 10, 12, 15, 19$ and $Y(1) = 14, 13, 18, 24$ (units 1 to 4, in order). Units 3 and 4 choose treatment, so the naive difference is $(18 + 24)/2 - (10 + 12)/2 = 10$. How much of this is selection bias?
questions.explanation: The treated units' untreated scores average $(15 + 19)/2 = 17$; the untreated units' average 11. Selection bias $= 17 - 11 = 6$. The rest, $21 - 17 = 4$, is the effect on the treated units, and $4 + 6 = 10$.

questions.stem: In the language of potential outcomes, what does random assignment accomplish?
choices: It reveals both potential outcomes for every unit
It guarantees the difference in means equals the average effect in every experiment
It removes chance variation from the estimate
It makes the selection-bias term zero on average, so the difference in group means is an unbiased estimate of the average effect
questions.explanation: Randomization makes the groups alike in their $Y(0)$ values on average. Any single randomization can still be off by chance (in the lesson's example one draw gave 7.5 when the true effect was 5), but there is no systematic error.

questions.stem: Group Y has a 12% rate among young people and 33% among old people. Using a standard population that is 70% young and 30% old, what is Group Y’s standardized rate?
questions.explanation: $0.70(12\%) + 0.30(33\%) = 8.4\% + 9.9\% = 18.3\%$. The simple average of 12% and 33% is 22.5%; swapping the weights gives 26.7%; adding the rates gives 45%.

questions.stem: After standardizing for math background, tutoring-center users pass calculus about 9 points more often than non-users. Why is this still not proof that tutoring causes passing?
choices: Unmeasured differences, such as motivation, may still differ between users and non-users
Standardization always exaggerates differences
The sample is too small for any conclusion
Pass rates cannot be compared across groups
questions.explanation: Adjustment removes only the confounders that were measured and used. Students who choose tutoring may differ in motivation or study habits, which could explain part or all of the gap.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a natural experiment?
choices: Researchers compare people who chose to move to a new city with people who stayed
A city lottery decides which applicants receive housing vouchers, and researchers compare later earnings of winners and losers
Towns that voted to build a park are compared with towns that voted against it
A random sample of adults is asked how often they exercise
questions.explanation: In a natural experiment, something like random assignment happens without the researcher imposing it. A lottery does exactly that. Moving and voting are choices, so the groups may differ in many ways; a survey assigns nothing.

questions.stem: Company X supplied 20,000 houses, with 300 cholera deaths; Company Y supplied 15,000 houses, with 45 deaths. Find each death rate per 10,000 houses and compare them.
choices: 300 and 45; X’s rate is about 6.7 times Y’s
15 and 3; X’s rate is 5 times Y’s
150 and 30; X’s rate is 5 times Y’s
150 and 45; X’s rate is about 3.3 times Y’s
questions.explanation: $300/20000 \times 10{,}000 = 150$ and $45/15000 \times 10{,}000 = 30$; $150/30 = 5$. Comparing raw counts (300 and 45) ignores that the companies supplied different numbers of houses; 150 and 45 converts only X's count to a rate; 15 and 3 are rates per 1,000.

questions.stem: Which of Bradford Hill’s viewpoints is generally treated as essential for a causal claim?
choices: Specificity: the cause produces only one effect
Analogy: similar causes are already known
Coherence: the claim fits textbook biology
Temporality: the cause comes before the effect
questions.explanation: An effect cannot come before its cause, so temporality is the one viewpoint that must hold. Hill himself said no single viewpoint was indispensable, and the others support a judgment rather than settle it; smoking, for example, fails specificity because it harms many organs.
