adding two successes and two failures in total, split between the groups
adding one success to each group
questions.explanation: For two groups, each gets one extra success and one extra failure, four added observations in all, which matches the "plus four" total. The one-sample version adds two of each to its single group.

questions.stem: The 95% Wilson interval computed from a sample consists of exactly the values $p_0$ that
choices: lie within $1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$ of $\hat{p}$
have probability at least 0.95 of producing the observed count
a two-sided one-proportion z test at $\alpha = 0.05$ would not reject
lie between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the sample
questions.explanation: The Wilson interval collects all $p_0$ with $|\hat{p} - p_0| \le 1.96\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$. That is exactly the non-rejection condition of the two-sided z test of $H_0: p = p_0$, whose standard deviation also uses $p_0$. The first choice describes the Wald interval.

questions.stem: "Student," who published the t distribution in 1908, was
choices: R. A. Fisher, writing about agricultural field trials
Karl Pearson, the editor of the journal that published the paper
a university student whose name was never discovered
W. S. Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin
questions.explanation: William Sealy Gosset worked with small samples at Guinness and published in Biometrika under the pen name Student. Fisher later recast the result into today's form; Pearson edited Biometrika.

questions.stem: With $n = 5$ observations from a normal population, an analyst uses $\bar{x} \pm 1.96\,s/\sqrt{n}$. Its true coverage, $2\,\text{tcdf}(1.96, 4) - 1$, is ___. Give 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\text{tcdf}(1.96, 4) \approx 0.9392$, so coverage $\approx 2(0.9392) - 1 = 0.878$, or 0.88. The "95%" interval captures $\mu$ only about 88% of the time; the correct multiplier is $t^* = 2.776$.

questions.stem: Why does a sample of $n$ values carry only $n - 1$ degrees of freedom for estimating spread?
choices: The deviations from $\bar{x}$ add to zero, so any $n - 1$ of them determine the last.
One observation is always discarded as a possible outlier.
The largest and smallest values are not used in computing $s$.
Dividing by $n - 1$ makes $s$ exactly equal to $\sigma$.
questions.explanation: Because $\sum(x_i - \bar{x}) = 0$, only $n - 1$ deviations are free to vary. Dividing by $n - 1$ makes $s^2$ unbiased for $\sigma^2$ on average, not equal to it, and $s$ itself still averages a little below $\sigma$.

questions.stem: For a random sample from a normal population, which facts combine to show that $(\bar{x} - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{n})$ has a t distribution with $n - 1$ df? Select all that apply.
choices: $(\bar{x} - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ is standard normal.
$(n - 1)s^2/\sigma^2$ has a chi-square distribution with $n - 1$ df.
$\bar{x}$ and $s$ are independent.
$s$ is exactly equal to $\sigma$.
The sample size is at least 30.
questions.explanation: $t = Z/(s/\sigma)$: a standard normal divided by an independent factor built from a chi-square variable. All three facts need a normal population; no minimum sample size is involved. If $s$ equaled $\sigma$, the statistic would simply be $Z$.

questions.stem: Writing $t = Z/(s/\sigma)$, why does $t$ have heavier tails than $Z$?
choices: Because $\bar{x}$ is more variable than $Z$ suggests
Because samples with an unusually small $s$ give unusually large values of $t$
Because $s$ is always larger than $\sigma$
Because $t$ is skewed to the right
questions.explanation: The denominator $s/\sigma$ is random and hovers around 1. When it happens to be small, $t$ is stretched far from 0, which puts extra probability in the tails, especially with few degrees of freedom. $t$ is symmetric, and $s$ is not always larger than $\sigma$ (on average it is slightly smaller).

questions.stem: In the lesson's simulation, 95% t intervals from a strongly right-skewed (exponential) population with $n = 10$ captured $\mu$ about 90% of the time. How were the misses distributed?
choices: Evenly: about half entirely above $\mu$ and half entirely below
Mostly entirely above $\mu$
There were almost no misses once $n$ reached 10
Mostly entirely below $\mu$
questions.explanation: About 9.5% of intervals lay entirely below $\mu$ and only 0.4% entirely above. Samples that miss the long right tail have both a small $\bar{x}$ and a small $s$, giving intervals that are too low and too short at the same time.

questions.stem: Match each population to how 95% t intervals for its mean behaved in the lesson's simulation.
choices: Coverage 95% for every sample size
Somewhat below 95% at n = 5, close to 95% by n = 10
Below 95% even at n = 30, with lopsided misses
Above 95%, but the intervals are wide
Exactly 95% only once n is at least 30
questions.explanation: For a normal population the t interval is exact at every $n$. Symmetric non-normal shapes like the uniform fall a little short at $n = 5$ (0.934) but are nearly fine by $n = 10$ (0.946). Strong skew still gave 0.926 at $n = 30$. Rare wild values inflate $s$, which raises coverage but makes intervals wide.

questions.stem: A random sample of 25 track gauge readings from a normal population has $\bar{x} = 80$ and $s = 8$. Using $t^* = 2.064$, the upper endpoint of the 95% prediction interval for one new reading is ___. Give 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: Margin $= t^* s\sqrt{1 + 1/n} = 2.064(8)\sqrt{1.04} \approx 16.51(1.0198) \approx 16.84$, so the upper endpoint is $80 + 16.84 = 96.84$, or 96.8. (The confidence interval for the mean would use $8/\sqrt{25} = 1.6$ and reach only 83.3.)

questions.stem: From the same sample, a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$ and a 95% prediction interval for one new observation are computed. As the sample size grows very large,
choices: both intervals shrink toward a single point
both intervals stay about the same width
the confidence interval shrinks toward a point, but the prediction interval settles near $\mu \pm 1.96\sigma$
the prediction interval shrinks toward a point, but the confidence interval settles near $\mu \pm 1.96\sigma$
questions.explanation: The confidence interval's margin $t^* s/\sqrt{n}$ goes to 0. The prediction interval's margin $t^* s\sqrt{1 + 1/n}$ approaches $1.96\sigma$, because a new individual still varies with SD $\sigma$ no matter how well $\mu$ is known.

questions.stem: Which statements about the prediction interval $\bar{x} \pm t^* s\sqrt{1 + 1/n}$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It needs a normal population, even when $n$ is large.
It is wider than the confidence interval for $\mu$ from the same data.
The 1 under the square root accounts for the variation of one new value around $\mu$.
The CLT justifies it for any population once $n \ge 30$.
It gives a range for the population mean.
questions.explanation: $\text{Var}(X_{\text{new}} - \bar{x}) = \sigma^2 + \sigma^2/n$: the $\sigma^2$ (the 1) is the new value's own spread, which makes the interval wider than $t^* s/\sqrt{n}$. The CLT is about averages, so it cannot make a single new value normal. A range for the mean is the confidence interval's job.

questions.stem: Two independent samples each have $n = 12$ and $s = 5$. Their Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom equal ___.
questions.explanation: $a = b = 25/12$, so df $= (2a)^2/(a^2/11 + a^2/11) = 4a^2/(2a^2/11) = 22$. With equal sizes and equal SDs, Welch's df reaches its maximum, $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 22$.

questions.stem: Two independent samples have $n_1 = 15$ and $n_2 = 40$. Whatever the sample SDs, the Welch–Satterthwaite df must lie between
choices: 14 and 53
15 and 55
14 and 39
1 and 54
questions.explanation: Welch df is never below $\min(n_1, n_2) - 1 = 14$ (the conservative choice) and never above $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 53$. It is near 14 when the smaller group contributes almost all of the uncertainty, and near 53 when the groups contribute in proportion to their degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Order these 95% critical values from LARGEST to SMALLEST.
choices: $t^*$ with df = 2
$t^*$ with df = 5
$t^*$ with df = 20
$z^*$ (standard normal)
questions.explanation: The values are 4.303, 2.571, 2.086 and 1.960. Fewer degrees of freedom mean heavier tails and a larger multiplier; as df grows, $t^*$ falls toward $z^* = 1.96$.

questions.stem: For random samples of 5 from a normal population, the long-run average of the sample standard deviation $s$ is
choices: exactly $\sigma$, because $s$ is unbiased
about $0.94\sigma$
about $1.06\sigma$
about $\sigma/\sqrt{5}$
questions.explanation: $s^2$ is unbiased for $\sigma^2$, but taking a square root pulls the average down, so $s$ averages about $0.94\sigma$ when $n = 5$ (about $0.97\sigma$ when $n = 10$). $\sigma/\sqrt{5}$ is the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$, a different quantity.

questions.stem: A one-sided test of $H_0: p = 0.80$ against $H_a: p < 0.80$ uses $n = 200$ and $\alpha = 0.05$. The curve is the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ if $H_0$ is true; the sample gave $\hat{p} = 0.74$, and $\hat{p} = 0.7535$ is the boundary of the rejection region. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A normal curve over a sample-proportion axis from 0.72 to 0.88, centered at 0.80 with a dotted center line (marker 1). A dashed vertical line at about 0.7535 (marker 2) and a solid vertical line at 0.74 (marker 3). The region left of the dashed line is shaded; the small tail left of the solid line is shaded darker (marker 4).

choices: Null value
Critical value
Observed statistic
p-value
Power
Margin of error
questions.explanation: 1: the curve is centered at the null value $p_0 = 0.80$, because it is drawn assuming $H_0$ is true. 2: the dashed line at 0.7535 ($z = -1.645$) is the critical value; everything to its left is the rejection region, with area $\alpha = 0.05$. 3: the solid line is the observed $\hat{p} = 0.74$ ($z = -2.12$). 4: the darker tail beyond the observed value is the p-value, about 0.017. Power needs a curve drawn for a specific alternative, and a margin of error belongs to a confidence interval.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a significance test in order.
choices: State $H_0$, $H_a$ and $\alpha$ before looking at the data
Name the test and check its conditions
Compute the test statistic and the p-value, assuming $H_0$ is true
Compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and conclude in context
questions.explanation: This is State, Plan, Do, Conclude. The hypotheses and $\alpha$ come first so the data can't influence them; the conditions are checked before any probability is trusted; the p-value has to exist before it can be compared with $\alpha$.

questions.stem: A test of $H_0: \mu = 80$ against $H_a: \mu \ne 80$ gives $z = -1.70$. The p-value, rounded to 3 decimal places, is ___.
questions.explanation: $P(Z \le -1.70) \approx 0.0446$. The alternative is two-sided, so double it: $2(0.0446) \approx 0.089$. (Forgetting to double gives 0.045, which would wrongly look significant at $\alpha = 0.05$.)

questions.stem: A test of $H_0: p = 0.5$ against $H_a: p > 0.5$ gives a p-value of 0.03. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: If $p$ really were 0.5, about 3% of samples would give a result at least as extreme as this one.
There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true.
At $\alpha = 0.05$ the result is statistically significant.
At $\alpha = 0.01$ the test shows that $p = 0.5$.
questions.explanation: The p-value is computed assuming $H_0$, so it is a probability about the data, not about $H_0$. Since $0.03 \le 0.05$, the result is significant at the 5% level. At $\alpha = 0.01$ we would fail to reject $H_0$, which is not the same as showing that $H_0$ is true.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean $\mu$ is $(48.2, 53.6)$. A two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ would reject which null hypothesis?
questions.explanation: A two-sided test at level $\alpha$ rejects exactly the null values that fall outside the $(1 - \alpha)$ confidence interval. Only 47.5 is outside $(48.2, 53.6)$. The other three values are plausible, so those tests would fail to reject.

questions.stem: The grid crosses the truth (columns: $H_0$ true, $H_0$ false) with the decision (rows: reject $H_0$, fail to reject $H_0$). Name each numbered cell.

image.alt: A two-by-two grid with column headings H0 is true and H0 is false and row headings Reject H0 and Fail to reject H0. Marker 1: reject, H0 true. Marker 2: reject, H0 false. Marker 3: fail to reject, H0 true. Marker 4: fail to reject, H0 false.

choices: Type I error
Power (correct rejection)
Correct decision, probability 1 − α
Type II error
p-value
Margin of error
questions.explanation: 1: rejecting a true $H_0$ is a Type I error (probability $\alpha$). 2: rejecting a false $H_0$ is the correct detection whose probability is the power, $1 - \beta$. 3: failing to reject a true $H_0$ is correct, with probability $1 - \alpha$. 4: failing to reject a false $H_0$ is a Type II error (probability $\beta$).

questions.stem: Test $H_0: \mu = 50$ against $H_a: \mu > 50$ with $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 2$ and $\alpha = 0.05$. The solid curve is the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ if $H_0$ is true; the dashed curve is the sampling distribution if the true mean is 55. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: Two normal curves over a sample-mean axis from 44 to 60: a solid one centered at 50 and a dashed one centered at 55. A vertical line at about 53.3 (marker 4). Marker 1 is on the small shaded area right of the line under the solid curve; marker 2 is on the shaded area left of the line under the dashed curve; marker 3 is on the large shaded area right of the line under the dashed curve.

choices: α, the Type I error probability
β, the Type II error probability
Power
Rejection cutoff
p-value
Confidence level
questions.explanation: The vertical line is the cutoff $50 + 1.645(2) = 53.29$: reject $H_0$ when $\bar{x}$ lands to its right. 1: the area right of the cutoff under the $H_0$ curve is $\alpha = 0.05$, the chance of rejecting when $H_0$ is true. 2: the area left of the cutoff under the true ($\mu = 55$) curve is $\beta \approx 0.20$, the chance of missing the effect. 3: the area right of the cutoff under the true curve is the power, about 0.80. A p-value would need an observed $\bar{x}$, which this picture doesn't have.

questions.stem: Match each description to its name.
left: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is false
The probability of rejecting $H_0$ when a specific alternative is true
The probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true
choices: Type I error
Type II error
Power
Significance level
p-value
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false alarm and a Type II error a missed effect. Power is the probability of correctly rejecting against a stated alternative ($1 - \beta$), and the significance level $\alpha$ is the Type I error probability, fixed before the data are collected. A p-value is computed from the data, after the fact.

questions.stem: A one-sided z test for a mean is planned. With everything else unchanged, which changes increase its power against a fixed alternative? Select all that apply.
choices: Increasing the sample size from 25 to 64
Raising $\alpha$ from 0.01 to 0.05
A true mean closer to the null value
Measuring more precisely, so $\sigma$ is smaller
Switching to a two-sided alternative
questions.explanation: A larger $n$ or a smaller $\sigma$ shrinks the standard error, so the two sampling distributions overlap less. A larger $\alpha$ moves the cutoff toward the null value, so more outcomes reject. A true mean closer to $\mu_0$ is a smaller effect, which is harder to detect. A two-sided test splits $\alpha$ between two tails, so it has less power in the true direction than the one-sided test.

questions.stem: Test $H_0: \mu = 50$ against $H_a: \mu > 50$ with $\sigma = 10$, $n = 25$ and $\alpha = 0.05$, so the test rejects when $\bar{x} \ge 53.29$. If the true mean is 54, the power, rounded to 2 decimal places, is ___.
questions.explanation: If $\mu = 54$, $\bar{x}$ is $N(54, 2)$. Power $= P(\bar{x} \ge 53.29) = P\!\left(Z \ge \dfrac{53.29 - 54}{2}\right) = P(Z \ge -0.355) \approx 0.64$. It lies between the lesson's 0.44 (for $\mu = 53$) and 0.80 (for $\mu = 55$), as it should.

questions.stem: A one-proportion z test of $H_0: p = 0.40$ uses a sample of $n = 150$. The standard error in the test statistic is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A test uses the null value: $SE = \sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n} = \sqrt{0.40(0.60)/150} = \sqrt{0.0016} = 0.04$. The sample proportion is not needed for the standard error.

questions.stem: Match each standard error to the procedure that uses it.
choices: One-proportion z test
One-proportion z interval
Two-proportion z test
Two-proportion z interval
questions.explanation: Tests compute probabilities assuming $H_0$, so they use what $H_0$ implies: the null value $p_0$ for one sample, and the pooled proportion $\hat{p}_c$ for two samples (since $H_0$ says $p_1 = p_2$). Intervals assume nothing about the parameter, so they use the sample proportions.

questions.stem: A one-proportion z test of $H_0: p = 0.06$ will use a simple random sample of 150 parts from a batch of 5,000. Which conditions are met? Select all that apply.
choices: Random: the data come from a simple random sample
10%: the sample is at most 10% of the batch
Large counts: $np_0 \ge 10$
Large counts: $n(1 - p_0) \ge 10$
questions.explanation: The sample is random, and $150 \le 0.10(5{,}000) = 500$. Large counts uses $p_0$: $150(0.06) = 9$, which is below 10, while $150(0.94) = 141$ is fine. With one large-counts check failing, the normal approximation is doubtful; an exact binomial calculation is the safer choice, as in the lesson's Example 4.

questions.stem: Put the calculation steps of a two-proportion z test in order.
choices: Compute the standard error from $\hat{p}_c$, $n_1$ and $n_2$
Divide $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ by the standard error to get $z$
Find the tail area(s) beyond $z$ named by $H_a$
Compare the p-value with $\alpha$
questions.explanation: Each step uses the result of the one before: the pooled standard error needs $\hat{p}_c$, the z statistic needs the standard error, the p-value needs $z$, and the decision needs the p-value.

questions.stem: Before an experiment, researchers stated that they expected treatment 1 to have a higher success rate than treatment 2. The two-proportion z test gives $z = 2.10$. What is the p-value?
questions.explanation: The alternative $H_a: p_1 > p_2$ was set in advance, so the p-value is the upper tail only: $P(Z \ge 2.10) \approx 0.0179$. Doubling (0.0357) is for a two-sided test, 0.9821 is the area to the left, and 0.0089 halves the tail instead of using it.

questions.stem: The picture shows eight operators' output with an old and a new jig (the differences match the lesson's Example 2). Why is a paired t test the right choice here rather than a two-sample t test?

image.alt: A slope graph joining each of eight operators' old-jig and new-jig outputs. Operators range from about 16 to 31 units per hour, and six of the eight lines rise by 2 to 5 units.

choices: Pairing uses twice as many observations as the two-sample test.
The two-sample test needs the two groups to have different sizes.
Each operator used both jigs, so the two columns are not independent; the differences remove the large operator-to-operator variation.
Most operators did worse with the new jig, which only a paired test can detect.
questions.explanation: The same operator appears in both columns, so the samples are dependent, and the two-sample test's independence condition fails. Working with each operator's difference removes the operator-to-operator spread (16 to 31 units), leaving the much smaller jig effect. Both tests use the same 16 numbers, the two-sample test doesn't need different sizes, and six of the eight operators improved.

questions.stem: Match each study to the significance test it calls for.
left: Mean weight of 30 randomly chosen bags compared with the labeled 500 g
Blood pressure of 20 patients measured before and after a medication
Test scores of 25 students taught online and 28 different students taught in person, randomly assigned
Defect rates of parts from two machines
choices: One-sample t test
Paired t test
Two-sample t test
Two-proportion z test
One-proportion z test
questions.explanation: One sample compared with a standard: one-sample t. The same patients measured twice: paired t on the differences. Two separate randomly assigned groups: two-sample t. Defect rates are proportions (a categorical response), so the two-machine comparison is a two-proportion z test, not a t test.

questions.stem: A random sample of $n = 16$ has $\bar{x} = 52.4$ and $s = 6$. For $H_0: \mu = 50$, the t statistic is $t =$ ___. Give only the number.
In which situations are the conditions for a one-sample t test for a mean met? Select all that apply.
choices: A random sample of 40 values whose dotplot is moderately skewed, with no outliers
A random sample of 10 values from a population known to be normal
A random sample of 12 values with one extreme outlier
The first 50 volunteers who answered an online ad
questions.explanation: With $n = 40 \ge 30$, moderate skew is fine (the central limit theorem helps). A small sample from a normal population is fine too. A small sample with an extreme outlier violates the normal condition, and volunteers who answer an ad are not a random sample, so the random condition fails.

questions.stem: Put the calculation steps of a paired t test in order.
choices: Subtract within each pair to get the differences
Find the mean $\bar{d}$ and standard deviation $s_d$ of the differences
Compute $t = \bar{d}/(s_d/\sqrt{n})$
Find the p-value from the t distribution with $n - 1$ df
questions.explanation: A paired t test is a one-sample t test on the differences, so the differences come first; their mean and SD give $t$, and $t$ gives the p-value, with $n$ the number of pairs.

questions.stem: A one-sided z test is run at significance level $\alpha$. What is the height of its power curve at the null value $\mu_0$?
choices: $\alpha$
$1 - \alpha$
questions.explanation: At $\mu = \mu_0$ the null hypothesis is true, so "power" there is the probability of rejecting a true $H_0$, which is the Type I error rate $\alpha$. The curve rises from $\alpha$ toward 1 as the true mean moves away from $\mu_0$ in the direction of $H_a$.

questions.stem: A one-sided z test at $\alpha = 0.05$ ($z_\alpha = 1.645$) should have power 0.80 ($z_\beta = 0.842$) to detect a mean 2 units above $\mu_0$. The individual measurements have $\sigma = 8$. The smallest sample size that does this is $n =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $n = \left(\dfrac{(1.645 + 0.842)(8)}{2}\right)^2 = (9.948)^2 \approx 98.96$. Always round up, to 99; with 98 the power would fall just short of 0.80.

questions.stem: A study was planned to detect a difference of 6 units. The investigators decide that a difference of 3 units also matters. Keeping $\alpha$, the power and $\sigma$ the same, the required sample size is multiplied by about
choices: $\sqrt{2}$
questions.explanation: $n = \left((z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma/\delta\right)^2$ depends on $1/\delta^2$. Halving $\delta$ multiplies $n$ by $2^2 = 4$. Small effects are expensive to detect.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: Power plotted against the true value of the parameter
The effect measured in standard deviations of individual values
Significant estimates from low-power studies overstate the effect
Power computed from the observed effect after the study
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
questions.explanation: A power curve shows power at every possible true value. The effect size $d = \delta/\sigma$ is measured in units of $\sigma$, not of the standard error. The winner's curse (a Type M error) is the exaggeration of effects that survive a low-power test. Observed power is computed after the fact and is just a restatement of the p-value. No test gives the probability that $H_0$ is true.

questions.stem: Which statements describe the power curve of a one-sided z test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ against $H_a: \mu > \mu_0$? Select all that apply.
choices: It equals $\alpha$ at $\mu = \mu_0$.
It rises toward 1 as the true mean increases above $\mu_0$.
A larger sample size makes it rise more steeply.
It equals $1 - \alpha$ at $\mu = \mu_0$.
It decreases as the true effect grows.
questions.explanation: At the null value the rejection probability is $\alpha$ (not $1 - \alpha$, which is the chance of correctly failing to reject). Bigger effects are easier to detect, so the curve rises with the true mean, and a larger $n$ shrinks the standard error, so the curve climbs faster. With $n = 25$ the lesson's curve is at 0.44 when $\mu = 53$; with $n = 100$ it is at 0.91.

questions.stem: A training program is expected to raise a test score by 6 points. Scores of individual students have a standard deviation of 15 points. What is the effect size $d$?
questions.explanation: $d = \delta/\sigma = 6/15 = 0.4$, a little under Cohen's rough "medium" of 0.5. Dividing the other way gives 2.5; 0.04 and 0.6 are slips with the decimal point or the subtraction.

questions.stem: Two independent groups of equal size will be compared with a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ ($z_{\alpha/2} = 1.960$). With $\sigma = 10$ in each group, the study needs power 0.80 ($z_\beta = 0.842$) to detect a difference of 5. How many subjects are needed in each group? ___
questions.explanation: $n = 2\left(\dfrac{(1.960 + 0.842)(10)}{5}\right)^2 = 2(5.604)^2 \approx 62.8$, rounded up to 63 per group (126 in all). Forgetting the factor 2 gives 32, too few.

questions.stem: The sample size formula gives $n = 95.2$. Why should the planner use 96 rather than 95?
choices: Sample sizes must be even numbers.
Rounding up makes $\alpha$ smaller.
The formula always underestimates by exactly one observation.
With 95 observations the power would be slightly below the target.
questions.explanation: Power increases with $n$, and 95.2 is the size that gives exactly the target power. Any smaller $n$, including 95, gives a little less (0.8996 instead of 0.90 in the lesson's Example 1), so round up. The significance level is fixed by the cutoff, not by the rounding.

questions.stem: A small study with power about 0.2 against a realistic effect finds a statistically significant improvement of 8 points. What is the most reasonable reading?
choices: The true effect is very likely 8 points or more, since the result survived a hard test.
The effect is probably real, but its true size is likely smaller than 8 points.
The result must be a Type I error, because the power was low.
Low power means the p-value was computed incorrectly.
questions.explanation: With low power, only estimates that happened to land far from 0 reach significance, so significant estimates tend to overstate the effect (the winner's curse). In the lesson's Example 4 the exaggeration averaged about 2.5 times. Low power does not make a significant result automatically false, and it doesn't affect how the p-value is computed.

questions.stem: A study finds p-value 0.30. A colleague plugs the observed effect into the power formula, gets "observed power" 0.18, and concludes that the effect might exist but the study lacked power. What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: Observed power is determined by the p-value, so it adds no new information; a confidence interval shows which effects are still plausible.
Observed power should be computed with $\alpha = 0.30$.
Power can only be computed for two-sided tests.
A p-value of 0.30 proves that the effect does not exist.
questions.explanation: For a given test, observed power is a fixed function of the p-value: a large p-value always comes with low observed power, so it cannot be independent evidence of anything. Power is for planning; after the study, the confidence interval reports which effect sizes the data rule out. A large p-value never proves the null hypothesis.

questions.stem: To plan the sample size for a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$, which value replaces $z_\alpha$ in the formula?
questions.explanation: A two-sided test puts $\alpha/2 = 0.025$ in each tail, so the cutoff is $z_{0.025} = 1.960$. 1.645 is the one-sided value, 0.842 is $z_\beta$ for power 0.80, and 2.576 is the two-sided value for $\alpha = 0.01$.

questions.stem: The sample size formula for a one-proportion test has two different square roots, $\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)}$ and $\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)}$. Why?
choices: One is for the sample and one is for the population.
One is for a one-sided test and one for a two-sided test.
Because the test pools the two proportions.
The SD of $\hat{p}$ depends on $p$, so it is different when $H_0$ is true (setting the cutoff) and when the alternative $p_1$ is true (giving the power).
questions.explanation: The cutoff is placed using the SD of $\hat{p}$ under $H_0$, $\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$, while the chance of landing beyond it is computed under the alternative, with SD $\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)/n}$. For means, $\sigma$ is the same under both hypotheses, so one $\sigma$ appears.

questions.stem: The z-based formula gives $n = 96$ for a study that will actually be analyzed with a t test (because $\sigma$ will be estimated). What should the planner expect?
choices: The t test needs far fewer observations, about half.
The t test needs slightly more observations, here about 97.
Exactly 96, since z and t tests have the same power.
Power cannot be computed for a t test.
questions.explanation: Critical values of $t$ are a little larger than those of $z$, so a t test needs slightly more data for the same power. Exact calculations (with the noncentral t distribution) give 97 for the lesson's Example 1. Usually the larger uncertainty is in the planning value of $\sigma$.

questions.stem: With everything else unchanged, which changes reduce the sample size needed for a test? Select all that apply.
choices: Deciding that only a larger effect is worth detecting
Using a larger planning value for $\sigma$
Accepting power 0.80 instead of 0.90
Lowering $\alpha$ from 0.05 to 0.01
Using matched pairs that reduce the SD of the differences
questions.explanation: $n = \left((z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma/\delta\right)^2$ shrinks when $\delta$ grows, when $z_\beta$ shrinks (lower power) and when the relevant SD shrinks, which is what good pairing does. A larger $\sigma$ and a smaller $\alpha$ (larger $z_\alpha$) both increase $n$.

questions.stem: Each bar is a 90% confidence interval for a difference, drawn against an equivalence margin $\pm\Delta$ (the shaded zone). Using a TOST at $\alpha = 0.05$, name the conclusion for each numbered interval.

image.alt: Four horizontal confidence intervals against an axis marked minus delta, 0 and plus delta, with the zone between the margins shaded. Interval 1 runs from inside the zone, across 0, to beyond plus delta. Interval 2 lies inside the zone and contains 0. Interval 3 lies entirely beyond plus delta. Interval 4 lies inside the zone, entirely to the right of 0.

choices: Inconclusive
Equivalent; the interval includes 0
Not equivalent
Equivalent; the interval excludes 0
Proves the difference is exactly 0
questions.explanation: TOST at $\alpha = 0.05$ concludes equivalence exactly when the 90% interval lies inside $(-\Delta, \Delta)$. Intervals 2 and 4 do; interval 4 also excludes 0, so the difference is real but too small to matter. Interval 1 contains 0 but reaches past $+\Delta$, so the data can't rule out an important difference: inconclusive. Interval 3 lies entirely beyond $+\Delta$: the difference is larger than the margin. No interval can show a difference is exactly 0.

questions.stem: In a TOST, the test against $-\Delta$ has p-value 0.003 and the test against $+\Delta$ has p-value 0.041. The TOST p-value is ___.
questions.explanation: Equivalence needs both one-sided tests to reject, so the evidence is only as strong as the weaker of the two: the TOST p-value is the larger p-value, 0.041. At $\alpha = 0.05$ equivalence is shown; at $\alpha = 0.01$ it is not.

questions.stem: A TOST at $\alpha = 0.05$ gives the same decision as checking whether which confidence interval lies inside $(-\Delta, \Delta)$?
choices: The 95% interval
The 90% interval
The 97.5% interval
The 99% interval
questions.explanation: Each one-sided test at level $\alpha$ matches one end of a $(1 - 2\alpha)$ interval, so $\alpha = 0.05$ goes with a 90% interval. Using the 95% interval would make the procedure stricter than the stated level.

questions.stem: A study comparing two gauges finds no significant difference (p-value 0.40). Why doesn't this show that the gauges are equivalent?
choices: A p-value of 0.40 is too small to support equivalence.
Equivalence can only be shown for proportions.
A small or noisy study can fail to detect even a large difference; the data may still allow differences bigger than any acceptable margin.
Ordinary tests can only be used for one-sided alternatives.
questions.explanation: Failing to reject "difference = 0" only says the data are consistent with 0. They may be consistent with large differences too, as in the lesson's 6-section study, whose 90% interval reached 0.45 mm. To support equivalence, the null hypothesis must be "the difference is at least $\Delta$," and the data must reject it.

questions.stem: Match each research goal to the null hypothesis its test uses.
left: Show that a new method gives different results from the old one
Show that two methods are practically the same
Show that a new treatment is not much worse than the standard
choices: The difference is 0
The difference is at least Δ in size
The new one is worse by Δ or more
The difference is less than Δ in size
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis is always what we want to find evidence against. To show a difference, test "no difference." To show equivalence, test "the difference is at least $\Delta$ in size" (TOST). To show non-inferiority, test "the new one is worse by at least $\Delta$." "Less than $\Delta$ in size" is what equivalence hopes to show, so it is the alternative, not a null.

questions.stem: A paired equivalence study has $\bar{d} = 0.5$, $SE = 0.2$ and margin $\Delta = 1$. What is the statistic $t_2 = (\bar{d} - \Delta)/SE$ for the test against $+\Delta$?
questions.explanation: $t_2 = (0.5 - 1)/0.2 = -2.5$, a lower-tail test of $H_{02}: \mu_d \ge 1$. The other statistic is $t_1 = (0.5 + 1)/0.2 = 7.5$. The positive 2.5 and the $-7.5$ come from sign slips.

questions.stem: With margin $\Delta = 0.30$, a study's 90% confidence interval for a difference is $(0.05, 0.22)$. Which statements are justified? Select all that apply.
choices: A TOST at $\alpha = 0.05$ concludes equivalence.
A two-sided test of "difference = 0" at $\alpha = 0.10$ would reject.
The true difference is exactly 0.
The study is inconclusive.
questions.explanation: The interval lies inside $(-0.30, 0.30)$, so equivalence is shown at $\alpha = 0.05$. It also excludes 0, and a 90% interval matches a two-sided test at 0.10, so that test rejects "difference = 0": the difference is real but small. That contradicts "exactly 0," and the study is not inconclusive.

questions.stem: Why can each of the two one-sided tests in a TOST use the full level $\alpha$ rather than $\alpha/2$?
choices: Because equivalence is claimed only when both tests reject, and if the true difference is outside the margin only one test's null hypothesis can be true, so a false claim has probability at most $\alpha$.
Because one-sided tests always have smaller error rates than two-sided tests.
Because the two tests are independent.
Because the margin $\Delta$ absorbs the extra error.
questions.explanation: If, say, $\theta \ge \Delta$, a false claim of equivalence requires test 2 to reject, which happens with probability at most $\alpha$ because test 2 is a valid level-$\alpha$ test there. Requiring test 1 to reject as well only lowers the chance. Splitting $\alpha$ is for "either one rejects" conclusions, like Bonferroni. The two tests use the same data, so they are not independent.

questions.stem: A non-inferiority test uses margin $\Delta = 0.08$. The observed difference (new − standard) is $-0.03$ with standard error 0.025. The test statistic is $z =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The test compares the estimate with $-\Delta$, not with 0: $z = \dfrac{-0.03 - (-0.08)}{0.025} = \dfrac{0.05}{0.025} = 2$, with one-sided p-value $P(Z \ge 2) \approx 0.023$.

questions.stem: Bioequivalence of a generic drug is usually shown by a 90% interval for the ratio of mean blood levels lying within 80% to 125%. Why is the upper limit 125% rather than 120%?
choices: Because generic drugs are allowed to be stronger than the original.
Because the 90% interval is wider on the upper side.
Because 120% was found to be unsafe.
Because the limits are symmetric on the log scale: a ratio of 0.80 one way is 1/0.80 = 1.25 the other way.
questions.explanation: Ratios are compared on the log scale, where $\ln 0.80 = -\ln 1.25$. A product with 80% of the reference's level means the reference has 125% of the product's, so the two limits describe the same size of difference in either direction.

questions.stem: A small study gives a 90% interval of $(-0.21, 0.45)$ for a mean difference, with margin $\Delta = 0.30$. An ordinary test of "difference = 0" has p-value 0.50. What is the right conclusion?
choices: The methods are equivalent, because the ordinary test was not significant.
Inconclusive: the data neither show equivalence nor show a difference, since the interval reaches past the margin and also contains 0.
The methods differ by more than the margin.
The methods are equivalent, because the interval contains 0.
questions.explanation: The interval includes 0, so there is no evidence of a difference, but it also reaches 0.45, beyond $+0.30$, so an important difference hasn't been ruled out. Only an interval entirely inside $(-0.30, 0.30)$ would show equivalence, and only one entirely beyond the margin would show a difference larger than $\Delta$.

questions.stem: A non-inferiority trial (higher cure rate is better, margin $\Delta = 0.10$) gives a 95% interval of $(-0.095, 0.015)$ for $p_{\text{new}} - p_{\text{std}}$. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The new treatment is non-inferior, and the trial gives no evidence that it is better or worse than the standard.
The new treatment is better than the standard.
The new treatment is worse by more than 10 points.
Nothing can be concluded, because the interval contains 0.
questions.explanation: Non-inferiority needs the lower bound above $-\Delta$: $-0.095 > -0.10$, so it is shown (at one-sided level 0.025). The interval contains 0, so there is no evidence of a real difference in either direction; "not much worse" is not "better." Containing 0 is not a problem for a non-inferiority claim.

questions.stem: Put the steps of an equivalence study analyzed by TOST in order.
choices: Choose the equivalence margin $\Delta$ before collecting data
Collect the data and compute the estimate and its standard error
Compute the two one-sided test statistics and their p-values
Take the larger p-value and compare it with $\alpha$
questions.explanation: The margin must be fixed first, so it can't be tuned to the results. The test statistics need the estimate and its standard error, and the decision uses the larger of the two p-values.

questions.stem: A study of 40,000 people finds that a new diet lowers weight by 0.2 kg on average (p-value < 0.001), with 90% interval $(0.12, 0.28)$ kg. A loss under 1 kg is considered unimportant. What is the best summary?
choices: The diet has a large and important effect, since the p-value is tiny.
The diet has no effect, since 0.2 kg is small.
The result is inconclusive.
The effect is real (the interval excludes 0) but practically negligible (the interval lies inside ±1 kg).
questions.explanation: Both questions can be asked of the same interval. It excludes 0, so the effect is statistically significant; it also lies entirely inside the margin of ±1 kg, so a TOST would conclude equivalence with "no effect" for practical purposes. A tiny p-value measures how surely the effect differs from 0, not how big it is.

questions.stem: In a paired study of 10 pairs, 7 differences are positive, 2 are negative and 1 is zero. The one-sided sign test p-value for "the median difference is positive" is ___ (4 decimal places).
questions.explanation: Drop the zero, leaving $n = 9$. Under $H_0$ the number of positive signs is $B(9, 0.5)$, so the p-value is $P(X \ge 7) = \dfrac{\binom{9}{7} + \binom{9}{8} + \binom{9}{9}}{2^9} = \dfrac{36 + 9 + 1}{512} \approx 0.0898$. Keeping the zero ($B(10, 0.5)$) would give a different, wrong answer.

questions.stem: Five paired differences are 4, −1, 6, 3 and 8. For the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the sum of the ranks of the positive differences is $W^+ =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Rank the sizes 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 as 1 to 5. Only the −1 (rank 1) is negative, so $W^+ = 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14$, which is also the total $5(6)/2 = 15$ minus 1. Ranking the signed values instead of their sizes is the common mistake.

questions.stem: Test $H_0: p = 0.5$ against $H_a: p > 0.5$ with an exact binomial test. In 12 independent trials there are 10 successes. What is the p-value?
questions.explanation: $P(X \ge 10) = \dfrac{\binom{12}{10} + \binom{12}{11} + \binom{12}{12}}{2^{12}} = \dfrac{66 + 12 + 1}{4096} \approx 0.0193$. 0.0161 is $P(X = 10)$ alone (not "at least as extreme"), 0.0386 doubles the tail for a two-sided test, and 0.0002 is $P(X = 12)$.

questions.stem: An exact test is called conservative. What does that mean?
choices: It always gives a smaller p-value than the normal approximation.
It can only be used for one-sided alternatives.
Its actual probability of a Type I error is at most the nominal $\alpha$, often less.
It assumes the population is normal.
questions.explanation: Discrete statistics allow only certain p-values, so "reject when p-value $\le \alpha$" usually has a true Type I error rate below $\alpha$, as in the lesson's coin example (0.0107 instead of 0.05). That protects against false alarms at some cost in power. Exact tests make no normality assumption.

questions.stem: With $n = 10$ trials, an exact binomial test of $H_0: p = 0.5$ against $H_a: p > 0.5$ rejects when the p-value is at most 0.05. If $H_0$ is true, what is the actual probability of a Type I error?
questions.explanation: $P(X \ge 8) = 56/1024 \approx 0.0547$ is above 0.05, but $P(X \ge 9) = 11/1024 \approx 0.0107$ is not, so the test rejects only when $X \ge 9$. The real Type I error rate is therefore 0.0107. No count gives exactly 0.05.

questions.stem: For the lesson's jig data, the paired t test gave a p-value of 0.0074 but the sign test gave 0.0625. What best explains the difference?
choices: The sign test made an arithmetic error by dropping the zero.
The sign test uses only the directions of the differences, not their sizes, so it has less power when the t test's conditions hold.
The t test is exact and the sign test is approximate.
The sign test is two-sided and the t test is one-sided.
questions.explanation: Both tests here are one-sided. The sign test throws away the sizes of the differences and keeps only their signs, so it needs stronger evidence to reject; in exchange it needs no normality assumption and isn't affected by outliers. The sign test is the exact one, and dropping the zero difference is the correct rule.

questions.stem: For the five differences 4, −1, 6, 3, 8 ($W^+ = 14$), what is the exact one-sided signed-rank p-value for "the differences tend to be positive"?
questions.explanation: All $2^5 = 32$ sign patterns are equally likely under $H_0$. $W^+ \ge 14$ means the negative ranks add to at most 1: either none negative or only rank 1 negative, 2 patterns. p-value $= 2/32 = 0.0625$. 0.0313 counts only the all-positive pattern, 0.1250 doubles for a two-sided test, and 0.1875 is the sign test's $P(X \ge 4) = 6/32$ for 4 positives out of 5.

questions.stem: Of the sign test, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and the paired t test, which makes the weakest assumption about the shape of the distribution of the differences?
choices: The sign test
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test
All three make the same assumption
The paired t test
questions.explanation: The sign test needs only that, under $H_0$, each nonzero difference is equally likely to be positive or negative (median 0). The signed-rank test adds symmetry about 0, and the t test needs the differences to be roughly normal (or the sample to be large). The price of the weaker assumptions is less power.

questions.stem: Match each test to the null distribution its p-value comes from.
choices: Binomial with n trials and the null value p0
Binomial with p = 0.5 for the nonzero differences
All 2^n equally likely sign patterns of the ranks
t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Normal curve with mean p0
questions.explanation: The exact binomial test uses $B(n, p_0)$ itself, and the sign test is the special case $B(n, 0.5)$ applied to signs. The signed-rank test lists every way of attaching signs to the ranks. The paired t test uses a t curve, which is exact only when the differences are normal. A normal curve with mean $p_0$ is the approximation the z test uses.

questions.stem: In which situations do the conditions for the usual z or t procedure fail, so that an exact test is the better choice? Select all that apply.
choices: A one-proportion test with $np_0 = 3$
Comparing two proportions when one expected count in the $2 \times 2$ table is 3.8
Eight paired differences that include one extreme outlier
A simple random sample of 500 with $np_0 = 150$ and $n(1 - p_0) = 350$
questions.explanation: Expected counts below 10 break the large counts condition for z tests (use the exact binomial or Fisher's test), and a small sample with an extreme outlier breaks the t test's normal condition (a sign or signed-rank test is safer). With 150 and 350 expected successes and failures, the z test is accurate.

questions.stem: The sign and signed-rank tests are called nonparametric. What does that mean?
choices: Their null distributions don't depend on a normal or other parametric model for the data.
They have no assumptions at all.
They can only be used with fewer than 30 observations.
They don't estimate anything, so they give no p-value.
questions.explanation: Their p-values come from counting equally likely sign patterns, not from a normal or t curve, so they are also called distribution-free. They still have assumptions: random data, and for the signed-rank test, symmetry. They give p-values, and they work for any sample size.

questions.stem: For the train-cancellation data ($n = 150$, $p_0 = 0.02$, 6 cancellations), a two-sided exact p-value is 0.164 by doubling the tail but 0.130 by summing all outcomes no more likely than 6. Why do the two conventions disagree?
choices: The binomial distribution with $p_0 = 0.02$ is lopsided, so the two tails are not mirror images.
One of the two calculations must contain an error.
Doubling is only allowed for proportions above 0.5.
The sample is too small for any two-sided test.
questions.explanation: With mean 3 and a floor at 0, $B(150, 0.02)$ is strongly skewed: the lower tail cannot mirror the upper one. The two rules handle that asymmetry differently, and both are in use, so a report should say which one it used. When $p_0 = 0.5$ the distribution is symmetric and the two agree.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test in order.
choices: Drop any differences that are exactly 0
Rank the remaining differences by absolute value
Add the ranks of the positive differences to get $W^+$
Find the share of the $2^n$ equally likely sign patterns with a $W^+$ at least as extreme
questions.explanation: Zeros are removed before ranking (they would otherwise take up ranks), the ranks are needed to form $W^+$, and $W^+$ is compared with its exact null distribution to get the p-value.

questions.stem: A paired study of 12 pairs has 8 positive differences, 1 negative and 3 equal to zero. Under $H_0$, the number of positive signs in the sign test has which distribution?
questions.explanation: Zero differences have no sign and are dropped, leaving $8 + 1 = 9$ nonzero differences, each positive with probability 0.5 under $H_0$: $B(9, 0.5)$. The p-value would be $P(X \ge 8) = 10/512 \approx 0.0195$.

questions.stem: The picture shows the chi-square distribution with 5 df for the fair-die test ($\chi^2 = 6.5$, $\alpha = 0.05$). Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A right-skewed chi-square density curve over an axis from 0 to 20. Marker 1 is at a solid line and triangle on the axis at 6.5. Marker 2 is at the top of a dashed line at about 11.07. Marker 3 is at the top of a dotted line at 5. Marker 4 is inside the shaded region to the right of 6.5.

choices: Observed chi-square statistic
Critical value for alpha = 0.05
Mean of the distribution (the df)
P-value
Expected count
Lower-tail area
questions.explanation: 1: the computed statistic, 6.5, sits on the axis. 2: the dashed line at 11.07 cuts off an upper-tail area of 0.05; a statistic beyond it would be significant. 3: a chi-square distribution's mean equals its df, here 5 (the peak is to the left of the mean because of the right skew). 4: the p-value is the whole area to the right of the observed statistic, about 0.26. Chi-square tests never use the lower tail.

questions.stem: In a goodness-of-fit test, a category has observed count 98 and expected count 80. Its contribution to $\chi^2$ is ___. Give the number to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Contribution $= (O - E)^2/E = (98 - 80)^2/80 = 324/80 = 4.05$. This is the fastener category in lesson 37's Example 1, the largest of the four contributions.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a chi-square goodness-of-fit test in order.
choices: State $H_0$, giving a proportion for every category
Compute the expected counts $np_i$
Check that every expected count is at least 5
Add the contributions $(O - E)^2/E$ to get $\chi^2$
Find the p-value as the upper-tail area beyond $\chi^2$
Compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and conclude in context
questions.explanation: The expected counts come from the proportions in $H_0$, and the large-counts condition is about expected counts, so it can only be checked after they are computed. The statistic needs the expected counts, the p-value needs the statistic, and the conclusion comes last.

questions.stem: Which statements about the chi-square goodness-of-fit test are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The p-value is the area in the upper tail of a chi-square distribution
The degrees of freedom equal the number of categories minus 1
Every observed count must be at least 5
A larger value of $\chi^2$ is stronger evidence against $H_0$
The statistic should be computed from percentages, not counts
questions.explanation: Only large values of $\chi^2$ count against $H_0$, so the p-value is always an upper-tail area, and df $= k - 1$. The large-counts condition is about expected counts; observed counts can be small or even 0. Percentages throw away the sample size, so the statistic must use counts.

questions.stem: Match each category's observed and expected counts to its contribution $(O - E)^2/E$.
questions.explanation: $5^2/20 = 1.25$; $(-8)^2/20 = 64/20 = 3.2$; $10^2/50 = 2$; $(-5)^2/50 = 0.5$. Notice that a miss of 10 counts for less when 50 were expected than a miss of 8 when 20 were expected. 0.25 is $5/20$, the miss divided by $E$ without squaring.

questions.stem: To find the expected count for the Under 30 / Train cell of the transit survey, which numbers do you use? Name each numbered part of the table.

image.alt: The transit survey table with rows Under 30, 30–50, Over 50 and Total, and columns Train, Bus, Car and Total. Four cells are shaded and numbered: 1 is the Under 30 row's Total, 60; 2 is the Train column's Total, 70; 3 is the bottom-right cell, 200; 4 is the Under 30 / Train cell, 30.

choices: Row total
Column total
Grand total
Observed count
Expected count
Degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: 1 (60) is the total of the Under 30 row, 2 (70) the total of the Train column, 3 (200) the grand total, and 4 (30) the observed count in the cell. The expected count is not in the table at all: it is computed as $60 \times 70/200 = 21$ and then compared with the observed 30.

questions.stem: In a two-way table with grand total 200, a cell's row total is 80 and its column total is 45. Under $H_0$, the expected count for that cell is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Expected $= \dfrac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}} = \dfrac{80 \times 45}{200} = 18$. (This is the 30–50 / Bus cell of the transit survey.)

questions.stem: Match each study to the procedure that fits it.
left: One random sample of 400 workers, each asked their shift and their commute mode
Separate random samples from three cities, each asked their preferred ticket type
One sample of 200 defects, compared with the historical percentages of four defect types
Two groups, a yes/no outcome, and the question "is group A's rate higher?"
choices: Test of independence
Test of homogeneity
Goodness-of-fit test
Two-proportion z test
t test for the slope
questions.explanation: One sample with two categorical variables per person: independence. Several samples (or treatment groups) and one variable: homogeneity. One variable against a claimed distribution: goodness of fit. A one-sided comparison of two proportions needs the z test, because chi-square tests are two-sided by nature. A slope test needs a quantitative response.

questions.stem: A chi-square test of independence is run on a table with 4 rows and 3 columns (not counting totals). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The total row and total column count toward $r$ and $c$
The test has $(4 - 1)(3 - 1) = 6$ degrees of freedom
$H_0$ says the two variables are independent in the population
A significant result on observational data shows that one variable causes the other
Each expected count is (row total)(column total)/(grand total)
questions.explanation: $r$ and $c$ count only the categories, so df $= 3 \times 2 = 6$. The null hypothesis is independence (no association), and expected counts come from the margins. A small p-value shows association; without random assignment it does not show causation.

questions.stem: The grid shows each cell's contribution to $\chi^2 = 24.45$ for the transit survey. Which conclusion does it support best?

image.alt: A 3 by 3 grid of contributions with observed and expected counts. Under 30: Train 3.86 above, Bus 3.13 above, Car 9.42 below. 30 to 50: Train 0.32 below, Bus 0.50 below, Car 1.06 above. Over 50: Train 1.71 below, Bus 0.91 below, Car 3.54 above.

choices: The 30–50 group drives the association, since it is the largest group
Every cell differs significantly from its expected count
Under-30 commuters drive much less than independence predicts, and over-50s drive more
Bus riders contribute most of the evidence of association
questions.explanation: The largest contribution, 9.42, is under-30 car commuters, below expectation (10 vs. 25.5); over-50 car commuters are above expectation (3.54). The 30–50 row's contributions are all small, so it fits independence well, and the bus column adds only about 4.5 of the 24.45. Small contributions such as 0.32 are not evidence of anything.

questions.stem: The picture shows the regression model $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A rising straight line with sideways bell curves centered on it at three x-values, all the same width. Marker 1 is on the straight line near its right end. Marker 2 is on the bell curve at the first x-value. Marker 3 is beside a short double arrow on the middle bell curve, running from the line down one unit of spread. Marker 4 is beside a vertical double arrow from the line up to an open circle above it at the third x-value.

choices: Population regression line
Distribution of y at one x
Standard deviation sigma
Error of one observation
Least-squares slope b
Correlation r
questions.explanation: 1 is the population line $\mu_y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, the mean response at each $x$. 2: at a fixed $x$, the $y$-values vary normally around that mean. 3: the spread of each normal curve is $\sigma$, the same at every $x$ (the Equal SD condition). 4: one observation sits above the line by its error $\varepsilon = y - \mu_y$. The statistic $b$ and the correlation $r$ come from a sample; they are not parts of the population model.

questions.stem: Name each numbered entry of this regression output (wear depth on tonnage, $n = 20$).

image.alt: A regression output table. Header: Predictor, Coef, SE Coef, T, P. Constant row: 1.84, 1.10, 1.67, 0.112. Tonnage row: 2.35, 1 marked; 0.82, 2 marked; 2.87, 3 marked; 0.010, 4 marked. Marker 5 is on the Constant row's Coef, 1.84. Below the table, S = 2.61 has marker 6, and R-sq = 31.3% is unmarked.

choices: Slope b
Standard error of the slope
t statistic for the slope
Two-sided p-value for the slope
Intercept a
Residual standard deviation s
Correlation r
One-sided p-value for the slope
questions.explanation: The row named after the explanatory variable (Tonnage) is about the slope: $b = 2.35$, $SE_b = 0.82$, $t = 2.35/0.82 = 2.87$ and the two-sided p-value 0.010 (halve it for a one-sided test when $b$ has the right sign). The Constant row gives the intercept $a = 1.84$. S is the residual standard deviation $s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n - 2)}$. The output does not print $r$; it could be found from R-sq.

questions.stem: Computer output gives slope $b = 2.35$ with $SE_b = 0.82$. The t statistic for $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is ___. Give the number to 2 decimal places.
Put the steps of a t test for the regression slope in order.
choices: State $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ and $H_a$ about the population slope
Check the LINER conditions with the scatterplot and residual plot
Compute $t = b/SE_b$
Find the p-value from a t distribution with $n - 2$ df
Compare with $\alpha$ and conclude in context
questions.explanation: As in every significance test: hypotheses first, then conditions (so you don't compute something that isn't valid), then the statistic, then its p-value (which needs $t$), and the conclusion last.

questions.stem: Which features would make a t test for the slope unreliable? Select all that apply.
choices: A clear curved pattern in the residual plot
Residuals that fan out as $x$ increases
Residuals scattered in a horizontal band of constant width
A strongly skewed residual distribution with an outlier, with $n = 8$
$x$ values spread widely across their range
questions.explanation: A curve breaks Linear, a fan breaks Equal SD, and strong skew with an outlier in a small sample breaks Normal. A horizontal band of constant width is exactly what the conditions want, and widely spread $x$ values make the slope more precise (larger $s_x$, smaller $SE_b$).

questions.stem: Which description defines the chi-square distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom?
choices: The distribution of the sum of $k$ independent standard normal variables
The distribution of the sum of the squares of $k$ independent standard normal variables
The distribution of a t statistic with $k$ df, squared
Any right-skewed distribution with mean $k$
questions.explanation: $\chi^2_k$ is the distribution of $Z_1^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2$ for independent standard normals. A sum of normals (without squaring) is normal, not chi-square. A squared $t$ with $k$ df has an F distribution, and "right-skewed with mean $k$" describes many distributions.

questions.stem: What are the mean and variance of a chi-square distribution with 6 degrees of freedom?
choices: Mean 6, variance 6
Mean 5, variance 10
Mean 6, variance 12
Mean 12, variance 6
questions.explanation: Each $Z^2$ has mean 1 and variance $E(Z^4) - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2$. Six independent terms: mean 6, variance 12. (Mean 5 would be the df for a 6-category goodness-of-fit test, not for $\chi^2_6$.)

questions.stem: The 0.05 critical value of the chi-square distribution with 1 df is 3.841, which is the square of ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\chi^2_1$ is the distribution of $Z^2$, so $P(\chi^2_1 \ge c) = P(|Z| \ge \sqrt{c})$. The two-sided 0.05 critical value of $Z$ is 1.96, and $1.96^2 = 3.8416$.

questions.stem: A claim says 25% of trips are late. In a random sample of 400 trips, 115 are late. What is the two-category goodness-of-fit statistic $\chi^2$?
In any goodness-of-fit test, why do the misses $O - E$ always add to zero?
choices: Because positive and negative misses are equally likely
Because $H_0$ is assumed true
Because each miss is divided by its expected count
Because the observed counts and the expected counts both add to $n$
questions.explanation: $\sum O = n$ and $\sum E = \sum np_i = n$, so $\sum (O - E) = 0$ for every data set, whether or not $H_0$ is true. That constraint is the reason one degree of freedom is lost.

questions.stem: A goodness-of-fit test has 8 categories, and $H_0$ is true. What is the expected value of the statistic $\chi^2$?
choices: 7, but only approximately for large $n$
7, exactly, for any sample size
8, exactly
0, since $H_0$ is true
questions.explanation: Each term has expected value $\text{Var}(O_i)/(np_i) = np_i(1 - p_i)/(np_i) = 1 - p_i$, so $E(\chi^2) = \sum (1 - p_i) = 8 - 1 = 7$. The calculation uses only the binomial variance, so it is exact for every $n$. Even when $H_0$ is true, chance misses make $\chi^2$ positive.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The degrees of freedom of a goodness-of-fit test grow with the sample size
Under $H_0$, the goodness-of-fit statistic averages exactly $k - 1$
For two categories, the goodness-of-fit $\chi^2$ equals the square of the one-proportion z statistic
A chi-square variable with 1 df is the square of a standard normal variable
For a 3 × 3 table, $\chi^2$ equals the square of a two-proportion z statistic
questions.explanation: df depends on the number of categories (and estimated parameters), never on $n$. $E(\chi^2) = k - 1$ exactly; two categories give $\chi^2 = z^2$ exactly; and $\chi^2_1 = Z^2$ by definition. The $\chi^2 = z^2$ link holds for 2 × 2 tables, not larger ones.

questions.stem: Counts of defects per box are tested against a binomial model with $p$ estimated from the data. After combining sparse values, 5 categories remain. How many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: df $= k - 1 - m = 5 - 1 - 1 = 3$: one df for the total and one for the estimated $p$. 4 forgets the estimated parameter; 2 subtracts it twice.

questions.stem: A normal model, with its mean and standard deviation estimated from the data, is tested by a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with 8 categories. The test has ___ degrees of freedom. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Two parameters are estimated, so df $= 8 - 1 - 2 = 5$. (As the lesson notes, if the mean and SD come from the raw data rather than the grouped counts, the true distribution lies between $\chi^2_5$ and $\chi^2_7$.)

questions.stem: Match each chi-square test to its degrees of freedom.
left: Goodness of fit, 6 categories, all proportions stated in $H_0$
Goodness of fit, 6 categories, binomial $p$ estimated from the data
Test of independence on a 3 × 4 table
Test of homogeneity on a 2 × 2 table
questions.explanation: $6 - 1 = 5$; $6 - 1 - 1 = 4$; $(3 - 1)(4 - 1) = 6$; $(2 - 1)(2 - 1) = 1$. 11 is $rc - 1$ for the 3 × 4 table, Pearson's original count before Fisher's correction.

questions.stem: Which argument explains why a test of independence on an $r \times c$ table has $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ degrees of freedom?
choices: There are $rc$ cells, and the largest row and column are dropped
Each row loses one df and each column loses one df, so $rc - r - c$
Start from $rc - 1$ free cells and subtract the $r - 1$ row proportions and $c - 1$ column proportions estimated from the margins
The statistic is a sum of $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ squared z statistics computed from the table's rows
questions.explanation: The rule df $= k - 1 - m$ with $k = rc$ cells and $m = (r - 1) + (c - 1)$ estimated parameters gives $rc - 1 - (r - 1) - (c - 1) = (r - 1)(c - 1)$. $rc - r - c$ is off by one, because it forgets that the total was already counted.

questions.stem: In the bulb-box example, the binomial model fit badly: there were more boxes with 0 defects and more with 3 or 4 than the model predicts. What is the most reasonable explanation?
choices: The sample of boxes was too large
Defective bulbs cluster in boxes, so bulbs in a box do not fail independently
The estimate of $p$ was too high
The expected counts were too small for any conclusion
questions.explanation: The binomial model needs independent bulbs with a common $p$. Too many empty boxes and too many bad ones is the signature of clustering, as when a box's bulbs share a bad batch. Large samples make the test more sensitive, not wrong, and the sparse categories were combined so every expected count was at least 5.

questions.stem: Put the steps of testing whether counts follow a binomial model with unknown $p$ in order.
choices: Estimate $p$ from the total count of successes
Compute the expected count for each value from the binomial model
Combine values whose expected counts are below 5
Add $(O - E)^2/E$ over the remaining categories
Use df = categories − 2 to find the p-value
questions.explanation: The expected counts need $\hat{p}$; which values to combine depends on the expected counts; the statistic is computed on the combined categories; and the df subtracts 1 for the total and 1 for the estimated $p$.

questions.stem: In the bulb-box example, suppose the supplier had claimed $p = 0.2$ and the test used the same 3 categories. How many degrees of freedom would the test have?
questions.explanation: A value stated in $H_0$ is not estimated from the data, so only the total costs a df: $3 - 1 = 2$. With $p$ estimated, the lesson used $3 - 1 - 1 = 1$.

questions.stem: In the transit survey, the 30–50 / Car cell has $O = 40$ and $E = 34$, with row total 80, column total 85 and $n = 200$. What is its adjusted residual?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{40 - 34}{\sqrt{34(1 - 0.40)(1 - 0.425)}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{11.73}} = \dfrac{6}{3.425} = 1.75$. 1.03 is the standardized residual $6/\sqrt{34}$, 1.06 is the cell's contribution $36/34$, and 6 is the raw miss.

questions.stem: For a cell with $O \ne E$, why is the adjusted residual always larger in size than the standardized residual $(O - E)/\sqrt{E}$?
choices: Because adjusted residuals use observed counts in the denominator
Because adjusted residuals are squared
Because standardized residuals have variance less than 1 under $H_0$, so the adjustment divides by a smaller number
Because adjusted residuals include a continuity correction
questions.explanation: With the margins fixed, cells can't vary as freely as independent counts, so $(O - E)/\sqrt{E}$ has variance below 1. Multiplying $E$ by $(1 - \text{row}/n)(1 - \text{col}/n) < 1$ shrinks the denominator and puts the residual on the standard normal scale.

questions.stem: The transit survey's adjusted residuals are: Under 30 / Train 2.91, Under 30 / Bus 2.40, Under 30 / Car −4.84, 30–50 / Car 1.75, Over 50 / Train −1.94, Over 50 / Car 2.97. Using the ±2 guideline, which cells depart from independence? Select all that apply.
choices: Under 30 / Train
Under 30 / Bus
Under 30 / Car
Over 50 / Train
Over 50 / Car
questions.explanation: Cells beyond ±2: 2.91, 2.40, −4.84 and 2.97. 1.75 and −1.94 are inside the band. With nine cells, values just past 2 deserve some caution: under a stricter ±3 cutoff only −4.84 would remain (2.97 narrowly misses).

questions.stem: A 3 × 4 table from $n = 500$ people gives $\chi^2 = 36$. What is Cramér's V?
questions.explanation: $\min(r - 1, c - 1) = \min(2, 3) = 2$, so $V = \sqrt{36/(500 \times 2)} = \sqrt{0.036} = 0.190$. 0.268 forgets the factor 2; 0.155 uses 3 instead of 2; 0.036 forgets the square root.

questions.stem: A 2 × 2 table with $n = 320$ gives $\chi^2 = 12.8$. The phi coefficient is $\phi =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\phi = \sqrt{\chi^2/n} = \sqrt{12.8/320} = \sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$, a small-to-moderate association by Cohen's rough conventions, even though $p \approx 0.0003$.

questions.stem: Every count in a two-way table is multiplied by 4 (same percentages, four times the people). What happens to $\chi^2$ and to Cramér's V?
choices: $\chi^2$ is multiplied by 4; V stays the same
Both stay the same
$\chi^2$ is multiplied by 16; V is multiplied by 4
$\chi^2$ is multiplied by 4; V is multiplied by 2
questions.explanation: Every $(O - E)^2$ grows by 16 and every $E$ by 4, so each contribution, and $\chi^2$, grows by 4. $V = \sqrt{\chi^2/(n \min(r-1, c-1))}$ has $n$ growing by 4 as well, so it is unchanged: more evidence, same strength.

questions.stem: A survey of 20,000 riders finds satisfaction of 51% on line A and 49% on line B, with $p = 0.005$ and $\phi = 0.02$. Which summary is best?
choices: The lines differ hugely in satisfaction
There is no real difference, since $\phi$ is small
The p-value is wrong because the sample is too large
There is convincing evidence of a difference, but the difference is very small
questions.explanation: The p-value says the 2-point difference is unlikely to be chance (evidence), and $\phi = 0.02$ says it is tiny (strength). Both are correct at once; whether 2 points matters is a practical judgment, not a statistical one.

questions.stem: In a tea-tasting test with 6 cups, 3 milk-first and 3 tea-first, the taster must pick the 3 milk-first cups. If she is only guessing, what is the probability that she gets all 3 right?
questions.explanation: There are $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ equally likely ways to choose 3 cups, and one is all correct: $1/20 = 0.05$. Even a perfect score would only just reach significance at $\alpha = 0.05$, which is why Fisher used 8 cups ($1/70 = 0.0143$). 0.125 is $(1/2)^3$, which wrongly treats the cups as independent guesses.

questions.stem: When is Fisher's exact test the right choice instead of the chi-square test?
choices: For a 2 × 2 table in which some expected count is below 5
For any table with more than 1,000 observations
For a goodness-of-fit test with many categories
Whenever the chi-square p-value is above 0.05
questions.explanation: Fisher's test computes the exact (hypergeometric) probabilities of 2 × 2 tables with the observed margins, so it needs no large-counts condition. Large samples are exactly where the chi-square approximation works well, and switching tests because of the p-value is never legitimate.

questions.stem: Match each tool to the question it answers.
choices: Is there convincing evidence of an association?
Which cells depart from independence?
How strong is the association?
What is the exact p-value for a small 2 by 2 table?
Does one variable cause the other?
questions.explanation: The p-value measures evidence, adjusted residuals locate it, and V measures strength on a 0-to-1 scale; Fisher's test replaces the chi-square p-value when counts are small. None of them settles causation, which depends on how the data were produced.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Fisher's exact test (one-sided) in order.
choices: Treat the row and column totals as fixed
Identify the tables (top-left counts) at least as extreme as the observed one in the direction of $H_a$
Compute the hypergeometric probability of each of those tables
Add those probabilities to get the p-value
Compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and conclude
questions.explanation: The possible tables, and so which ones are at least as extreme, are only defined once the margins are fixed; the probabilities are computed for exactly those tables, then added to give the p-value, and the conclusion comes last.

questions.stem: For the brake-pad table (1 of 10 new pads and 6 of 10 old pads failed), the chi-square test gives $p = 0.019$ and Fisher's two-sided test gives $p = 0.057$. Which p-value should be reported, and why?
choices: 0.019, because chi-square tests are more powerful
The average, 0.038
0.057, because the expected counts (3.5) are below 5, so the chi-square approximation is not valid
0.019, because Fisher's test only works for one-sided alternatives
questions.explanation: Expected failures are $10 \times 7/20 = 3.5$ in each row, so the chi-square curve can't be trusted; here it gives a p-value far too small. Fisher's test has a two-sided version (0.057) and a one-sided one (0.0286, used in the lesson for $H_a$: the new design fails less often).

questions.stem: A 2 × 2 table has row totals 5 and 5, and 4 of the 10 units failed. With the margins fixed and no association, the probability that none of the first row's 5 units failed is ___. Give the answer to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: $P(a = 0) = \dfrac{\binom{5}{0}\binom{5}{4}}{\binom{10}{4}} = \dfrac{1 \times 5}{210} = 0.0238$: all 4 failures must come from the second row.

questions.stem: A planner wants an interval for the average wear of all rail segments that carry 30 million tons per year. Which interval fits?
choices: A prediction interval at $x^* = 30$
A confidence interval for the slope
A confidence interval for the mean response at $x^* = 30$
A one-sample t interval for the mean wear
questions.explanation: "The average of all segments at 30" is the mean response $\mu_y$ at $x^* = 30$. A prediction interval is for one segment, the slope interval is about the change per million tons, and a one-sample t interval ignores tonnage altogether.

questions.stem: A regression on $n = 10$ points has $\bar{x} = 50$, $s_x = 10$ and $s = 4$. What is $SE_{\hat{\mu}}$, the standard error of the mean response, at $x^* = 65$?
questions.explanation: $(n - 1)s_x^2 = 9 \times 100 = 900$, so $SE_{\hat{\mu}} = 4\sqrt{1/10 + 15^2/900} = 4\sqrt{0.35} = 2.37$. 2.28 uses $n s_x^2 = 1000$; 2.00 drops the $1/n$ term; 4.65 is the prediction standard error $4\sqrt{1.35}$.

questions.stem: At some $x^*$, a regression has residual SD $s = 4$ and $SE_{\hat{\mu}} = 3$. The standard error for predicting one new $y$ there is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $SE_{\text{pred}} = \sqrt{s^2 + SE_{\hat{\mu}}^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$. Adding the two (7) is the classic slip: variances add, not standard deviations.

questions.stem: Which changes make a 95% confidence interval for the mean response narrower? Select all that apply.
choices: A larger sample size $n$
Choosing $x^*$ closer to $\bar{x}$
A larger residual SD $s$
More widely spread $x$ values (larger $s_x$)
A 99% confidence level instead
questions.explanation: $SE_{\hat{\mu}} = s\sqrt{1/n + (x^* - \bar{x})^2/((n - 1)s_x^2)}$ shrinks with larger $n$, smaller $|x^* - \bar{x}|$ and larger $s_x$ (a larger $n$ also lowers $t^*$). A larger $s$ and a higher confidence level both widen it.

questions.stem: As the sample size grows without limit (conditions holding), what happens to a 95% prediction interval at a fixed $x^*$?
choices: Its width shrinks toward 0
Its width approaches about $2 \times 1.96\sigma$, never less
Its width grows without limit
It becomes the same as the confidence interval for the slope
questions.explanation: $SE_{\hat{\mu}} \to 0$, but $SE_{\text{pred}} = \sqrt{s^2 + SE_{\hat{\mu}}^2} \to \sigma$ and $t^* \to 1.96$, so the interval approaches $\hat{y} \pm 1.96\sigma$. A new individual's own scatter never averages away.

questions.stem: Where along the $x$-axis are the confidence and prediction bands narrowest?
choices: At the smallest $x$ in the data
At $x = 0$
At the largest $x$ in the data
At $\bar{x}$, the mean of the $x$ values
questions.explanation: Both standard errors contain $(x^* - \bar{x})^2$, which is 0 at $x^* = \bar{x}$ and grows in both directions. At $\bar{x}$ only the height of the line is uncertain; farther out, error in the slope adds to it.

questions.stem: A railway regresses fuel use on train weight. Match each question to the procedure that answers it.
left: Mean fuel use of all 800-ton trains
Extra mean fuel use for each additional ton
Is there any linear relationship at all?
choices: Confidence interval for the mean response
Prediction interval
Confidence interval for the slope
t test for the slope
Chi-square test of independence
questions.explanation: An average over all trains of one weight is the mean response; one particular train needs a prediction interval; "per additional ton" is the slope; and "any relationship" is the test of $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$. A chi-square test is for categorical variables.

questions.stem: A random sample of 14 pairs has $r = 0.5$. What is the t statistic for $H_0: \rho = 0$?
questions.explanation: $t = r\sqrt{n - 2}/\sqrt{1 - r^2} = 0.5\sqrt{12}/\sqrt{0.75} = 1.732/0.866 = 2.00$, with 12 df. 1.73 forgets to divide by $\sqrt{1 - r^2}$; 2.16 uses $\sqrt{n}$ instead of $\sqrt{n - 2}$; 2.31 divides by $1 - r^2$ without the square root.

questions.stem: For a sample of $n = 27$ pairs with $r = 0.6$, the t statistic for testing $\rho = 0$ is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $t = 0.6\sqrt{25}/\sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 3/0.8 = 3.75$, with 25 df. This is the same $t$ that $b/SE_b$ would give for the slope.

questions.stem: Why does the Normal condition matter more for a prediction interval than for a confidence interval for the slope?
choices: Because a prediction interval is about one new error $\varepsilon$, which the Central Limit Theorem does not make normal
Because prediction intervals use $z^*$ instead of $t^*$
Because the slope is never affected by skewness
Because prediction intervals use df $= n - 1$
questions.explanation: Estimates such as $b$ and $\hat{\mu}$ are averages of many errors, so they are close to normal for large $n$ even when the errors aren't. A single new $y$ carries one error with whatever shape the error distribution has, so skewed residuals make a prediction interval wrong at any $n$.

questions.stem: In the lesson's rail example, the 95% prediction interval at 30 million tons is 8.18 to 12.82 mm. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: 95% of all segments carrying 30 million tons have mean wear in this range
We are 95% confident that the slope is between 8.18 and 12.82
We are 95% confident that one new segment carrying 30 million tons will have wear between 8.18 and 12.82 mm
The mean wear at 30 million tons is exactly 10.5 mm
questions.explanation: A prediction interval is about a single new value. The mean-response interval (9.34 to 11.66 mm) is the one about the average of all such segments; 10.5 is only the estimate of that mean, and the slope is about 0.30 mm per million tons.

questions.stem: In the lesson's rail example ($\bar{x} = 20$), put these 95% intervals in order from narrowest to widest.
choices: Mean response at $x^* = 20$
Mean response at $x^* = 30$
One new segment at $x^* = 20$
One new segment at $x^* = 30$
questions.explanation: Half-widths: 0.58, 1.16, 2.09 and 2.32 mm. Mean-response intervals are narrower than prediction intervals, and each kind widens as $x^*$ moves away from $\bar{x}$.

cards.back: $n$ values drawn with replacement from the $n$ data values. Some repeat, some are left out.
SD of the statistic over thousands of bootstrap samples. Estimates the statistic's SE.
$\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\cdot s/\sqrt{n}$: slightly below the usual $s/\sqrt{n}$.
2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the bootstrap distribution. Rough, and often too narrow, for small $n$.
Without replacement every resample is the data reordered, so the statistic never varies.

cards.front: Chance a value is left out of a bootstrap resample
