Find the mean and the sample standard deviation of the number of defects (3 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$n = \sum f = {nn}$ and $\sum fx = {sx}$, so $\bar{x} = {sx}/{nn} =$ **{mn:dp3}**.
$\sum f(x - \bar{x})^2 = {ss:num4}$, so $s^2 = {ss:num4}/({nn} - 1)$ and $s =$ **{sd:dp3}**.

drills.title: Median of grouped data by interpolation

calc.lb: if(half <= k1, 0, if(half <= k2, wid, if(half <= k3, 2*wid, if(half <= k4, 3*wid, 4*wid))))
calc.below: if(half <= k1, 0, if(half <= k2, k1, if(half <= k3, k2, if(half <= k4, k3, k4))))
calc.inbin: if(half <= k1, c1, if(half <= k2, c2, if(half <= k3, c3, if(half <= k4, c4, c5))))

drills.prompt:
Waiting times (minutes), grouped into bins:

| Minutes | 0–<{b1} | {b1}–<{b2} | {b2}–<{b3} | {b3}–<{b4} | {b4}–<{b5} |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count | {c1} | {c2} | {c3} | {c4} | {c5} |

Estimate the median by linear interpolation (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$n = {nn}$, so the median is at position $n/2 = {half}$. The cumulative counts are {k1}, {k2},
{k3}, {k4}, {nn}, so position {half} falls in the bin starting at $L = {lb}$, which holds
$f = {inbin}$ values with $F = {below}$ values below it. Median
$\approx {lb} + \dfrac{{half} - {below}}{{inbin}} \times {wid} =$ **{med:dp2}** minutes.

drills.title: Combine two groups' means and SDs
drills.prompt:
Section A: $n = {na}$, mean {ma}, standard deviation {sa}. Section B: $n = {nb}$, mean {mb},
standard deviation {sb}. Find the mean and the sample standard deviation of all {nt} scores
combined (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Mean: $\dfrac{{na}({ma}) + {nb}({mb})}{{nt}} =$ **{mc:dp2}**. Within groups:
$({na} - 1)({sa})^2 + ({nb} - 1)({sb})^2 = {within}$. Between groups:
${na}({ma} - {mc:num4})^2 + {nb}({mb} - {mc:num4})^2 = {between:num4}$.
$s^2 = \dfrac{{within} + {between:num4}}{{nt} - 1} = {vc:num4}$, so $s =$ **{sc:dp2}**.

drills.title: Plotting position and expected z-score
drills.prompt:
A normal probability plot uses plotting positions $(i - 0.5)/n$. For the value in
position {i} (counting from the smallest) of a sample of {n} values, find the plotting
position (4 decimal places) and the expected z-score (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Plotting position: $p = \dfrac{{i} - 0.5}{{n}} =$ **{pp:dp4}**. Expected z-score: the
z with that area to its left, $z = \Phi^{-1}({pp:dp4}) \approx$ **{zz:dp2}**. (Positions
below 0.5 give negative z-scores.)

drills.title: Mean and SD from a normal probability plot
drills.prompt:
A normal probability plot (data value up, expected z-score across) is close to a
straight line through the points $({za}, {xa})$ and $({zb}, {xb})$. Estimate the mean
and the standard deviation of the data.
drills.solution:
Normal data follow $x \approx \mu + \sigma z$, so the slope estimates the SD and the
value at $z = 0$ estimates the mean. Slope:
$\dfrac{{xb} - ({xa})}{{zb} - ({za})} =$ **{slope}**. At $z = 0$:
${xa} - ({slope})({za}) =$ **{icpt}**.

drills.title: Fraction out of specification
drills.prompt:
Part lengths are normal with mean {mu} mm and standard deviation {sd} mm. The
specification is {lsl} to {usl} mm. What proportion of parts are out of specification?
Give 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Lower limit: $z = \dfrac{{lsl} - {mu}}{{sd}} = {zl:num2}$, and $\Phi({zl:num2}) = {pl:num4}$.
Upper limit: $z = \dfrac{{usl} - {mu}}{{sd}} = {zu:num2}$, and $1 - \Phi({zu:num2}) = {pu:num4}$.
Both tails count: ${pl:num4} + {pu:num4} =$ **{pout:dp4}**.

drills.title: Capability indices Cp and Cpk
drills.prompt:
A specification is {lsl} to {usl}. The process mean is {mu} and its standard deviation
is {sd}. Find $C_p$ and $C_{pk}$ (2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$C_p = \dfrac{\text{USL} - \text{LSL}}{6\sigma} = \dfrac{{usl} - {lsl}}{6({sd})} \approx$ **{cp:dp2}**.
Distances to the limits: ${usl} - {mu} = {du}$ and ${mu} - {lsl} = {dl}$. Use the nearer one:
$C_{pk} = \dfrac{\min({du}, {dl})}{3({sd})} \approx$ **{cpk:dp2}**.

drills.title: Largest SD for a target Cpk
drills.prompt:
A specification is {lsl} to {usl}, and the process mean is {mu}. What is the largest
standard deviation that gives $C_{pk}$ of at least {ck}? Give 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
The nearer limit is $\min({usl} - {mu}, {mu} - {lsl}) = {dn}$ away. Since
$C_{pk} = \dfrac{{dn}}{3\sigma} \ge {ck}$, we need $\sigma \le \dfrac{{dn}}{3({ck})} \approx$ **{smax:dp3}**.

drills.title: Split SST into SSR and SSE
drills.prompt:
For the points $({x1}, {y1}),\ ({x2}, {y2}),\ ({x3}, {y3}),\ ({x4}, {y4}),\ ({x5}, {y5})$,
split the total sum of squares $\text{SST} = \sum (y - \bar{y})^2$ into the regression sum of
squares SSR and the residual sum of squares SSE of the least-squares line. Keep full precision
(don't round the slope or SSR) until the end, then give SSR and SSE to 2 decimal places and
$r^2$ to 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
$\bar{x} = {mx:num4}$, $\bar{y} = {my:num4}$, $S_{xy} = {sxy:num4}$, $S_{xx} = {sxx:num4}$, and
$\text{SST} = S_{yy} = {sst:num4}$. The slope is $b = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = {bb:num4}$, so
$\text{SSR} = b^2 S_{xx} = S_{xy}^2/S_{xx} =$ **{ssr:dp2}**. Then
$\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSR} =$ **{sse:dp2}**, and
$r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST} =$ **{r2:dp3}**.

drills.title: SSE and s from summary statistics
drills.prompt:
A least-squares regression on $n = {nn}$ points has $s_y = {sy}$ and $r = {rr}$. Find the
residual sum of squares SSE (1 decimal place) and the standard deviation of the residuals $s$
(2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$\text{SST} = (n - 1)s_y^2 = {df1} \times {sy}^2 = {sst:dp0}$. Since $\text{SSE} = \text{SST}(1 - r^2)$,
$\text{SSE} = {sst:dp0}(1 - ({rr})^2) =$ **{sse:dp1}**. Then
$s = \sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n - 2)} = \sqrt{{sse:sig8}/{dfr}} =$ **{sres:dp2}**.

drills.title: Predict a retest score
drills.prompt:
A test and a retest both have mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}, and scores on the two
have correlation $r = {rr}$. A student scored {xs} on the first test. Use the least-squares
line to predict the student's retest score, and find how many points closer to the mean the
prediction is than the first score. Give both to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
The first score is $z = ({xs} - {mu})/{sd} = {zx:num4}$. The line predicts
$\hat{z} = r z = {rr} \times ({zx:num4}) = {zy:num4}$, so the predicted retest is
${mu} + ({zy:num4})({sd}) =$ **{pred:dp1}**. (With equal SDs this is just
${mu} + {rr}({xs} - {mu})$.) The first score was {ad} points from the mean; the prediction is
${rr} \times {ad} = {pd:num4}$ points from it, which is ${ad} - {pd:num4} =$ **{closer:dp1}** points closer.

drills.title: The two regression slopes
drills.prompt:
Two variables have $r = {rr}$, $s_x = {sx}$ and $s_y = {sy}$. Find the slope of the
least-squares line for predicting $y$ from $x$, and the slope of the line for predicting $x$
from $y$ (3 decimal places each).
drills.solution:
Predicting $y$ from $x$: $b = r\,s_y/s_x = {rr} \times {sy}/{sx} =$ **{byx:dp3}**.
Predicting $x$ from $y$: $b = r\,s_x/s_y = {rr} \times {sx}/{sy} =$ **{bxy:dp3}**.
Check: the product is ${prod:num4} = r^2$. The second slope is not the reciprocal of the
first.

drills.title: Relative risk and odds ratio
drills.prompt:
A cohort study records whether people were exposed to a risk factor and whether they later
developed a condition.

| | Condition | No condition |
|---|---|---|
| Exposed | {aa} | {bb} |
| Not exposed | {cc} | {dd} |

Find the relative risk (exposed ÷ not exposed) and the odds ratio, each to 2 decimal places.
Keep full precision (don't round the risks) until the end.
drills.solution:
Risks: exposed ${aa}/{n1} \approx {p1:num4}$, not exposed ${cc}/{n2} \approx {p2:num4}$. Relative
risk $= \dfrac{{aa}/{n1}}{{cc}/{n2}} =$ **{rrisk:dp2}** (dividing the unrounded risks). Odds ratio
$= \dfrac{ad}{bc} = \dfrac{{aa} \times {dd}}{{bb} \times {cc}} = \dfrac{{adp:dp0}}{{bcp:dp0}} =$ **{orr:dp2}**.

drills.title: Crude and standardized rates
drills.prompt:
A hospital treated {n1} mild cases, of whom {s1} survived, and {n2} severe cases, of whom {s2}
survived. Find (a) its overall (crude) survival rate and (b) its standardized survival rate for
a standard population that is {ww}% mild and {w2}% severe. Give both as percents to 1 decimal
place.
drills.solution:
(a) Crude: $\dfrac{{s1} + {s2}}{{n1} + {n2}} = \dfrac{{st:dp0}}{{nt:dp0}} =$ **{crude:dp1}%**.
(b) Stratum rates: mild ${s1}/{n1} = {p1}\%$, severe ${s2}/{n2} = {p2}\%$. Weight them by the
standard mix and add: ${ww}\% \times {p1}\% + {w2}\% \times {p2}\% =$ **{adj:dp1}%**. The crude rate
uses the hospital's own mix ({n1} mild to {n2} severe), so it changes with the case mix; the
standardized rate doesn't.

drills.title: Weighted estimate from a stratified sample
drills.prompt:
A survey splits a population into two strata. Stratum A has {biga} people, and a simple random
sample of {na} of them includes {xa} who say yes. Stratum B has {bigb} people, and a simple random
sample of {nb} of them includes {xb} who say yes. Find the sampling weight of each respondent in
stratum A, and estimate the proportion of the whole population who would say yes (as a decimal,
to 3 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Weight in A: $N_A/n_A = {biga:dp0}/{na} =$ **{wa}** (each respondent stands for {wa} people).
Stratum results: $\hat{p}_A = {xa}/{na} = {pa:num4}$ and $\hat{p}_B = {xb}/{nb} = {pb:num4}$.
Population shares: A is {biga} of {biga} + {bigb}, about {sa:num4}; B about {sb:num4}.
Estimate: ${sa:num4}({pa:num4}) + {sb:num4}({pb:num4}) \approx$ **{est:dp3}**.
(The unweighted proportion, {unw:dp3}, would treat both strata as if they were sampled at the same rate.)

drills.title: Neyman allocation
drills.prompt:
A factory wants the mean daily output of its machines. Stratum 1 has {big1} older machines whose
daily output has standard deviation about {s1} units; stratum 2 has {big2} newer machines with
standard deviation about {s2} units. Using Neyman allocation, how should a sample of {nn} machines
be split between the strata?
drills.solution:
Neyman allocation: $n_h = n \cdot \dfrac{N_h S_h}{\sum N_k S_k}$.
$N_1 S_1 = {big1}({s1}) = {p1:dp0}$ and $N_2 S_2 = {big2}({s2}) = {p2:dp0}$.
Stratum 1: ${nn} \times {p1:dp0}/({p1:dp0} + {p2:dp0}) =$ **{n1}**. Stratum 2: ${nn} - {n1} =$ **{n2}**.

drills.title: Design effect of a cluster sample
drills.solution:
$\text{deff} \approx 1 + (m - 1)\rho = 1 + ({mm} - 1)({rho}) =$ **{dfx:dp2}**.
Effective sample size: $n/\text{deff} = {nn:dp0}/{dfx:dp2} \approx$ **{neff:int}**.

drills.title: Main effects and interaction in a 2 × 2 experiment
drills.prompt:
A $2 \times 2$ greenhouse experiment crosses fertilizer (none or added) with watering (light or
heavy). Mean yields in grams per plant: no fertilizer, light watering {m11}; no fertilizer, heavy
watering {m12}; fertilizer, light watering {m21}; fertilizer, heavy watering {m22}. Find the main
effect of adding fertilizer, the main effect of heavy watering, and the interaction measured as
(effect of fertilizer with heavy watering) minus (effect of fertilizer with light watering).
Give signed values.
drills.solution:
Fertilizer: average with it $({m21} + {m22})/2$ minus average without it $({m11} + {m12})/2$, which is **{mainf}**.
Heavy watering: $({m12} + {m22})/2 - ({m11} + {m21})/2 =$ **{maini}**.
Simple effects of fertilizer: heavy watering ${m22} - {m12} = {effhi}$; light watering ${m21} - {m11} = {efflo}$.
Interaction: ${effhi} - ({efflo}) =$ **{inter}**. (Zero would mean parallel lines on an interaction plot.)

drills.title: Standardized rates
drills.prompt:
Two clinics report recovery rates by severity. Clinic A: {ra1}% of mild cases and {ra2}% of severe
cases recover. Clinic B: {rb1}% of mild cases and {rb2}% of severe cases recover. Using a standard
population that is {ww}% mild and {w2}% severe, find each clinic's standardized recovery rate, in
percent to 1 decimal place.
drills.solution:
Apply each clinic's rates to the same mix of patients.
Clinic A: $({ww} \times {ra1} + {w2} \times {ra2})/100 =$ **{sta:dp1}%**.
Clinic B: $({ww} \times {rb1} + {w2} \times {rb2})/100 =$ **{stb:dp1}%**.
Because both use the same severity mix, the difference no longer reflects which clinic sees more severe cases.

drills.title: Comparing rates per 10,000
drills.prompt:
During an epidemic, households supplied by water company A had {da} deaths among {housa} houses,
and households supplied by company B had {db} deaths among {housb} houses. Find each company's death
rate per 10,000 houses (to 1 decimal place) and how many times larger A's rate is than B's (to 2
decimal places).
drills.solution:
Rate A: ${da}/{housa:dp0} \times 10{,}000 =$ **{ratea:dp1}**. Rate B: ${db}/{housb:dp0} \times 10{,}000 =$ **{rateb:dp1}**.
Ratio: $\dfrac{{da}/{housa:dp0}}{{db}/{housb:dp0}} \approx$ **{ratio:dp2}**. Rates per house, not raw death counts, make
the companies comparable when they supply different numbers of houses.

drills.title: Two draws without replacement
drills.prompt:
A bin holds {rr} red and {bb} blue tokens. Two tokens are drawn at random **without
replacement**. Find the probability that both are red, and the probability that exactly one
is red. Give each to 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Multiplication rule: $P(\text{both red}) = \dfrac{{rr}}{{nn}} \cdot \dfrac{{rm1}}{{nm1}} =$ **{pboth:num4}**.
Exactly one red happens as red then blue or blue then red, two paths with the same product:
$2 \cdot \dfrac{{rr}}{{nn}} \cdot \dfrac{{bb}}{{nm1}} =$ **{pone:num4}**.

drills.title: Probability of the condition after a negative test
drills.prompt:
A condition has prevalence {prev}. A test has sensitivity {sens} and specificity {spec}. A
randomly chosen person tests **negative**. What is the probability that they have the condition
anyway? Give 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
False negatives: ${prev} \times {miss:num2} = {fn:sig4}$. True negatives: ${healthy:num2} \times {spec} = {tn:sig4}$.
$P(-) = {pneg:sig4}$, so $P(D \mid -) = \dfrac{{fn:sig4}}{{pneg:sig4}} =$ **{post:sig3}**.
A negative result lowers the probability below the prior of {prev}.

drills.title: Inclusion–exclusion with three events
where: ra + rb + rc + rab + rac + rbc + rabc <= tot - 20

calc.uni: na + nb + nc - nab - nac - nbc + rabc

drills.prompt:
A survey of {tot} households asked which of three streaming services they pay for. {na} pay for
service A, {nb} for B and {nc} for C; {nab} pay for both A and B, {nac} for both A and C, {nbc}
for both B and C, and {rabc} pay for all three. How many households pay for at least one of the
services, and how many pay for none?
drills.solution:
Add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple:
${na} + {nb} + {nc} - {nab} - {nac} - {nbc} + {rabc} =$ **{uni}**. None: ${tot} - {uni} =$ **{none}**.

drills.title: The birthday problem
drills.prompt:
Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore February 29) and independent people. In a group of
{nn} people, find (a) the probability that at least two share a birthday and (b) the probability
that at least one of the other {oth} people shares **your** birthday. Give 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
(a) $P(\text{all different}) = \dfrac{365}{365} \cdot \dfrac{364}{365} \cdots \dfrac{365 - {oth}}{365} = {pall:num4}$, so
$P(\text{shared}) = 1 - {pall:num4} =$ **{pany:num4}**.
(b) Each other person misses your birthday with probability $\tfrac{364}{365}$:
$1 - (364/365)^{{oth}} =$ **{pme:num4}**. Part (a) is much larger because the group has {pairs:int} pairs, and only
{oth} of them include you.

drills.title: The matching problem
drills.prompt:
At a party, {nn} guests leave their coats, and the coats are handed back completely at random.
In how many of the {tot:int} possible ways of returning the coats does **nobody** get their own coat,
and what is the probability of that? Give the probability to 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
By inclusion–exclusion, $P(\text{no match}) = \dfrac{1}{0!} - \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} - \cdots \pm \dfrac{1}{{nn}!} =$ **{pno:num4}**.
The number of such arrangements is $P(\text{no match}) \times {tot:int} =$ **{nder}** (a shortcut: $n!/e$ rounded to the
nearest whole number). So the chance at least one guest gets their own coat is {pat:num4}, close to $1 - 1/e \approx 0.632$.

drills.title: Converting between probability and odds
drills.prompt:
(a) An event has probability {pp}. What are its odds (in favor)? Give 3 significant figures.
(b) Another event has odds of {aa} to {bb} in favor. What is its probability? Give 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
(a) Odds $= \dfrac{p}{1 - p} = \dfrac{{pp}}{{qq:num2}} =$ **{od:sig3}**.
(b) Odds of {aa} to {bb} mean {aa} occurrences for every {bb} non-occurrences, so
$p = \dfrac{{aa}}{{aa} + {bb}} = \dfrac{{aa}}{{sm}} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Bayes with odds and a likelihood ratio
drills.prompt:
A test has sensitivity {sens} and specificity {spec}. It is used where the prevalence is
{prev:num4}. Find the likelihood ratio of a positive result, $\text{LR}_+$, to 2 decimal places, and
the probability that a person who tests positive has the condition, to 4 decimal places (carry the
unrounded likelihood ratio into this step).
drills.solution:
$\text{LR}_+ = \dfrac{\text{sensitivity}}{1 - \text{specificity}} = \dfrac{{sens}}{{fpr:num2}} =$ **{lr:num2}**.
Prior odds $= {prev:num4}/(1 - {prev:num4}) = {po:sig4}$. Posterior odds $= {po:sig4} \times {lr:sig4} = {pso:sig4}$.
Probability $= \dfrac{{pso:sig4}}{1 + {pso:sig4}} =$ **{post:num4}**.

drills.title: Several independent positive results
drills.prompt:
A condition has prior probability {prev}. Each positive result of a test has likelihood ratio
{lr}, and the results are conditionally independent. A person tests positive {kk} times. Find the
posterior odds (3 significant figures) and the posterior probability (4 decimal places).
drills.solution:
Prior odds $= {prev}/(1 - {prev}) = {po:sig4}$. Each positive multiplies the odds by {lr}, so
{kk} positives multiply them by ${lr}^{{kk}} = {mult:int}$: posterior odds $= {po:sig4} \times {mult:int} =$ **{pso:sig3}**.
Probability $= \dfrac{{pso:sig4}}{1 + {pso:sig4}} =$ **{post:num4}**.

drills.title: Coupon collector expected wait
drills.prompt:
Each box of a snack contains one of {n} different stickers, each equally likely and independent
from box to box. What is the expected number of boxes you must buy to collect all {n} stickers?
Give 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Split the wait into stages. With $k$ stickers already collected, a box is new with probability
$({n} - k)/{n}$, so that stage is geometric with mean ${n}/({n} - k)$. Adding the stage means
(linearity), the expected total is
${n}\left(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac1{{n}}\right) = {n} \times {H:num4} =$ **{E:num2}** boxes.
The last sticker alone takes {last} boxes on average.

drills.title: Expected number of matching pairs
drills.prompt:
Each of {n} people independently picks a whole number from 1 to {d}, all equally likely. What
is the expected number of pairs of people who pick the same number? Give 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Give each of the $\binom{{n}}{2} = {pairs}$ pairs an indicator that equals 1 if the two pick the
same number. For one pair, the second person matches the first with probability $1/{d}$. By
linearity of expectation (no independence needed), the expected number of matching pairs is
${pairs}/{d} =$ **{E:num2}**.

drills.title: Expected number of empty categories
drills.prompt:
A dispatcher assigns {b} repair jobs to {k} crews. Each job goes to a crew chosen at random, all
crews equally likely, independently of the other jobs. What is the expected number of crews that
get no jobs at all? Give 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Give each crew an indicator that equals 1 if it gets no jobs. A crew misses one job with
probability $\tfrac{{k} - 1}{{k}}$, and all {b} jobs with probability
$\left(\tfrac{{k} - 1}{{k}}\right)^{{b}} = {q:num4}$. Adding over the {k} crews:
${k} \times {q:num4} =$ **{E:num2}** crews.

drills.title: Covariance and correlation from a joint table
drills.prompt:
$X$ and $Y$ each take the values 0 and 1, with joint probabilities

| | $Y = 0$ | $Y = 1$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X = 0$ | {p00} | {p01} |
| $X = 1$ | {p10} | {p11} |

Find $\text{Cov}(X, Y)$ (4 decimal places) and the correlation $\rho$ (3 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$\mu_X = P(X = 1) = {p10} + {p11} = {mx:num2}$ and $\mu_Y = P(Y = 1) = {p01} + {p11} = {my:num2}$.
Only the cell $X = Y = 1$ contributes to $E(XY)$, so $E(XY) = {p11}$.
$\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E(XY) - \mu_X\mu_Y = {p11} - ({mx:num2})({my:num2}) =$ **{cov:num4}**.
A 0/1 variable has variance $p(1-p)$, so $\sigma_X = {sx:num4}$ and $\sigma_Y = {sy:num4}$, and
$\rho = \text{Cov}/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y) =$ **{rho:dp3}**.

drills.title: SD of a weighted sum with correlation
drills.prompt:
Investment A has a return SD of {sa} percentage points and investment B an SD of {sb}, with
correlation $\rho = {rho}$ between their returns. You put a fraction {w} of your money in A and
the rest in B, so your return is $R = {w}A + {v:num1}B$. Find the SD of $R$ in percentage points
(2 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$\text{Var}(R) = a^2\sigma_A^2 + b^2\sigma_B^2 + 2ab\rho\,\sigma_A\sigma_B$ with $a = {w}$, $b = {v:num1}$:
${va:num4} + {vb:num4} + ({cv:num4}) = {var:num4}$, so $\sigma_R = \sqrt{{var:num4}} =$ **{sd:num2}**.

drills.title: Sampling without replacement (finite population correction)
drills.prompt:
A lot of {N} items contains {K} defectives. An inspector draws {n} items at random **without
replacement**; $X$ is the number of defectives drawn. Find the SD of $X$, and the SD a binomial
model would (wrongly) give. Use 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
$p = {K}/{N} = {p:num4}$. Binomial variance: $np(1-p) = {vb:num4}$, so the binomial SD is
**{sdb:dp3}**. Without replacement, multiply the variance by the finite population correction
$\tfrac{N - n}{N - 1} = \tfrac{{N} - {n}}{{N} - 1} = {f:num4}$: $\text{Var}(X) = {vb:num4} \times {f:num4}$,
so $\sigma_X =$ **{sdh:dp3}**.

drills.title: Plus four interval for a proportion
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} train departures finds {xx} that left late. Construct a plus four
confidence interval at level {lev} for the proportion of all departures that leave late.
Give the endpoints to 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
Add two successes and two failures: $\tilde{p} = \dfrac{{xx} + 2}{{nn} + 4} = {pt:num4}$.
$SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{\tilde{p}(1 - \tilde{p})}{{nt}}} \approx {se:num4}$, and $ME = {lev:num4}({se:num4}) \approx {me:num4}$.
Interval: ${pt:num4} \pm {me:num4}$, from **{lo:dp3}** to **{hi:dp3}**. (The point estimate is still
$\hat{p} = {ph:num4}$; only the interval is centered at $\tilde{p}$.)

drills.title: Wilson score interval
drills.prompt:
In a random sample of {nn} rail bearings, {xx} show wear beyond the limit. Find the 95% Wilson
score interval for the proportion of all bearings with excess wear (use $z^* = 1.96$). Give
the endpoints to 3 decimal places.
drills.solution:
$\hat{p} = {xx}/{nn} = {ph:num4}$ and $z^{*2}/n = 3.8416/{nn} \approx {kz:num4}$.
Center: $\dfrac{\hat{p} + z^{*2}/(2n)}{1 + z^{*2}/n} \approx {cen:num4}$.
Half-width: $\dfrac{1.96}{1 + z^{*2}/n}\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \dfrac{z^{*2}}{4n^2}} = \dfrac{1.96}{1 + {kz:num4}}\sqrt{{vv:dp6} + {kk:dp6}} \approx {hw:num4}$.
Interval: from **{lo:dp3}** to **{hi:dp3}** (a lower endpoint of 0 occurs when $\hat{p} = 0$).

drills.title: Upper bound after zero successes (rule of three)
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} signal relays is tested and none fails. Find the exact one-sided 95%
upper bound $1 - 0.05^{1/n}$ for the failure rate, and the rule-of-three approximation. Give
both to 4 decimal places.
drills.solution:
The largest $p$ with $(1 - p)^{{nn}} \ge 0.05$ is $1 - 0.05^{1/{nn}} = 1 - {root:dp4} =$ **{exact:dp4}**.
The rule of three gives $3/{nn} =$ **{three:dp4}**, a close approximation because
$(1 - p)^n \approx e^{-np}$ and $e^{-3} \approx 0.05$.

drills.title: True coverage of a z interval that uses s
drills.prompt:
An analyst with $n = {nn}$ observations from a normal population reports
$\bar{x} \pm z^* s/\sqrt{n}$ as a {lev} confidence interval. Find its true coverage,
$2\,\text{tcdf}(z^*, n - 1) - 1$ (3 decimal places), and the t critical value that should have been
used (3 decimal places).
drills.solution:
With $s$ in place of $\sigma$, the standardized statistic has a t distribution with
df $= {dfree}$. $\text{tcdf}({lev:num4}, {dfree}) \approx {cdf:num4}$, so the true coverage is
$2({cdf:num4}) - 1 \approx$ **{cover:dp3}**, not {nominal:dp3}. The correct multiplier leaves the
same middle area at df = {dfree}: $t^* = \text{invT}({area:num4}, {dfree}) \approx$ **{ts:dp3}**.

drills.title: Prediction interval for one new observation
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} loading times from a normal population has $\bar{x} = {xbar}$ min and
$s = {sx}$ min. Find a 95% prediction interval for the loading time of one new train.
Give the endpoints to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
df $= {dfree}$, $t^* \approx {ts:dp3}$, and $\sqrt{1 + 1/{nn}} \approx {fac:num4}$.
Margin $= t^* s\sqrt{1 + 1/n} = {ts:dp3}({sx})({fac:num4}) \approx {me:num4}$.
Interval: ${xbar} \pm {me:num4}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}** min. (The confidence interval for
the mean would have margin only {cme:num4}.)

drills.title: Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
drills.prompt:
Two independent samples: $n_1 = {n1}$, $s_1 = {s1}$ and $n_2 = {n2}$, $s_2 = {s2}$. Find the
Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (2 decimal places) and the conservative df,
$\min(n_1, n_2) - 1$.
drills.solution:
$a = s_1^2/n_1 = {va:num4}$ and $b = s_2^2/n_2 = {vb:num4}$.
df $= \dfrac{(a + b)^2}{a^2/(n_1 - 1) + b^2/(n_2 - 1)} \approx$ **{dfw:num2}**.
Conservative df $=$ **{dmin}**. Welch's value always lies between {dmin} and $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = {dmax}$.

drills.title: Sample size for a one-sided z test of a mean
drills.prompt:
A one-sided z test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ at $\alpha = {al}$ should have power {pw} to detect a true
mean {del} units above $\mu_0$. The standard deviation of individual measurements is $\sigma = {sig}$.
What is the smallest sample size that does this? Use $z$ values to 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
$z_\alpha = {za:dp3}$ and $z_\beta = {zb:dp3}$. Then
$n = \left(\dfrac{({za:dp3} + {zb:dp3})({sig})}{{del}}\right)^2 \approx {nraw:num2}$. Always round up: $n =$ **{nn:int}**.

drills.title: Power of a one-proportion z test
drills.prompt:
A one-proportion z test of $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_a: p < {p0}$ uses $n = {nn}$ and
$\alpha = 0.05$. Find the cutoff for $\hat{p}$ (reject when $\hat{p}$ is at or below it; 4 decimals),
and the power of the test if the true proportion is {p1:num2} (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
Under $H_0$: $SE = \sqrt{{p0}(1 - {p0})/{nn}} \approx {se0:num4}$, so reject when
$\hat{p} \le {p0} - 1.645({se0:num4}) \approx$ **{cut:num4}**. If $p = {p1:num2}$, the SD of $\hat{p}$ is
$\sqrt{{p1:num2}(1 - {p1:num2})/{nn}} \approx {se1:num4}$, and the power is
$P\!\left(Z \le \dfrac{{cut:num4} - {p1:num2}}{{se1:num4}}\right) = P(Z \le {zz:num2}) \approx$ **{pw:dp3}**.

drills.title: Sample size per group for comparing two means
drills.prompt:
Two independent groups of equal size will be compared with a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$.
The common standard deviation is about $\sigma = {sig}$, and the study should have power {pw} to
detect a difference in means of {del}. How many subjects are needed in each group? Use $z$ values
to 3 decimals.
drills.solution:
Two-sided, so use $z_{\alpha/2} = {za:dp3}$; for power {pw}, $z_\beta = {zb:dp3}$.
$n = 2\left(\dfrac{({za:dp3} + {zb:dp3})({sig})}{{del}}\right)^2 \approx {nraw:num2}$, rounded up to
**{nn:int}** per group ({tot:int} subjects in all).

drills.title: Two one-sided tests (TOST) for paired data
drills.prompt:
Two measuring methods are compared on {nn} items. The differences have $\bar{d} = {dbar}$ and
$s_d = {sd}$ (no strong skew or outliers). The equivalence margin is $\Delta = {del}$. Find the two TOST
statistics $t_1 = (\bar{d} + \Delta)/SE$ and $t_2 = (\bar{d} - \Delta)/SE$ (3 decimals) and the TOST
p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$SE = {sd}/\sqrt{{nn}} \approx {se:num4}$, df $= {dfree}$.
$t_1 = ({dbar} + {del})/{se:num4} \approx$ **{t1:dp3}**, upper-tail p-value $\approx {p1:num4}$.
$t_2 = ({dbar} - {del})/{se:num4} \approx$ **{t2:dp3}**, lower-tail p-value $\approx {p2:num4}$.
The TOST p-value is the larger: **{pt:num4}**. Equivalence is shown at level $\alpha$ only if this is at most $\alpha$.

drills.title: Equivalence from a 90% confidence interval
drills.prompt:
A paired study of {nn} items gives mean difference $\bar{d} = {dbar}$ and $s_d = {sd}$. Find the 90%
confidence interval for $\mu_d$ (3 decimals each). Then find the equivalence margin $\Delta$
at which a TOST at $\alpha = 0.05$ has p-value exactly 0.05, so that any larger margin shows equivalence (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$SE = {sd}/\sqrt{{nn}} \approx {se:num4}$, and for 90% with df $= {dfree}$, $t^* \approx {ts:dp3}$.
Interval: ${dbar} \pm {ts:dp3}({se:num4}) =$ (**{lo:dp3}**, **{hi:dp3}**). TOST at 0.05 succeeds exactly
when this 90% interval lies inside $(-\Delta, \Delta)$, so the boundary is the larger endpoint size:
**{mg:dp3}**. At that margin one of the one-sided tests has p-value exactly 0.05; any larger margin puts the interval strictly inside and gives equivalence.

drills.title: Non-inferiority test for two proportions
drills.prompt:
In a randomized trial, {x1} of {n1} patients on a new treatment were cured, compared with {x2} of
{n2} on the standard treatment. Test non-inferiority with margin $\Delta = {del}$:
$H_0: p_{\text{new}} - p_{\text{std}} \le -{del}$ against $H_a: p_{\text{new}} - p_{\text{std}} > -{del}$, using the
unpooled standard error. Find $z$ (2 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat{p}_{\text{new}} = {p1:num4}$, $\hat{p}_{\text{std}} = {p2:num4}$, difference $= {diff:num4}$.
$SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{{p1:num4}(1 - {p1:num4})}{{n1}} + \dfrac{{p2:num4}(1 - {p2:num4})}{{n2}}} \approx {se:num4}$.
$z = \dfrac{{diff:num4} + {del}}{{se:num4}} \approx$ **{zz:num2}**; p-value $= P(Z \ge z) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Exact binomial test (one-sided)
drills.prompt:
Under $H_0: p = {p0}$, a process produces successes independently. In {nn} trials there were {xx}
successes. Find the exact binomial p-value for $H_a: p > {p0}$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Under $H_0$, $X \sim B({nn}, {p0})$ with mean {mu:num2}. The p-value is
$P(X \ge {xx}) = 1 - P(X \le {xm}) = 1 - \text{binomcdf}({nn}, {p0}, {xm}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Sign test for paired data
drills.prompt:
In a paired study with {tot} pairs, {npos} differences (after − before) are positive, {nneg} are
negative and {nzero} are exactly 0. Use the sign test of $H_0$: the median difference is 0, against
$H_a$: the median difference is positive. How many differences does the test use, and what is the
p-value (4 decimals)?
drills.solution:
Drop the zero differences (there are {nzero}): $n = {npos} + {nneg} =$ **{nn:int}**. Under $H_0$ the number of
positive signs is $B({nn:int}, 0.5)$, so the p-value is $P(X \ge {npos}) = 1 - \text{binomcdf}({nn:int}, 0.5, {nm:int}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Two-sided exact binomial p-value by doubling
drills.prompt:
Test $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_a: p \ne {p0}$ with an exact binomial test. In {nn} independent trials there
were {xx} successes. Find the two-sided p-value using the doubling convention: twice the smaller of
$P(X \ge {xx})$ and $P(X \le {xx})$, capped at 1 (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Under $H_0$, $X \sim B({nn}, {p0})$ with mean {mu:num2}. Upper tail: $P(X \ge {xx}) = 1 - \text{binomcdf}({nn}, {p0}, {xm}) \approx {up:num4}$.
Lower tail: $P(X \le {xx}) = \text{binomcdf}({nn}, {p0}, {xx}) \approx {dn:num4}$. Double the smaller: p-value $\approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Two-category chi-square equals z squared
drills.solution:
Expected counts: {e1} defective and {e2} not. The observed counts miss them by {u} and by its
opposite, so
$\chi^2 = \dfrac{({u})^2}{{e1}} + \dfrac{({u})^2}{{e2}} =$ **{chi:dp3}**.
For z: $\hat{p} = {o1}/{nn} = {ph:num4}$, $SE = \sqrt{{p0}(1 - {p0})/{nn}} = {se:num4}$, so
$z = ({ph:num4} - {p0})/{se:num4} =$ **{zz:num2}**. Check: $z^2 \approx {chi:dp3}$, and both tests give the
two-sided p-value {pv:num4}.

drills.title: Degrees of freedom with estimated parameters

choices.label: a distribution whose proportions are all stated in $H_0$
a binomial model, with $p$ estimated from the data
a normal model, with the mean and SD estimated from the data

drills.prompt:
A chi-square goodness-of-fit test checks the fit of {mm}. After combining sparse categories,
the test uses {kk} categories and gives $\chi^2 = {chi}$. Find the degrees of freedom and the
p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
df $=$ categories $- 1 -$ parameters estimated $= {kk} - 1 - {mval} =$ **{dfree}**. p-value
$= P(\chi^2_{{dfree}} \ge {chi}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Adjusted residual for a cell
drills.prompt:
A random sample of passengers is classified by ticket type and by line:

| | Single | Return | Pass | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Line A | {aa} | {ab} | {ac} | {r1} |
| Line B | {ba} | {bb} | {bc} | {r2} |
| Total | {c1} | {c2} | {c3} | {tot} |

Find the adjusted residual for the cell Line A, Single (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
Expected count: $E = {r1} \times {c1}/{tot} = {ee:num4}$. Then
$\dfrac{O - E}{\sqrt{E(1 - {r1}/{tot})(1 - {c1}/{tot})}} = \dfrac{{aa} - {ee:num4}}{\sqrt{{ee:num4}(1 - {r1}/{tot})(1 - {c1}/{tot})}} =$ **{adj:num2}**.
(The standardized residual $(O - E)/\sqrt{E}$ is only {std:num2}.)

drills.title: Chi-square and Cramér's V

calc.chi: (aa - eaa)^2/eaa + (ab - eab)^2/eab + (ac - eac)^2/eac + (ba - eba)^2/eba + (bb - ebb)^2/ebb + (bc - ebc)^2/ebc

where: min(eaa, eab, eac, eba, ebb, ebc) >= 5
drills.prompt:
A random sample of commuters is classified by shift and by how they get to work:

| | Train | Bus | Car |
|---|---|---|---|
| Day shift | {aa} | {ab} | {ac} |
| Night shift | {ba} | {bb} | {bc} |

Find $\chi^2$ for a test of independence (2 decimals) and Cramér's V (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
Totals: rows {r1}, {r2}; columns {c1}, {c2}, {c3}; grand {tot}. Expected counts: {eaa:num2},
{eab:num2}, {eac:num2} (day) and {eba:num2}, {ebb:num2}, {ebc:num2} (night).
$\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E =$ **{chi:num2}**. The table is 2 × 3, so $\min(r - 1, c - 1) = 1$ and
$V = \sqrt{{chi:num2}/{tot}} =$ **{vv:dp3}**.

drills.title: Fisher's exact test (one-sided)

funcs.h(j): nCr(n1, j)*nCr(n2, kk - j)/nCr(n1 + n2, kk)

drills.prompt:
A new part is fitted to {n1} randomly chosen machines and the old part to {n2} others. Failures:

| | Failed | Did not fail | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| New | {a} | {b} | {n1} |
| Old | {c} | {d} | {n2} |
| Total | {kk} | {nk} | {tot} |

Some expected counts are below 5, so use Fisher's exact test of $H_a$: the new part fails less
often. Find the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
With the margins fixed, the number of new-part failures $A$ is hypergeometric:
$P(A = j) = \dfrac{\binom{{n1}}{j}\binom{{n2}}{{kk} - j}}{\binom{{tot}}{{kk}}}$.
Tables at least as extreme as the observed one have $A \le {a}$. $P(A = 0) = {p0:num4}$,
$P(A = 1) = {p1:num4}$, $P(A = 2) = {p2:num4}$; add those with $j \le {a}$: p-value $=$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Confidence interval for a mean response
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ points gives $\hat{y} = {aa} + {bb}x$, with $\bar{x} = {xbar}$,
$s_x = {sx}$ and residual SD $s = {sres}$. Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean response at
$x^* = {xs}$ (endpoints to 2 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat{y} = {aa} + {bb}({xs}) = {yh:num4}$. $SE_{\hat{\mu}} = {sres}\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{{nn}} + \dfrac{({xs} - {xbar})^2}{{nm1}({sx})^2}} = {sem:num4}$.
df $= {dfree}$, $t^* = {ts:dp3}$. Interval: ${yh:num4} \pm {ts:dp3}({sem:num4})$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Prediction interval for one new value
drills.prompt:
A regression on $n = {nn}$ points gives $\hat{y} = {aa} + {bb}x$, with $\bar{x} = {xbar}$,
$s_x = {sx}$ and residual SD $s = {sres}$. Find a 95% prediction interval for one new observation
at $x^* = {xs}$ (endpoints to 2 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat{y} = {aa} + {bb}({xs}) = {yh:num4}$. $SE_{\text{pred}} = {sres}\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{{nn}} + \dfrac{({xs} - {xbar})^2}{{nm1}({sx})^2}} = {sep:num4}$.
df $= {dfree}$, $t^* = {ts:dp3}$. Interval: ${yh:num4} \pm {ts:dp3}({sep:num4})$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: t test for a correlation
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} pairs has correlation $r = {r}$. Test $H_0: \rho = 0$ against
$H_a: \rho \ne 0$. Find $t$ (3 decimals, with its sign) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$t = \dfrac{r\sqrt{n - 2}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}} = \dfrac{{r}\sqrt{{dfree}}}{\sqrt{1 - ({r})^2}} =$ **{tt:dp3}**, df $= {dfree}$.
Two-sided p-value $= 2P(t_{{dfree}} \ge |{tt:dp3}|) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.
